charlotte-harbor.s: Charlotte Harbor is a large estuary on the Gulf coast of south-western Florida, fed by the Peace and Myakka rivers. Its rich fisheries supported the Calusa, whose shell-mound towns lined its shores and islands, such as Pineland.

charlottetown-conference.s: The Charlottetown Conference was a meeting of delegates from the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, held at Charlottetown in September 1864. Called to discuss a union of the Maritime colonies, it was turned by the Canadian delegates into…

canar-province.s: Cañar is a province in the southern highlands of Ecuador, north of Azuay, with its capital at Azogues. It takes its name from the Cañari people, who lived there before the Inca conquest, and many of its inhabitants still identify as Cañari and speak Kichwa.

cuenca-ecuador.s: Cuenca is the third-largest city of Ecuador and capital of Azuay province, in the southern highlands. It stands on the site of the Cañari centre of Guapondelig and the Inca city of Tomebamba, and was founded as a Spanish city in 1557.

cuenca-spain.s: Cuenca is a city in Castilla–La Mancha, central Spain, capital of the province of the same name, built on a rocky ridge between the gorges of the Júcar and Huécar rivers. Taken from the Muslims by Alfonso VIII of Castile in 1177, it became a bishopric with one of Spain's…

cantabria.s: Cantabria is an autonomous community and historic region of northern Spain, on the Bay of Biscay between Asturias and the Basque Country, with its capital at Santander. Its name comes from the Cantabri, the Iron Age people whom Rome subdued in the Cantabrian Wars of 29–19 BCE.

canterbury.s: Canterbury is a cathedral city in Kent, south-east England. As Durovernum Cantiacorum it was the chief town of the Cantiaci under Rome, and it became the capital of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Kent, where Augustine founded in 597 the see whose archbishop heads the English Church.

cassivellaunus.s: Cassivellaunus was a British war leader who led the resistance to Julius Caesar's second invasion of Britain in 54 BCE. Ruling north of the Thames, he harassed the Romans with chariot warfare, but after the Trinovantes and other peoples went over to Caesar and his stronghold…

cunobelinus.s: Cunobelinus was a king of the Catuvellauni who ruled much of south-eastern Britain from about 9 to 40 CE from his capital at Camulodunum, modern Colchester. He issued many gold coins with an ear of grain, and Suetonius calls him king of the Britons.

chen-jiongming.s: Chen Jiongming was a Chinese military leader and governor of Guangdong. He brought Sun Yat-sen back to Guangzhou in 1920 and backed his government, but he favoured a federal China and opposed Sun's plans for a northern campaign.

cape-province.s: The Cape Province was the largest of the four provinces of the Union, and later Republic, of South Africa, formed from the Cape Colony in 1910, with its capital at Cape Town. It kept a limited non-racial franchise longer than the other provinces, until apartheid laws removed it.

concepcion-chile.s: Concepción is a city in south-central Chile near the mouth of the Biobío river, founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1550. As the main Spanish base on the frontier of the Arauco War it housed the colony's army.

ciudad-vieja.s: Ciudad Vieja is a town in the Almolonga valley of Guatemala, the site of the second Spanish capital, Santiago de los Caballeros, founded there in 1527. On the night of 10–11 September 1541 a flood of water and mud from the Volcán de Agua destroyed the city, killing the…

cuiaba.s: Cuiabá is the capital of the Brazilian state of Mato Grosso, near the geographical centre of South America. It was founded in 1719 after bandeirantes from São Paulo found gold in the area, and miners reached it by long river convoys.

caete.s: The Caeté were a Tupi-speaking people of the north-eastern coast of Brazil, between Pernambuco and the São Francisco river. They resisted the first Portuguese settlers of Pernambuco.

caral.s: Caral is an archaeological site in the Supe valley of Peru, about 23 km from the coast, and the largest centre of the Norte Chico or Caral-Supe civilisation. Its platform mounds, sunken circular plazas and houses date from about 2600 BCE, making it one of the oldest cities in…

cayambi.s: The Cayambi, or Kayambi, are an indigenous people of the northern Ecuadorian highlands around the Cayambe volcano. Allied with the Caranqui, they resisted the Inca conquest for years in the late 15th century before Huayna Capac defeated them at Lake Yahuarcocha.

cochasqui.s: Cochasquí is an archaeological site in Pichincha province, northern Ecuador, with fifteen truncated earthen pyramids, some with long ramps, and many burial mounds. It was built by the Caranqui and related peoples from around 950 until the Inca conquest.

constantius-i.s: Constantius I, known as Chlorus, was a Roman emperor of the Tetrarchy, made Caesar in the west under Maximian in 293 and senior emperor in 305. He took Boulogne from the usurper Carausius in 293 and recovered Britain from Allectus in 296.

carlism.s: Carlism is a Spanish traditionalist and legitimist political movement that arose in 1833 in support of Infante Carlos María Isidro's claim to the throne against his niece Isabella II. Strong in Navarre, the Basque Country and Catalonia, it defended Catholicism and regional…

chartres.s: Chartres is a city on the River Eure in northern France, the Gallo-Roman Autricum, chief town of the Carnutes. It later became a seat of the counts of Blois and a centre of learning in the 11th and 12th centuries.

carpathian-sich.s: The Carpathian Sich was a Ukrainian paramilitary force formed in Carpatho-Ukraine in November 1938, during its autonomy within Czechoslovakia. It drew local youths and volunteers from Galicia and clashed with Czechoslovak troops in March 1939.

ciudad-real.s: Ciudad Real is a city in Castile-La Mancha, central Spain, and the capital of the province of the same name. King Alfonso X founded it in 1255 as Villa Real to strengthen royal power in La Mancha against the military orders, and it became a city in 1420.

complutum.s: Complutum was a Roman city in central Hispania, on the site of modern Alcalá de Henares near Madrid, which grew from a settlement of the Carpetani. It flourished in the imperial period, with a forum and rich houses with mosaics.

carpathian-mountains.s: The Carpathian Mountains form an arc about 1,500 km long across central and eastern Europe, from Slovakia through Poland, Ukraine and Romania to the Iron Gates on the Danube. They enclose the Pannonian Basin, which the Hungarians entered across their passes in 895.

carlisle.s: Carlisle is a city in Cumbria, north-west England, near the Scottish border, on the site of the Roman town of Luguvalium close to Hadrian's Wall. It was the centre of the civitas of the Carvetii and later a stronghold disputed between England and Scotland, with a castle and a…

cumbria.s: Cumbria is a county of north-west England, bordering Scotland, created in 1974 mainly from Cumberland and Westmorland. It includes the Lake District and the western end of Hadrian's Wall.

chalons-en-champagne.s: Châlons-en-Champagne, formerly Châlons-sur-Marne, is a city on the Marne in north-eastern France and the prefecture of the Marne department. As Durocatalaunum it was the town of the Catalauni and a late Roman bishopric.

catania.s: Catania is a city on the east coast of Sicily at the foot of Mount Etna, founded as the Greek colony of Catana in 729 BCE and known to the Romans as Catina. It has repeatedly been damaged by Etna and earthquakes; after the eruption of 1669 and the earthquake of 1693 it was…

charondas.s: Charondas was a lawgiver of the Greek city of Catana in Sicily, probably in the 6th century BCE. His laws, known for their detailed provisions on family, property and contracts, were adopted by other Chalcidian colonies in Sicily and southern Italy, including Rhegion.

caratacus.s: Caratacus was a British chieftain, son of Cunobelinus of the Catuvellauni, who led resistance to the Roman invasion of 43 CE. After the fall of his homeland he continued the war among the Silures and Ordovices of Wales, until he was defeated around 50.

chechnya.s: Chechnya is a republic of the Russian Federation in the North Caucasus, with its capital at Grozny. Its people fought Russian conquest in the 19th-century Caucasian War, many under Imam Shamil, were deported en masse to Central Asia in 1944, and fought two wars against Russia…

county-wicklow.s: County Wicklow is a county on the east coast of Ireland, south of Dublin, known for the Wicklow Mountains and the early monastic site of Glendalough. Its mountains long sheltered Gaelic clans such as the O'Byrnes and O'Tooles, who resisted English rule from Dublin.

cavaillon.s: Cavaillon is a town on the Durance in Provence, southern France, the Cabellio of the Cavares and a Roman colony, where a small Roman arch survives. It belonged to the papal Comtat Venaissin until 1791 and was one of the four towns where the 'Pope's Jews' were allowed to live;…

cimbri.s: The Cimbri were an ancient people, probably from northern Jutland, whose migration with the Teutones and others shook the Roman Republic from 113 BCE. They defeated Roman armies at Noreia and at Arausio in 105 BCE, one of Rome's worst defeats, and wandered through Gaul and…

cap-vert.s: Cap-Vert is the peninsula on the coast of Senegal that forms the westernmost point of mainland Africa. Named Cabo Verde by Portuguese navigators in 1444, it shelters the island of Gorée and is occupied today by the city of Dakar.

cayuga-lake.s: Cayuga Lake is the longest of the Finger Lakes of central New York, about 61 km long, with the city of Ithaca at its southern end. It lay at the heart of the homeland of the Cayuga, one of the five original nations of the Iroquois Confederacy, who lived in villages along its…

chronicle-of-chicxulub.s: The Chronicle of Chicxulub is an account of the Spanish conquest of Yucatán written in the Yucatec Maya language by Nakuk Pech, a noble of the Ceh Pech province, in the mid-16th century. It records the arrival of the Spaniards and presents the Pech lords as early allies of…

cerdanya.s: Cerdanya is a high Pyrenean valley of the upper Segre, divided between Catalonia in Spain and the French department of Pyrénées-Orientales. It takes its name from the ancient Cerretani, became a Carolingian county and later passed to the counts of Barcelona.

calafell.s: Calafell is a coastal town in the Baix Penedès, in the province of Tarragona, Catalonia. It contains Alorda Park, a fortified settlement of the Iberian Cessetani occupied from about the 5th to the 2nd century BCE, which has been excavated and partly reconstructed as an…

camp-de-tarragona.s: The Camp de Tarragona is a coastal plain and historic region of southern Catalonia around the cities of Tarragona and Reus, enclosed by the Prades mountains and other coastal ranges. In antiquity it was the land of the Iberian Cessetani and the hinterland of Roman Tarraco.

council-of-chalcedon.s: The Council of Chalcedon was the fourth ecumenical council of the Christian Church, held in 451 at Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from Constantinople, under Emperor Marcian. It defined Christ as one person in two natures, divine and human, and raised the see of Constantinople…

chalcidice.s: Chalcidice is a peninsula of northern Greece in Central Macedonia, ending in three prongs: Kassandra, Sithonia and Mount Athos. It took its name from the many colonies founded there by Chalcis and other Greek cities from the 8th century BCE, which later formed the Chalcidian…

chimalpahin.s: Chimalpahin, in full Domingo Francisco de San Antón Muñón Chimalpahin Quauhtlehuanitzin, was a Nahua historian born in 1579 at Amaquemecan (Amecameca) in Chalco. Working in Mexico City, he wrote annals and histories in Nahuatl covering the peoples of Chalco and central Mexico…

chandrapur.s: Chandrapur, historically Chanda, is a city in eastern Maharashtra, India, near the confluence of the Wardha and Erai rivers. It was the capital of the Gond kingdom of Chanda from the 15th or 16th century, and its stone walls and the Mahakali temple date from that period.

chittagong.s: Chittagong, officially Chattogram, is the main port and second-largest city of Bangladesh, on the Karnaphuli river near the Bay of Bengal. A trading port since ancient times, it was contested by Bengal, Tripura and Arakan, held by the Arakanese kingdom of Mrauk U in the 16th…

chenani-nashri-tunnel.s: The Chenani-Nashri Tunnel is a road tunnel of about 9.2 kilometres on the Jammu–Srinagar highway in Jammu and Kashmir, India, running beneath the Patnitop range between Chenani in Udhampur district and Nashri in Ramban district. Opened in April 2017, it was then India's…

cen-peng.s: Cen Peng was a general of Emperor Guangwu of the Eastern Han dynasty, counted among the Twenty-Eight Generals of Yuntai. In 35 CE he broke through the Chengjia defences on the Yangtze with a fleet and advanced deep into Sichuan, but was assassinated in his camp by an agent…

cheraman-perumal-nayanar.s: Cheraman Perumal Nayanar was a Chera king of Kerala and one of the 63 Nayanars, the Tamil Shaiva poet-saints, probably active in the early 9th century. A close friend of the saint Sundarar, he is credited with Shaiva hymns preserved in the eleventh book of the Tirumurai.

cherokee-phoenix.s: The Cherokee Phoenix was the first newspaper published by a Native American nation in the United States, printed at New Echota, Georgia, from 1828 in English and in Cherokee using Sequoyah's syllabary. Edited first by Elias Boudinot, it carried laws, news and arguments against…

chickamauga-cherokee.s: The Chickamauga Cherokee were a band of Cherokee who, under the war leader Dragging Canoe, refused to accept land cessions to colonists and moved in 1777 to the Chickamauga Creek area near modern Chattanooga, Tennessee. Allied with the British and later supplied by Spain, they…

chhota-udaipur.s: Chhota Udaipur is a town in eastern Gujarat, India, and the headquarters of Chhota Udaipur district, created in 2013. It was the capital of the princely state of Chhota Udaipur, founded by Khichi Chauhan Rajputs who fled Champaner after its capture by Mahmud Begada in 1484.

chorotega.s: The Chorotega are an Indigenous people of the Pacific coast of Central America, living at the Spanish conquest in what are now western Nicaragua and the Nicoya peninsula of Costa Rica. Speakers of an Oto-Manguean language related to languages of southern Mexico, they are…

cajamarca.s: Cajamarca is a city in the northern highlands of Peru, capital of the Cajamarca region. An Inca administrative centre with baths and temples, it was where Francisco Pizarro and his small Spanish force ambushed the Inca emperor Atahualpa on 16 November 1532, capturing him and…

communist-international.s: The Communist International, or Comintern, was the organisation of the world's communist parties founded in Moscow in March 1919 under the leadership of Lenin and the Russian Bolsheviks. It worked for world revolution and directed member parties in line with Soviet policy,…

chang-jun.s: Chang Jun was a Chinese official sent by Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty in 607 as envoy to Chi Tu, the "Red Earth" kingdom of South-East Asia. He sailed from Guangzhou with Wang Junzheng, and his report, preserved in the Book of Sui, describes Chi Tu's court, its Buddhist and…

chosokabe-motochika.s: Chōsokabe Motochika (1539–1599) was a daimyo of Tosa province on the Japanese island of Shikoku. Succeeding his father Kunichika in 1560, he unified Tosa by 1575 and by 1585 controlled most of Shikoku, relying on part-time farmer-soldiers called ichiryō gusoku.

chosokabe-morichika.s: Chōsokabe Morichika (1575–1615) was the last Chōsokabe lord of Tosa, a son of Motochika. He joined the western army at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, and after its defeat lost his domain, which passed to Yamauchi Kazutoyo.

chosokabe-nobuchika.s: Chōsokabe Nobuchika (1565–1587) was the eldest son and heir of Chōsokabe Motochika. Sent with his father to support Toyotomi Hideyoshi's invasion of Kyushu against the Shimazu, he was killed at the Battle of Hetsugigawa in the winter of 1586–87.

carrigafoyle-castle.s: Carrigafoyle Castle is a tower house on the Shannon estuary near Ballylongford in north County Kerry, Ireland, built in the late 15th century by the O'Connor Kerry. It guarded the approaches to the Shannon, and during the Second Desmond Rebellion in 1580 it was besieged and…

clonfert.s: Clonfert is a village in east County Galway, Ireland, where St Brendan the Navigator founded a monastery around 557. The monastery became a major centre of learning and the seat of a medieval bishopric.

county-kerry.s: County Kerry is a county in the south-west of Ireland, in the province of Munster, with its county town at Tralee. Its name comes from the Ciarraige, the "people of Ciar", who held the north of the county in the early Middle Ages.

circassians.s: The Circassians, who call themselves Adyghe, are a people of the North-West Caucasus speaking Northwest Caucasian languages. Organised in princely and more egalitarian tribal societies, they resisted the Russian Empire in the Russo-Circassian War until 1864, when most were…

consulta-of-lyon.s: The Consulta of Lyon was an assembly of some 450 delegates of the Cisalpine Republic convened by Napoleon Bonaparte at Lyon from December 1801 to January 1802. It adopted a new constitution, transformed the Cisalpine into the Italian Republic and elected Napoleon its…

carlos-frederico-lecor.s: Carlos Frederico Lecor (1764–1836) was a Portuguese general who commanded the invasion of the Banda Oriental, modern Uruguay, in 1816 against José Artigas. He entered Montevideo in January 1817 and governed the territory, annexed in 1821 as the Cisplatine Province, with the…

chutia-people.s: The Chutia are an ethnic group of Assam in north-eastern India, of Bodo-Kachari origin. Their medieval kingdom, centred on Sadiya in the upper Brahmaputra valley, flourished from about the 13th century until the Ahom king Suhungmung annexed it in 1523–24.

camden-south-carolina.s: Camden is a town in Kershaw County, South Carolina, on the Wateree River, and one of the oldest inland towns in the state, settled in the 1730s. During the American Revolutionary War the British defeated an American army under Horatio Gates near the town in August 1780.

catawba-people.s: The Catawba are a Native American people of the Carolina piedmont, living along the Catawba River on the border of North and South Carolina. Speakers of a Siouan language, they absorbed remnants of neighbouring peoples, including those of the former chiefdom of Cofitachequi,…

chocho-people.s: The Chocho, who call themselves Ngiwa, are an Indigenous people of the Mixteca Alta in north-western Oaxaca, Mexico, centred on the Coixtlahuaca valley. Their language belongs to the Popolocan branch of the Oto-Manguean family and is closely related to Popoloca.

collasuyu.s: Collasuyu, in Quechua Qullasuyu, was the southern and largest of the four quarters (suyus) of the Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu. Named after the Colla people of the Lake Titicaca basin, it stretched from south of Cuzco across the Altiplano of present-day Bolivia into northern…

comas-district.s: Comas is a district of northern Lima, Peru, in the lower Chillón valley. Before the Spanish conquest the area belonged to the coastal lordship of Collique, whose fortified centre, the Fortaleza de Collique, survives in the district.

cariboo.s: The Cariboo is a region of the interior plateau of British Columbia, Canada, between the Coast and Cariboo mountains. Gold was discovered on its creeks in the early 1860s, and the Cariboo Gold Rush made Barkerville its booming centre and led to the building of the Cariboo…

cariboo-wagon-road.s: The Cariboo Wagon Road was a road built between 1860 and 1865 by the colony of British Columbia from the lower Fraser valley through the Fraser Canyon to the goldfields at Barkerville. Constructed partly by the Royal Engineers and partly by private contractors, it ran about…

colonial-sugar-refining-company.s: The Colonial Sugar Refining Company was an Australian sugar company founded in Sydney in 1855. It expanded into Fiji in the 1880s, where it came to dominate the sugar industry, owning mills and estates worked largely by indentured labourers from India and later leasing land to…

compagnie-des-iles-de-lamerique.s: The Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique was a French chartered company founded in 1635 under Cardinal Richelieu to colonise the Caribbean. It succeeded the Compagnie de Saint-Christophe and sponsored the settlement of Guadeloupe and Martinique in 1635.

charles-lienard-de-lolive.s: Charles Liénard de l'Olive was a French colonist who, with Jean du Plessis d'Ossonville, led the first French settlement of Guadeloupe in June 1635 for the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique. The settlers suffered famine and disease, and after du Plessis died he governed the…

cape-mesurado.s: Cape Mesurado is a headland on the coast of Liberia, at the mouth of the Mesurado River. Agents of the American Colonization Society acquired it from local Dei rulers in December 1821, and from 1822 settlers founded the town of Monrovia there.

charlestown-saint-kitts-and-nevis.s: Charlestown is the capital of the island of Nevis in Saint Kitts and Nevis, on its western coast. Founded by English settlers in the 17th century, it was a busy sugar port and the centre of colonial government on the island.

cupids.s: Cupids, originally Cuper's Cove, is a town on Conception Bay in Newfoundland, Canada. John Guy founded it in 1610 for the London and Bristol Company as the first English colony in Newfoundland, one of the earliest in North America after Jamestown.

constitution-act-1982.s: The Constitution Act, 1982 is part of the Constitution of Canada, enacted together with the Canada Act 1982 of the British Parliament. It patriated the constitution, ending the need for British approval of amendments, set out a domestic amending formula and entrenched the…

clayton-bulwer-treaty.s: The Clayton–Bulwer Treaty was signed in 1850 by the United States and Britain, represented by John M. Clayton and Sir Henry Bulwer.

coxen-hole.s: Coxen Hole is the main town of the island of Roatán and capital of the Bay Islands department of Honduras. Settled by English-speaking islanders in the 19th century, it was the seat of the British Colony of the Bay Islands from 1852 to 1860.

cedula-of-population.s: The Cédula de Población was a royal decree issued by Charles III of Spain in 1783 to encourage the settlement of Trinidad. It offered free land, tax exemptions and other privileges to Catholic immigrants from friendly nations, with additional land for each enslaved person they…

chaguaramas.s: Chaguaramas is a peninsula and bay at the north-western tip of Trinidad, west of Port of Spain. Leased to the United States in 1941 under the destroyers-for-bases agreement, it became a US naval base.

college-of-william-and-mary.s: The College of William & Mary is a public university in Williamsburg, Virginia, founded by royal charter in 1693 under King William III and Queen Mary II. It is the second-oldest institution of higher education in the United States, after Harvard.

coolgardie.s: Coolgardie is a town in the Goldfields region of Western Australia. Gold was found there in 1892 by Arthur Bayley and William Ford, starting a rush that briefly made it the third-largest town in the colony.

claros.s: Claros was an ancient sanctuary and oracle of Apollo in Ionia, on the west coast of Asia Minor, in the territory of Colophon near modern Ahmetbeyli in Turkey. Its oracle, delivered through a priest who drank from a sacred spring, was among the most famous of the Greek world…

colorado.s: Colorado is a state of the western United States, crossed by the Rocky Mountains and the high plains to their east. Its eastern plains were part of the hunting lands of the Comanche, Cheyenne and Arapaho before American settlement.

coahuila.s: Coahuila is a state of northern Mexico bordering Texas, with its capital at Saltillo. Under Spanish rule it was a frontier province of New Spain exposed to Apache and Comanche raids, and from 1824 it was joined with Texas as the Mexican state of Coahuila y Tejas until the…

comanche.s: The Comanche, who call themselves Numunuu, are a Native American people who split from the Shoshone and moved onto the southern Plains in the early 18th century. Mastering the horse, they built a powerful raiding and trading domain, Comancheria, from Kansas to northern Mexico,…

canberra.s: Canberra is the capital of Australia, built in the Australian Capital Territory as a compromise between the rival cities of Sydney and Melbourne. The site was chosen in 1908 and named in 1913, and the city was planned by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion…

convention-parliament-1660.s: The Convention Parliament of 1660 was an English parliament elected without royal writ after General George Monck restored the members excluded from the Long Parliament. Meeting in April 1660, it accepted Charles II's Declaration of Breda and proclaimed him king, ending the…

crema.s: Crema is a town in Lombardy, northern Italy, on the Serio river between Milan and Cremona. Allied with Milan against Cremona, it was besieged and destroyed by Frederick Barbarossa in 1159–1160, then rebuilt.

cathedral-of-saint-tryphon.s: The Cathedral of Saint Tryphon is the Roman Catholic cathedral of Kotor in Montenegro, consecrated in 1166 and dedicated to the city's patron saint, whose relics it holds. A Romanesque church with two west towers, it was rebuilt after earthquakes in 1667 and 1979.

corpus-christi-feast.s: Corpus Christi is a Christian feast honouring the Eucharist, celebrated on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday. It began at Liège in 1246 after the visions of Juliana of Cornillon, and Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole Church in 1264.

cangrande-i-della-scala.s: Cangrande I della Scala was lord of Verona from 1311 to 1329 and the most powerful of the Scaliger family. Imperial vicar and Ghibelline leader, he conquered Vicenza, Padua and Treviso, making Verona the leading power of north-eastern Italy.

carraresi.s: The Carraresi, or da Carrara, were a family who ruled Padua as lords from 1318, with interruptions, until 1405. Patrons of Petrarch and of artists, they made Padua a cultural centre but were caught between Verona, Milan and Venice.

carrara.s: Carrara is a town in northern Tuscany at the foot of the Apuan Alps, famous for its white marble, quarried since Roman times. Michelangelo chose blocks there for his sculptures.

certosa-di-pavia.s: The Certosa di Pavia is a Carthusian monastery north of Pavia in Lombardy, founded in 1396 by Gian Galeazzo Visconti as a family mausoleum. Built over more than a century, it combines late Gothic and Renaissance styles, and its marble façade, carved from the 1490s, is among…

collegiata-san-gimignano.s: The Collegiata is the main church of San Gimignano in Tuscany, consecrated in 1148. Its interior is covered with 14th-century frescoes of the Old and New Testaments by Sienese painters, including Bartolo di Fredi, and its Santa Fina chapel was frescoed by Domenico Ghirlandaio.

carpentras.s: Carpentras is a town in Provence, south-eastern France, the capital of the papal Comtat Venaissin from 1320 until 1791. Its Jewish community, one of the four of the Pope's Jews, lived in an enclosed street, and its synagogue, founded in 1367, is the oldest still in use in France.

comtadin-jews.s: The Comtadin Jews, or Pope's Jews, were the Jewish communities of the papal territories of Avignon and the Comtat Venaissin, where they found refuge after expulsions from France in the 14th century. From the 17th century they were confined to four communities, at Avignon,…

cape-mount.s: Cape Mount is a headland and coastal district in north-western Liberia, near the border with Sierra Leone, home mainly to the Vai people. From the 18th century its anchorage was a centre of trade, including the slave trade, between the interior and European ships.

condroz.s: The Condroz is a plateau region of southern Belgium, in the provinces of Namur and Liège, south of the Meuse. Its name comes from the Condrusi, a people of Gaul recorded by Julius Caesar.

congo-reform-association.s: The Congo Reform Association was a humanitarian campaign founded in 1904 by the journalist E. D.

couserans.s: The Couserans is a historic region of the central French Pyrenees, in the upper Salat valley, now in the department of Ariège. Its name comes from the Consoranni, a people of Roman Gaul.

cooch-behar-palace.s: Cooch Behar Palace, also called the Victor Jubilee Palace, is a royal residence in Cooch Behar, West Bengal, built in 1887 for Maharaja Nripendra Narayan in a style inspired by the Italian Renaissance and Buckingham Palace. A two-storey brick building with a domed central…

coosa-river.s: The Coosa River flows about 450 km from north-western Georgia through Alabama, where it joins the Tallapoosa to form the Alabama River. Its valley was home to the Mississippian chiefdom of Coosa, visited by Hernando de Soto in 1540, and later to Upper Creek towns.

coosawattee-river.s: The Coosawattee River is a river in north-west Georgia, in the United States, which joins the Conasauga near Calhoun to form the Oostanaula. In the 14th to 16th centuries its valley was home to Mississippian towns, among them the Little Egypt site near Carters, which…

ciaran-of-saighir.s: Ciarán of Saigir, also called Ciarán the Elder, was an early Irish saint, traditionally regarded as the first bishop of Ossory and as active even before Saint Patrick. He founded a monastery at Saigir, now Seir Kieran in County Offaly, which became the burial place of the…

clonakilty.s: Clonakilty is a market town in West Cork, Ireland, at the head of Clonakilty Bay on the Atlantic coast. It was developed as a plantation town in the early 17th century by Richard Boyle, 1st Earl of Cork, and received a royal charter in 1613.

chersicrates.s: Chersicrates was a member of the Bacchiad ruling clan of Corinth who, according to Strabo, led the Corinthian colonists who founded Corcyra on the island of Corfu, traditionally around 733 BCE. Strabo says that Archias, the founder of Syracuse, left him with part of his…

carduchi.s: The Carduchi were a warlike people of the mountains of south-eastern Anatolia, north of the Tigris, in the region later called Corduene. Xenophon describes how the Greek mercenaries of the Ten Thousand fought their way through their country for seven days during the retreat of…

county-carlow.s: County Carlow is one of the smallest counties of Ireland, in the province of Leinster, crossed by the rivers Barrow and Slaney. In early medieval times it lay within the lands of the Uí Chennselaig kings of south Leinster.

county-kilkenny.s: County Kilkenny is a county in the south-east of Ireland, in the province of Leinster, centred on the city of Kilkenny on the River Nore. It corresponds broadly to the early medieval kingdom of Osraige.

corseul.s: Corseul is a village in the Côtes-d'Armor department of Brittany, France, whose name preserves that of the Coriosolites. In the Roman period it was Fanum Martis, the capital of their civitas, a planned town with a forum and public buildings.

caithness.s: Caithness is a historic county in the far north-east of mainland Scotland, bounded by the Pentland Firth and the North Sea. It is rich in Iron Age brochs and was part of Pictish territory before Norse settlers from Orkney took it over in the 9th century; the earls of Orkney…

cheshire.s: Cheshire is a county in north-west England, between the Welsh border and the Pennines, with Chester as its historic county town. In the Iron Age it formed part of the territory of the Cornovii, and its brine springs have been exploited for salt since prehistoric times.

corte.s: Corte is a town in the mountainous centre of Corsica, overlooked by a citadel on a rocky spur above the Tavignano and Restonica rivers. Pasquale Paoli made it the capital of the independent Corsican Republic from 1755 and founded a university there in 1765.

chyhyryn.s: Chyhyryn is a small town on the Tiasmyn river in the Cherkasy region of central Ukraine. Under Bohdan Khmelnytsky it became the residence of the hetman and the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate from the late 1640s.

council-of-clermont.s: The Council of Clermont was a church council held by Pope Urban II at Clermont in Auvergne in November 1095. Besides decrees on church reform, it ended with Urban's sermon of 27 November calling on western Christians to aid the Byzantines and free Jerusalem, which launched the…

conflent.s: Conflent is a historic district of Northern Catalonia in the eastern Pyrenees, now in the French department of Pyrénées-Orientales, centred on the valley of the Têt and the town of Prades. In the Middle Ages it belonged to the county of Cerdanya, and it contains the…

chretien-de-troyes.s: Chrétien de Troyes was a French poet of the late 12th century who wrote at the court of Marie de Champagne and later for Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders. His verse romances, including Erec and Enide, Lancelot, Yvain and Perceval, shaped the legends of King Arthur, and…

carignan-ardennes.s: Carignan is a small town on the Chiers in the Ardennes department of north-eastern France, known until 1662 as Ivoix or Yvois. A Roman settlement and medieval fortified town, it belonged to the County of Chiny and then to Luxembourg, and changed hands repeatedly between Spain…

carcassonne.s: Carcassonne is a city in the Aude department of southern France, on the route between the Mediterranean and Toulouse. Its fortified upper town, the Cité, with a double ring of walls and 52 towers, was the seat of counts and then of the Trencavel viscounts, whose surrender to…

celle.s: Celle is a town on the Aller in Lower Saxony, Germany, on the southern edge of the Lüneburg Heath. From the late 14th century it was the residence of the Guelph dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg ruling the Principality of Lüneburg, whose palace still stands.

charles-edzard-prince-of-east-frisia.n: Charles Edzard, Prince of East Frisia
charles-edzard-prince-of-east-frisia.s: Charles Edzard was the last prince of East Frisia of the Cirksena dynasty, ruling from 1734 to 1744. His reign was troubled by conflict with the East Frisian estates and the town of Emden.

charles-ii-of-navarre.s: Charles II, called the Bad, was king of Navarre from 1349 and count of Évreux, a grandson of Louis X of France through his mother Joan II. Holding large lands in Normandy, he intrigued against John II and Charles V of France, switching between the English and French during the…

canche.s: The Canche is a river of northern France, about 90 kilometres long, flowing west through the Pas-de-Calais department to the English Channel at Étaples. In the Middle Ages its valley marked the southern limit of the County of Flanders, and the early medieval trading port of…

catharism.s: The Cathars were a Christian dualist movement of the 12th and 13th centuries, strongest in Languedoc and northern Italy, who believed the material world was the creation of an evil principle. Led by ascetic 'perfects', they rejected the sacraments and hierarchy of the Catholic…

chlodwig-zu-hohenlohe-schillingsfurst.s: Chlodwig zu Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst (1819–1901) was a German statesman who served as prime minister of Bavaria from 1866 to 1870, governor of Alsace-Lorraine from 1885 and Chancellor of the German Empire and Prussian prime minister from 1894 to 1900. A liberal Catholic…

community-of-true-inspiration.s: The Community of True Inspiration (the Inspirationists) is a Radical Pietist movement founded in Germany in 1714 by Eberhard Ludwig Gruber and Johann Friedrich Rock, who held that God still spoke through inspired prophets. Persecuted elsewhere, its members found refuge in the…

charroux.s: Charroux is a village in the Vienne department of western France that grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in the late 8th century and renowned for its relics. A church council held there in 989 issued the first known decrees of the Peace of God.

cluny-abbey.s: Cluny Abbey was a Benedictine monastery at Cluny in Burgundy, founded in 910 by Duke William I of Aquitaine and placed directly under the pope, free from lay and episcopal control. Under abbots such as Odo, Odilo and Hugh it led a reform movement and headed hundreds of…

cardona.s: Cardona is a town in central Catalonia on the Cardener river, famous for its salt mountain, mined since antiquity, and its hilltop castle. The castle, seat of the viscounts and later dukes of Cardona, was one of the strongest in Catalonia and held out until September 1714,…

christian-rantzau.s: Christian Rantzau was a Holstein noble and Danish statesman who served Frederick III of Denmark as governor of the royal parts of Schleswig-Holstein and later as the leading member of his government. In 1649 he bought the district of Barmstedt from the Duke of…

conques.s: Conques is a village in the Aveyron department of southern France, in the Rouergue hills. Its abbey church of Sainte-Foy, a major stop on the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela, holds the relics of Saint Faith and a famous gold reliquary statue of the saint.

carrion-de-los-condes.s: Carrión de los Condes is a town on the Carrión river in the province of Palencia, Castile and León. Its name recalls the counts of the Banu Gómez family who held it in the 10th and 11th centuries, and the infantes de Carrión of the Cantar de mio Cid.

camino-de-santiago.s: The Camino de Santiago, or Way of St James, is the network of pilgrimage routes leading to the shrine of the apostle St James at Santiago de Compostela in Galicia. From the 9th and especially the 11th and 12th centuries it drew pilgrims from across Europe, and the main route…

chambery.s: Chambéry is a city in the French Alps, historic capital of Savoy, set between the Bauges and Chartreuse massifs. The counts of Savoy bought it in 1232, made it their capital in 1295 and kept the Holy Shroud in its castle chapel from 1502 until 1578.

christian-ernst-count-of-stolberg-wernig.s: Christian Ernst was Count of Stolberg-Wernigerode from 1710 until his death in 1771. A devout Pietist with close ties to Halle, he reformed church and school life in his small territory in the northern Harz and supported missions.

compromise-of-caspe.s: The Compromise of Caspe was the agreement of 1412 by which nine delegates from Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia, meeting at Caspe, chose a new king after Martin the Humane died without a legitimate heir in 1410. They selected the Castilian prince Ferdinand of Antequera over…

conrad-i-of-wurttemberg.s: Conrad of Wirtemberg is the first known lord of Württemberg, recorded between 1081 and 1110. He built the castle on the Wirtemberg hill above the Neckar near Stuttgart, from which the dynasty and later the state took their name.

capo-colonna.s: Capo Colonna is a cape on the Ionian coast of Calabria, south of Crotone, in southern Italy. It was the site of the sanctuary of Hera Lacinia, the main religious centre of the Greek cities of southern Italy, whose temple of the 5th century BCE was later plundered for building…

crotone.s: Crotone is a city on the Ionian coast of Calabria, southern Italy, on the site of the Greek colony of Croton, founded around 710 BCE. Ancient Croton was famed for its athletes, such as the wrestler Milo, for its physicians and as the home of Pythagoras and his community.

council-negri.s: The Council Negri is the legislature of Sarawak, first convened in 1867 under the Brooke rajahs and one of the oldest legislative bodies in South-East Asia. In 1946 it narrowly approved the cession of Sarawak to the British crown.

cobbold-commission.s: The Cobbold Commission was a commission of enquiry set up by Britain and Malaya in 1962, chaired by Lord Cobbold, to find out whether the peoples of North Borneo and Sarawak supported joining the proposed Federation of Malaysia. It found about two-thirds in favour, subject to…

coxcox.s: Coxcox was a ruler of Culhuacan in the Valley of Mexico in the early 14th century, known from Mexica chronicles. According to tradition he allowed the wandering Mexica to settle at Tizaapan as his vassals and used them in war, but drove them out after they sacrificed a Culhua…

campi-flegrei.s: The Campi Flegrei, or Phlegraean Fields, is a large volcanic caldera west of Naples, in southern Italy. Its craters, hot springs and fumaroles surround Pozzuoli and the ancient sites of Cumae and Baiae, and in antiquity the area was linked with the entrance to the underworld…

cumaean-sibyl.s: The Cumaean Sibyl was the prophetess who presided over the oracle of Apollo at Cumae, the Greek colony near Naples. Roman tradition said she sold the Sibylline Books to King Tarquin, and in Virgil's Aeneid she guides Aeneas through the underworld.

codex-cumanicus.s: The Codex Cumanicus is a manuscript compiled in the late 13th and early 14th centuries for Italian merchants and Franciscan missionaries working in the lands of the Golden Horde. It contains a Latin–Persian–Cuman glossary, Cuman riddles and Christian texts in Cuman, and is the…

cyzicene.s: Cyzicenes were electrum coins struck by the Greek city of Cyzicus on the Sea of Marmara from the 6th to the 4th century BCE. Usually staters of about 16 grams, marked with the city's tuna-fish emblem beneath a changing main design, they were among the most widely used coins in…

county-antrim.s: County Antrim is a county in the north-east of Northern Ireland, between Lough Neagh and the North Channel, and includes much of Belfast. Its coast, with the basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway, lies only some 20 kilometres from Scotland.

canusium.s: Canusium, modern Canosa di Puglia, was one of the main towns of the Daunians in northern Apulia, famed for its rich chamber tombs and painted pottery. It sided with Rome in the Samnite Wars, and after the Roman defeat at Cannae in 216 BCE it sheltered the surviving soldiers.

cromarty-firth.s: The Cromarty Firth is a sea inlet in Easter Ross in the Scottish Highlands, separating the Black Isle from the mainland to the north. Its deep, sheltered waters made Invergordon an important naval base in both world wars, and in recent decades it has been used for building and…

chester.s: Chester is a city in Cheshire, north-west England, on the River Dee near the Welsh border. It began as the Roman legionary fortress of Deva Victrix, founded in the 70s CE, and became a key base against the Welsh.

county-waterford.s: County Waterford is a county in the province of Munster, in the south-east of Ireland, named after the city of Waterford, founded by Vikings in the early 10th century. In the early Middle Ages its lands belonged to the Déisi, and the monastery of Lismore was one of Ireland's…

carthach-of-lismore.s: Carthach, also called Mochuda, was an Irish monk and saint who died in 637. He founded and ruled a monastery at Rahan in the midlands but was expelled from there around 636 and led his community south to Lismore, in the lands of the Déisi.

caesar-rodney.s: Caesar Rodney was an American politician from Delaware and a signer of the Declaration of Independence. On the night of 1–2 July 1776 he rode about 80 miles to Philadelphia to break a tie in Delaware's delegation and cast its vote for independence.

cyprus-convention.s: The Cyprus Convention was a secret agreement signed on 4 June 1878 between Britain and the Ottoman Empire. Britain undertook to defend the Ottoman lands in Asia against Russia, and in return the sultan allowed it to occupy and administer Cyprus while keeping formal sovereignty.

convention-of-london-1786.s: The Convention of London was signed by Britain and Spain on 14 July 1786. Britain agreed to evacuate its settlers from the Mosquito Coast of Central America, and in return Spain enlarged the area of the Bay of Honduras in which British woodcutters could cut logwood and…

carmarthen.s: Carmarthen is the county town of Carmarthenshire in south-west Wales, on the River Tywi. It began as Moridunum, the Roman town of the Demetae, which had an amphitheatre and is among the westernmost Roman towns in Britain.

carmarthenshire.s: Carmarthenshire is a county in south-west Wales, the largest of the historic Welsh counties, with Carmarthen as its county town and Llanelli as its largest town. It covers the valley of the Tywi and the uplands around it.

chhindwara-district.s: Chhindwara district is a district of Madhya Pradesh, India, on the Satpura plateau, with its headquarters at the town of Chhindwara. It has a large Gond population and was the heartland of the Gond kingdom of Deogarh, whose rulers founded Nagpur.

chamunda.s: Chamunda is a fierce form of the Hindu mother goddess Devi, one of the seven or eight Matrikas. In the Devi Mahatmya she is created from the goddess's anger and slays the demons Chanda and Munda, from whom she takes her name.

cirencester.s: Cirencester is a market town in Gloucestershire, England, in the southern Cotswolds. As Corinium Dobunnorum it was the civitas capital of the Dobunni and the second-largest town of Roman Britain.

corinium-dobunnorum.s: Corinium Dobunnorum was the Roman town at Cirencester in Gloucestershire, England. It grew beside a fort built soon after the conquest of 43 CE and became the civitas capital of the Dobunni, with a forum, basilica and amphitheatre.

cotswolds.s: The Cotswolds are a range of limestone hills in south-central England, mainly in Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire. Sheep farming made the region rich from the Middle Ages, when its wool was exported across Europe, leaving a legacy of stone-built market towns and large churches.

ceylon-independence-act-1947.s: The Ceylon Independence Act 1947 was an act of the British Parliament that granted independence to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, as a dominion within the Commonwealth. It came into force on 4 February 1948, together with the Soulbury Constitution and agreements with Britain on…

c-rajagopalachari.s: C. Rajagopalachari, known as Rajaji, was an Indian independence leader, lawyer and writer who served as Governor-General of India from 1948 to 1950, the only Indian to hold the office.

commission-of-government.s: The Commission of Government was the unelected body that governed Newfoundland from 1934 to 1949. Facing bankruptcy in the Great Depression, the dominion gave up self-government, and a governor and six commissioners appointed from London, three from Britain and three from…

clichy.s: Clichy is a town on the Seine immediately north-west of Paris, in the Hauts-de-Seine department of France. In the Merovingian period it was the site of a royal villa where Dagobert I held court and was married, and church councils met there in the 7th century.

chronicle-of-fredegar.s: The Chronicle of Fredegar is a Latin chronicle compiled in Frankish Gaul, probably in Burgundy, around 660, and attributed since the 16th century to an otherwise unknown 'Fredegar'. Drawing on earlier works such as Gregory of Tours, it continues the history of the Franks to…

cenad.s: Cenad is a village in Timiș county, western Romania, on the Mureș river near the Hungarian border. As Morisena it was the seat of the local ruler Ahtum around 1000; after his defeat by King Stephen I of Hungary it took the name Csanád from the victorious commander and in 1030…

csanad-commander.s: Csanád was a Hungarian commander of the early 11th century in the service of King Stephen I. According to the Legend of Saint Gerard, he had served Ahtum, the ruler of the lower Mureș region, before going over to Stephen, and he led the royal army that defeated and killed Ahtum.

carloman-mayor-of-the-palace.s: Carloman was the eldest son of Charles Martel and Frankish mayor of the palace in Austrasia from 741 to 747, ruling jointly with his brother Pepin the Short. He campaigned against the Alemanni, Bavarians and Saxons, crushing Alemannic resistance at Cannstatt in 746, and…

carloman-of-bavaria.s: Carloman of Bavaria was a Carolingian king of Bavaria from 876 and of Italy from 877, the eldest son of Louis the German. After Emperor Louis II died in 875 without a son, Carloman contested Italy with Charles the Bald and took the Italian crown after Charles's death.

chernivtsi.s: Chernivtsi is a city in western Ukraine on the Prut river, the historic capital of Bukovina. Under Austrian rule from 1775 it was known as Czernowitz and grew into a multinational, largely German-speaking city with a large Jewish population and a university founded in 1875.

citeaux-abbey.s: Cîteaux Abbey, south of Dijon in Burgundy, was founded in 1098 by Robert of Molesme and a group of monks seeking a stricter observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict. It became the mother house of the Cistercian order, which spread across Europe under Bernard of Clairvaux.

cesare-d-este-duke-of-modena.s: Cesare d'Este was Duke of Modena and Reggio from 1597. As cousin and heir of Duke Alfonso II of Ferrara, he expected to inherit Ferrara too, but Pope Clement VIII refused to recognise him, arguing that his line was illegitimate, and in 1598 Ferrara was annexed to the Papal…

catherine-jagiellon.s: Catherine Jagiellon was a Polish princess, daughter of Sigismund I the Old, who in 1562 married Duke John of Finland, the future John III of Sweden. When his brother Eric XIV imprisoned John at Gripsholm in 1563, she chose to share his captivity.

conrad-i-of-germany.s: Conrad I was King of East Francia from 911 to 918, the first king not of the Carolingian line. A member of the Conradine family and Duke of Franconia, he was elected after the death of Louis the Child but struggled against the dukes of Saxony, Bavaria and Swabia and against…

codex-diplomaticus-cajetanus.s: The Codex Diplomaticus Cajetanus is a collection of medieval charters from Gaeta and its district, published by the monks of Monte Cassino from 1887. Its documents, beginning in the 9th century, are the main source for the society, economy and rulers of the Duchy of Gaeta,…

cumans.s: The Cumans were a Turkic nomadic people of the Eurasian steppe, closely linked with the Kipchaks and called Polovtsians in Russian sources. From the mid-11th century they dominated the steppe north of the Black Sea, raiding and allying with Kievan Rus', Byzantium, Hungary and…

casimir-ii-of-leczyca.s: Casimir II of Łęczyca (c. 1261–1294) was a Polish prince of the Piast dynasty, a son of Casimir I of Kuyavia.

charles-duke-of-lower-lorraine.s: Charles (953–c. 993) was a Carolingian prince, younger son of the West Frankish king Louis IV and brother of King Lothair.

christian-thomasius.s: Christian Thomasius (1655–1728) was a German jurist and philosopher, one of the founders of the early German Enlightenment. Forced out of Leipzig for his views, he moved to Halle in 1690 and helped found its university.

camera-degli-sposi.s: The Camera degli Sposi ('Bridal Chamber') is a room in the Castle of San Giorgio in Mantua frescoed by Andrea Mantegna between about 1465 and 1474 for Ludovico III Gonzaga. Its walls show the marquis with his family and court, and its ceiling has a painted oculus opening on to…

chelmno-land.s: Chełmno Land is a historical region of northern Poland on the right bank of the Vistula, around the town of Chełmno (Kulm). Konrad I of Masovia granted it to the Teutonic Order in the 1220s as a base for the conquest of the pagan Prussians, and it became the core of the…

charlotte-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.s: Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz (1744–1818) was the wife of George III and queen consort of Great Britain and Ireland from 1761. A princess of the small ducal house of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, she bore fifteen children, including the future George IV and William IV.

conrad-ii-count-of-dachau.s: Conrad II (d. 1159) was a Bavarian count of Dachau to whom Frederick Barbarossa gave the title Duke of Merania around 1152, making him its first holder.

cesare-beccaria.s: Cesare Beccaria (1738–1794) was an Italian jurist, philosopher and economist of the Milanese Enlightenment. His treatise On Crimes and Punishments (1764) condemned torture and the death penalty and argued that punishments should be proportionate and aimed at preventing crime…

ciro-menotti.s: Ciro Menotti (1798–1831) was an Italian patriot from Carpi in the Duchy of Modena. He conspired for a revolution in central Italy and hoped for the support of Duke Francis IV, but the duke had him arrested on the eve of the revolt of February 1831.

charles-of-austria-bishop-of-wroclaw.s: Archduke Charles of Austria (1590–1624), a son of Archduke Charles II of Inner Austria, was Bishop of Wrocław from 1608, Bishop of Brixen from 1613 and from 1619 Grand Master of the Teutonic Order. A leading figure of the Counter-Reformation in Silesia, he founded a Jesuit…

counter-reformation.s: The Counter-Reformation was the period of Catholic renewal and response to the Protestant Reformation, from the mid-16th to the mid-17th century. Its programme was set by the Council of Trent (1545–1563), which defined doctrine and reformed the clergy, and it was carried…

congress-of-troppau.s: The Congress of Troppau was a conference of the powers of the Holy Alliance held in late 1820 at Troppau (Opava) in Austrian Silesia. Called by Metternich after the liberal revolution in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, it produced the Troppau Protocol, by which Austria,…

czestochowa.s: Częstochowa is a city in the Silesian Voivodeship of southern Poland, on the Warta river. It is famous for the Jasna Góra Monastery, founded in 1382 by Pauline monks, which houses the icon of the Black Madonna and is the main Catholic pilgrimage site in Poland.

cieszyn.s: Cieszyn (German: Teschen) is a town in southern Poland on the Olza river, which since 1920 has formed the border with the Czech town of Český Těšín. From 1290 it was the seat of the Duchy of Cieszyn, ruled by a branch of the Piasts until 1653 and then by the Habsburgs.

casimir-i-of-opole.s: Casimir I of Opole (c. 1178–1230) was a Piast duke of Opole and Racibórz in Upper Silesia from 1211, a son of Mieszko IV Tanglefoot.

congress-of-gniezno.s: The Congress of Gniezno was a meeting in March 1000 between Emperor Otto III and Duke Bolesław I the Brave of Poland at the tomb of Saint Adalbert in Gniezno. Otto founded an archbishopric there with dependent bishoprics at Kraków, Wrocław and Kołobrzeg, giving Poland its own…

coburg.s: Coburg is a town in Upper Franconia, Bavaria, Germany, dominated by the fortress of Veste Coburg, where Martin Luther stayed in 1530. It was the residence of the Ernestine dukes of Saxe-Coburg and later of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, whose family supplied monarchs to Belgium,…

camerino.s: Camerino is a hill town in the Marche region of central Italy, in the province of Macerata. From the thirteenth century until 1539 it was ruled by the Varano family, who made it a small Renaissance court, and it then returned to the Papal States.

conrad-iii-of-germany.s: Conrad III was King of Germany from 1138 to 1152, the first ruler of the Hohenstaufen dynasty. His election began the long rivalry between the Hohenstaufen and the Welfs.

conradin.s: Conradin was the last legitimate member of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, Duke of Swabia and claimant to the kingdoms of Sicily and Jerusalem. At fifteen he invaded Italy to recover Sicily from Charles of Anjou, but was defeated at the Battle of Tagliacozzo in 1268.

conrad-i-duke-of-zahringen.s: Conrad I was Duke of Zähringen from 1122 until his death in 1152. Together with his brother Berthold III he founded the town of Freiburg im Breisgau in 1120.

cunipert.s: Cunipert was King of the Lombards, co-ruler with his father Perctarit from 680 and sole king from 688 to 700. Early in his reign the rebel duke Alahis seized Pavia, but Cunipert defeated and killed him at Coronate in 689.

county-of-arnsberg.s: The County of Arnsberg was a territory of the Holy Roman Empire in Westphalia, centred on the castle and town of Arnsberg on the Ruhr. Its counts held much of the Sauerland and competed with the archbishops of Cologne.

christoph-duke-of-wurttemberg.s: Christoph was Duke of Württemberg from 1550 to 1568, succeeding his father Ulrich. With the reformer Johannes Brenz he organised a Lutheran territorial church, set out in the Great Church Order of 1559, and created a system of schools and monastic seminaries to train clergy.

constantine-bodin.s: Constantine Bodin was King of Duklja from about 1081 to around 1101, son of Mihailo I. In 1072 Bulgarian rebels proclaimed him tsar as Peter III, but the Byzantines defeated and captured him.

cornwall.s: Cornwall is a county in the far south-west of England, a peninsula bounded by the Atlantic and the English Channel. It was home to the British kingdom of Dumnonia and its Cornish-speaking successors, and was absorbed by Wessex by the tenth century, keeping its Celtic language…

chinsurah.s: Chinsurah is a town on the Hooghly River in West Bengal, India, about 35 kilometres north of Kolkata. From the 17th century it was the main base of the Dutch East India Company in Bengal, trading in textiles, silk, saltpetre and opium.

christiaan-huygens.s: Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician, physicist and astronomer. In 1655 he discovered Saturn's moon Titan and explained the planet's rings, and in 1656 he invented the pendulum clock, greatly improving timekeeping.

cornelis-lampsins.s: Cornelis Lampsins was a merchant and burgomaster of Vlissingen in Zeeland. With his brother Adriaan he sponsored the Dutch colonisation of Tobago from 1654, settling planters and enslaved Africans there.

cape-araxos.s: Cape Araxos is the north-western tip of the Peloponnese in Greece, in western Achaea, where the Gulf of Patras opens into the Ionian Sea. In antiquity it marked the boundary between Achaea and Elis, near the city of Dyme.

choros-oirats.s: The Choros are a clan of the Oirat Mongols and one of the four main groups of the Four Oirat confederation. In the 17th century their leaders founded and ruled the Dzungar Khanate, which dominated Central Asia until the Qing conquest of 1755 to 1758.

chester-le-street.s: Chester-le-Street is a town in County Durham in north-east England, on the site of a Roman fort. From 883 to 995 it was the seat of the community of Saint Cuthbert, which had left Lindisfarne with the saint's relics to escape Viking raids.

clan-sinclair.s: Clan Sinclair is a Scottish clan of Norman origin based in Caithness and Orkney. In 1379 Henry Sinclair was invested as Earl of Orkney by the king of Norway, and his descendants held the earldom until William Sinclair gave it up to James III of Scotland in 1470.

carrick-on-suir.s: Carrick-on-Suir is a town on the River Suir in County Tipperary, Ireland. It was a seat of the Butler earls of Ormond, and its Ormond Castle includes an Elizabethan manor house built by Thomas Butler, 10th Earl of Ormond, around 1565, the finest of its kind in Ireland.

carrickfergus.s: Carrickfergus is a town on the northern shore of Belfast Lough in County Antrim, Northern Ireland. Its castle was built by John de Courcy after his invasion of Ulster in 1177 and became the centre of the earldom of Ulster.

coleraine.s: Coleraine is a town on the River Bann in County Londonderry, Northern Ireland. Mount Sandel nearby holds remains of one of the earliest known settlements in Ireland, about 9,000 years old.

clandeboye-oneills.s: The Clandeboye O'Neills, in Irish Clann Aodha Buidhe, were a branch of the O'Neill dynasty of Tyrone that crossed the River Bann in the 14th century. They took over much of south Antrim and north Down from the declining earldom of Ulster and formed the lordship of Clandeboye.

chera-dynasty.s: The Chera dynasty was one of the three crowned dynasties of ancient Tamilakam, with the Cholas and Pandyas, ruling the Malabar Coast and the Kongu country of southern India. The edicts of Ashoka name them as the Keralaputras, and Sangam poems praise their kings, who grew rich…

charles-eliot-diplomat.s: Sir Charles Eliot was a British diplomat, linguist and scholar who served as Commissioner of the East Africa Protectorate from 1900 to 1904. He promoted European settlement in the Kenya highlands, setting aside land at the expense of the Maasai and other Africans, and resigned…

clough-oughter-castle.s: Clough Oughter Castle is a ruined circular tower on a small island in Lough Oughter, County Cavan, Ireland, built in the early 13th century. It became a stronghold of the O'Reilly lords of East Breifne.

cuttack.s: Cuttack is a city in Odisha, India, at the head of the Mahanadi delta. It became the capital of the Eastern Ganga kings in the 12th century and remained the main city of Odisha under the Gajapatis, Mughals, Marathas and British, with the Barabati Fort as its stronghold.

county-dublin.s: County Dublin is a county in the province of Leinster on the east coast of Ireland, containing the capital, Dublin. Created after the Anglo-Norman conquest, it formed the core of the English Pale in the later Middle Ages.

catuvolcus.s: Catuvolcus was an elderly king of the Eburones in northern Gaul who shared rule with Ambiorix. He joined the rising of 54 BCE that destroyed a Roman force at Atuatuca.

chenes.s: Chenes is a region of northern Campeche state in Mexico, and the name of a Maya architectural style of the Late Classic period that developed there. Chenes buildings are known for facades covered with stone mosaic masks, often framing doorways in the shape of a monster's open…

coptos.s: Coptos, modern Qift, was an ancient Egyptian city on the east bank of the Nile north of Thebes. It was the starting point of desert routes through the Wadi Hammamat to the Red Sea and to stone quarries and gold mines, and the cult centre of the fertility god Min.

ceres.s: Ceres was the Roman goddess of agriculture, grain crops and fertility, closely identified with the Greek Demeter. Her temple on the Aventine Hill in Rome, traditionally dedicated in 493 BCE, was a centre of the plebeians.

chinguetti.s: Chinguetti is a desert town in the Adrar region of central Mauritania, founded in the 13th century as a stop on trans-Saharan caravan routes. It became a centre of Islamic learning, with family libraries of manuscripts, and gave its name to the whole country in Arabic as Bilad…

charles-stoddart.s: Charles Stoddart was a British army officer sent to Bukhara in 1838 to reassure Emir Nasrullah about British aims in Afghanistan and to seek the release of Russian captives. Accused of slighting the emir, he was thrown into a vermin-infested pit and held for years.

chefchaouen.s: Chefchaouen is a town in the Rif mountains of north-western Morocco. It was founded in 1471 by the sharif Ali ibn Rashid as a fortified base for raids on the Portuguese enclaves on the coast, and Muslim and Jewish refugees from Spain later settled there.

cadmus.s: Cadmus was a legendary hero of Greek myth, a Phoenician prince and brother of Europa, who founded the city of Thebes in Boeotia, whose citadel was called the Cadmea after him. Herodotus credits him with bringing the alphabet to Greece.

catherine-of-braganza.s: Catherine of Braganza was a Portuguese princess who became queen of England, Scotland and Ireland as the wife of Charles II from 1662 to 1685. Her dowry included Tangier and Bombay, giving England its first footholds in North Africa and India.

cayster-river.s: The Cayster, now the Küçük Menderes, is a river in western Turkey that flows into the Aegean near the ruins of Ephesus. The ancient city was founded near its mouth, but the silt the river carried steadily filled the harbour and pushed the coastline westwards, so that Ephesus…

chaonia.s: Chaonia was the north-western region of ancient Epirus, on the Ionian coast in present-day southern Albania, home of the Chaonians, one of the three main Epirote peoples. Its chief town was Phoenice, and Butrint lay within it.

claude-dabbeville.s: Claude d'Abbeville was a French Capuchin friar who joined the expedition that founded the colony of Equinoctial France on the island of Maranhão in Brazil in 1612. His history of the Capuchin mission, published in 1614, is a major source on the Tupinambá.

capuchins.s: The Capuchins are a Catholic order of friars, a reformed branch of the Franciscans founded in Italy in the 1520s and approved by the pope in 1528. Known for their brown habits with long pointed hoods, simple living and popular preaching, they became leading agents of the…

county-donegal.s: County Donegal is a county in the north-west of Ireland, part of the province of Ulster but in the Republic of Ireland. In the Middle Ages it was largely the lordship of Tír Chonaill, ruled by the O'Donnells, whose leaders took part in the Flight of the Earls from Rathmullan…

carlos-de-urrutia.s: Carlos de Urrutia was a Spanish officer born in Veracruz who served as governor and captain general of Santo Domingo from 1813 to 1818, during the period of restored Spanish rule known as España Boba. His order that soldiers farm plots of land earned him the nickname Carlos…

cartersville-georgia.s: Cartersville is a city in north-western Georgia, in the United States, the seat of Bartow County. It lies on the Etowah River near the Etowah Indian Mounds, the remains of a major Mississippian town occupied from around 1000 to 1550, now a state historic site.

cherokee.s: The Cherokee are an Iroquoian-speaking Native American people whose homeland lay in the southern Appalachians. In the early 19th century they adopted a written constitution and the syllabary created by Sequoyah.

campo-della-fiera.s: Campo della Fiera is an archaeological site at the foot of the cliff of Orvieto, in Umbria, central Italy. Excavations led by Simonetta Stopponi since 2000 have uncovered temples, a sacred way and votive offerings used from the 6th century BCE into Roman times.

communist-party-of-nepal-maoist-centre.s: The Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre) is a Nepalese party led by Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda). As the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) it waged an armed insurgency, the People's War, from 1996 to 2006, in which some 17,000 people died.

communist-party-of-nepal-unified-marxist.s: The Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist–Leninist) is one of Nepal's largest parties, formed in 1991 by the merger of two communist parties that had joined the 1990 People's Movement. Its leader Man Mohan Adhikari formed a minority government in 1994, and it has since led…

congress-of-oriente.s: The Congress of Oriente was an assembly of the Federal League convened by José Gervasio Artigas at Arroyo de la China, now Concepción del Uruguay, in June 1815. Delegates from the Eastern Province, Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Santa Fe, Córdoba and Misiones discussed independence…

certosa-situla.s: The Certosa Situla is a bronze bucket of about 500 BCE found in the 19th century in a grave of the Certosa cemetery of Etruscan Felsina, now Bologna. Its embossed decoration, arranged in four bands, shows a procession of soldiers, a religious procession with offerings, scenes…

carl-gustaf-emil-mannerheim.s: Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim was a Finnish soldier and statesman who served as a general in the Russian imperial army before leading the White forces to victory in the Finnish Civil War of 1918. He was regent of Finland in 1918–1919, commanded the Finnish army in the Winter War…

christian-social-party-austria.s: The Christian Social Party was an Austrian Catholic conservative party founded in 1891 and led in its early years by Karl Lueger, mayor of Vienna. It was strongest among the peasantry, the clergy and the lower middle class, and after 1920 it dominated the governments of the…

carbonaria-portugal.s: The Carbonária was a Portuguese secret revolutionary society founded in 1896, modelled on the Italian Carbonari and linked to republican and freemason circles. It recruited among workers, soldiers and sailors and organised armed cells against the monarchy, and some of its…

chaoyang-liaoning.s: Chaoyang is a city in western Liaoning province in north-eastern China. As Longcheng, the dragon city, it was founded in 342 by Murong Huang as the capital of the Former Yan, and it was later the last capital of the Later Yan and the capital of the Northern Yan until the…

compagnie-de-lorient.s: The Compagnie de l'Orient was a French trading company chartered in 1642 under Cardinal Richelieu to trade and found colonies in the Indian Ocean, especially in Madagascar. It sent Jacques Pronis to found Fort-Dauphin in south-east Madagascar in 1643, and Étienne de Flacourt…

chalon-sur-saone.s: Chalon-sur-Saône is a city in Burgundy in eastern France on the river Saône. As the Roman Cabillonum it was a river port and later a bishopric, and in the 6th century the Merovingian king Guntram made it the capital of his Frankish kingdom of Burgundy.

chlothar-i.s: Chlothar I was a Merovingian king of the Franks, the youngest son of Clovis I. On his father's death in 511 he received a share of the kingdom around Soissons, and with his brothers he conquered the Burgundian kingdom in 534 and took part in the conquest of Thuringia.

columbanus.s: Columbanus was an Irish monk from Bangor who travelled to Gaul around 590 and founded monasteries at Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaine in the Frankish kingdom of Burgundy. His strict monastic rule and Irish customs, such as the dating of Easter, brought him into conflict with…

chilperic-i.s: Chilperic I was a Merovingian king of the Franks who ruled the western kingdom of Neustria from Soissons from 561 until his murder in 584. A son of Chlothar I, he fought long wars against his brothers Sigebert I and Guntram, and his feud with Austrasia, waged with his wife…

chattuarii.s: The Chattuarii were a Germanic people of the lower Rhine, mentioned by Roman writers from the 1st century CE. They are counted among the older peoples who merged into the Frankish confederation from the 3rd century, and a district on the lower Rhine, the Hattuarian gau,…

counts-feud.s: The Count's Feud was a Danish civil war of 1534 to 1536, named after Count Christopher of Oldenburg, who led Lübeck's forces in the name of the deposed King Christian II. Lübeck under Jürgen Wullenwever, allied with Copenhagen, Malmö and rebellious peasants, opposed the…

charles-iii-of-the-united-kingdom.n: Charles III of the United Kingdom
charles-iii-of-the-united-kingdom.s: Charles III is King of the United Kingdom and of fourteen other Commonwealth realms, including Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The eldest son of Elizabeth II, he was Prince of Wales from 1958, the longest-serving heir apparent in British history, and succeeded his mother on…

colonia-claudia-ara-agrippinensium.s: Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium was the Roman city that became Cologne. Founded on the site of the main settlement of the Ubii, it received the rank of a colony in 50 CE under Emperor Claudius at the request of his wife Agrippina, who had been born there.

crescentia-of-kaufbeuren.s: Crescentia of Kaufbeuren, born Anna Höss, was a Franciscan nun in the convent of Kaufbeuren in Bavarian Swabia, of which she became mother superior in 1741. Known for her mystical piety and sought out for advice by visitors of every rank, she was beatified in 1900 and…

christoph-schappeler.s: Christoph Schappeler was a preacher in Memmingen from 1513 who led the city's turn to the Reformation. In 1525 he helped Sebastian Lotzer draft the Twelve Articles, the main programme of the rebels in the German Peasants' War, and after the peasants' defeat he fled to St.

castra-regina.s: Castra Regina was a Roman legionary fortress on the Danube completed in 179 CE under Marcus Aurelius for the Third Italian Legion, on the site of the later city of Regensburg. It guarded the frontier of the province of Raetia, and parts of its walls, including the Porta…

church-of-saints-peter-and-paul-rosheim.n: Church of Saints Peter and Paul, Rosheim
church-of-saints-peter-and-paul-rosheim.s: The Church of Saints Peter and Paul in Rosheim, Alsace, is a Romanesque church built in the middle of the 12th century of yellow sandstone. Its sculpted decoration, octagonal crossing tower and harmonious proportions make it one of the finest Romanesque buildings in Alsace.

church-of-sainte-foy-selestat.s: The Church of Sainte-Foy in Sélestat, Alsace, is a Romanesque church built in the 12th century for a priory dependent on the abbey of Conques. Built of red and yellow sandstone, with an octagonal crossing tower, it is one of the major Romanesque buildings of Alsace.

christian-social-union-in-bavaria.s: The Christian Social Union in Bavaria is a conservative political party founded in 1945 that operates only in Bavaria, where it has led the state government almost continuously since 1946. In federal politics it forms a joint parliamentary group with the Christian Democratic…

cloppenburg.s: Cloppenburg is a town in Lower Saxony, Germany, in the Oldenburg Münsterland. It belonged to the Prince-Bishopric of Münster until 1803, when it passed to Oldenburg, and so remained Catholic within the largely Lutheran duchy.

chemnitz.s: Chemnitz is a city in Saxony, Germany, which grew in the 19th century into one of the leading centres of German textile and machine-building industry, nicknamed the Saxon Manchester. From 1953 to 1990 the East German government named it Karl-Marx-Stadt, and a giant head of…

carl-zeiss-ag.s: Carl Zeiss AG is a German optics company that began as a workshop opened in Jena in 1846 by Carl Zeiss. With the physicist Ernst Abbe and the glassmaker Otto Schott it became a world leader in microscopes, lenses and precision optics.

cremieux-decree.s: The Crémieux Decree was a decree issued by the French Government of National Defence on 24 October 1870, named after the justice minister Adolphe Crémieux. It granted French citizenship to the Jews of Algeria, while Muslim Algerians remained subjects without full citizenship,…

cholon.s: Cholon (Chợ Lớn, 'big market') is the Chinese quarter of Ho Chi Minh City in southern Vietnam. Founded by Chinese settlers in the late 18th century, it grew under French rule into a separate city and the main rice-trading centre of the Mekong delta, before being joined…

coup-of-18-brumaire.s: The Coup of 18 Brumaire was the seizure of power in France by Napoleon Bonaparte on 9–10 November 1799 (18–19 Brumaire, Year VIII, in the revolutionary calendar). With the help of the director Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès and of troops who dispersed the legislative councils,…

committee-of-public-safety.s: The Committee of Public Safety was the executive body set up by the French National Convention in April 1793 to direct the war and suppress internal revolt. Dominated from July 1793 by Maximilien Robespierre and his allies, it ran the Reign of Terror, in which thousands of…

charlesfort.s: Charlesfort was a short-lived French Huguenot outpost built in 1562 by Jean Ribault on Parris Island, in present-day South Carolina. Ribault left a small garrison there while he returned to France, but supplies failed to arrive and the men abandoned it in 1563.

cayenne.s: Cayenne is the capital of French Guiana, an overseas department of France on the north-east coast of South America. French settlers established a post there in 1643, and after Dutch and English interludes France held it from 1676.

conakry.s: Conakry is the capital and largest city of Guinea, on the Kaloum peninsula and Tombo Island on the Atlantic coast. France occupied the island in 1887, and Conakry became the capital of the colony of French Guinea in the early 1890s, linked by railway to Kankan on the Niger…

chandannagar.s: Chandannagar, formerly Chandernagore, is a city on the Hooghly River north of Kolkata in West Bengal, India. Established as a French trading post in the 1670s and fortified from 1688, it was one of France's chief settlements in India.

corcyre-department.s: Corcyre was a French department created in 1797 from the former Venetian Ionian Islands after the Treaty of Campo Formio, named after the ancient Greek name of Corfu. Centred on Corfu, it was one of three departments, with Ithaque and Mer-Égée, into which France organised the…

casablanca.s: Casablanca is the largest city of Morocco and its chief port, on the Atlantic coast. Rebuilt in the 18th century on the site of the ruined town of Anfa, it was bombarded and occupied by France in 1907, and under the protectorate Resident-General Hubert Lyautey developed its…

can-vuong.s: The Cần Vương ('Aid the King') movement was a Vietnamese uprising against French rule launched in July 1885, when the regent Tôn Thất Thuyết fled Huế with the boy emperor Hàm Nghi and issued an edict calling on scholars and people to resist. Led by local scholar-gentry, it…

compagnie-de-saint-christophe.s: The Compagnie de Saint-Christophe was a French colonial company founded in 1626 under the patronage of Cardinal Richelieu to settle and exploit the island of Saint Christopher (Saint Kitts) in the Caribbean. Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc led its colonists, who shared the island…

christiansted.s: Christiansted is the largest town on Saint Croix in the United States Virgin Islands. It grew from the French settlement of Bassin and was laid out by the Danes after they bought the island from France in 1733, becoming the capital of the Danish West Indies from 1755 to 1871.

charles-leclerc-general.s: Charles Victoire Emmanuel Leclerc was a French general and the husband of Napoleon's sister Pauline Bonaparte. In 1801–1802 he led the large expedition sent to Saint-Domingue to restore French authority; he seized Toussaint Louverture by treachery and deported him to France,…

committee-of-togolese-unity.s: The Committee of Togolese Unity was a political party in French Togoland, founded in 1941 as a cultural association and turned into a nationalist party after 1946 under Sylvanus Olympio. It petitioned the United Nations for independence and for the unification of the Ewe…

cossus-cornelius-lentulus.s: Cossus Cornelius Lentulus was a Roman aristocrat and general of the reign of Augustus, consul in 1 BCE. As proconsul of Africa around 6 CE he defeated the Gaetuli, Berber peoples of the Saharan fringe who had risen against the client king Juba II of Mauretania.

chandradeva.s: Chandradeva was the founder of the Gahadavala dynasty of northern India, ruling from about 1089 to 1103. He took Kannauj after the decline of the Pratiharas and extended his authority over Varanasi, Ayodhya and the Doab.

chaitanya-mahaprabhu.s: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was a Bengali saint and the inspiration of Gaudiya Vaishnavism, a devotional movement centred on Krishna and Radha. Born at Nabadwip in 1486, he spread congregational chanting of Krishna's names and spent his later years at Puri, near the Jagannath temple,…

carita-parahyangan.s: The Carita Parahyangan is an Old Sundanese palm-leaf manuscript, usually dated to the late 16th century. It narrates the history of the Sundanese kingdoms of Galuh and Sunda from the 7th century to the fall of Pakuan Pajajaran, listing kings and the lengths of their reigns.

ciamis.s: Ciamis is a town and regency in West Java, Indonesia, in hill country near the border with Central Java. It lies in the old heartland of the Sundanese kingdom of Galuh, whose royal centre at Kawali, with its 14th-century inscriptions, is in the regency.
