chicama-valley.s: The Chicama Valley is a river valley on the desert north coast of Peru, just north of Trujillo. Watered by irrigation since ancient times, it was a heartland of the Moche culture, whose major site of El Brujo stands near its mouth, and later of the Chimú, who linked it to the…

cupisnique.s: Cupisnique was a culture of the north coast of Peru, flourishing from about 1500 to 500 BCE in valleys such as Jequetepeque, Chicama and Moche. Its people built platform mounds and temples decorated with painted clay friezes of feline and serpent deities, and they made fine…

chisinau.s: Chișinău, formerly Kishinev, is the capital and largest city of Moldova. A small market town under the Principality of Moldavia, it became the administrative centre of Bessarabia after the Russian annexation of 1812 and grew rapidly in the 19th century; the pogrom of 1903…

chugoku-region.s: The Chūgoku region is the western end of Honshu, the main island of Japan, made up of the prefectures of Hiroshima, Okayama, Shimane, Tottori and Yamaguchi. Its mountains divide a Sea of Japan coast from the Inland Sea coast.

chouf.s: The Chouf is a mountainous region of Mount Lebanon, south-east of Beirut, traditionally the heartland of the Druze community. Its lords, first the Ma'n and then the Shihab emirs, governed Mount Lebanon from towns such as Deir al-Qamar and Beiteddine under Ottoman rule.

chattahoochee-river.s: The Chattahoochee is a river of the south-eastern United States, rising in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Georgia and forming part of the boundary between Georgia and Alabama. Joining the Flint, it forms the Apalachicola.

creek-war.s: The Creek War of 1813 to 1814 began as a civil war among the Muscogee between the Red Sticks, who resisted American expansion, and those friendly to the United States. American militia and regulars under Andrew Jackson, with Cherokee and Lower Muscogee allies, crushed the Red…

carrowmore.s: Carrowmore is a large cemetery of megalithic tombs on the Cúil Irra peninsula near Sligo in north-west Ireland. Its dozens of passage tombs and stone circles, some dated to the 4th millennium BCE, are among the oldest in Ireland.

connachta.s: The Connachta were a group of early Irish dynasties who claimed descent from the legendary king Conn of the Hundred Battles and gave their name to the province of Connacht. Their main branches, the Uí Briúin, Uí Fiachrach and Uí Ailello, ruled the province, and the O'Connor…

county-sligo.s: County Sligo is a county in the province of Connacht in north-west Ireland, on the Atlantic coast, with the town of Sligo as its county seat. It is rich in prehistoric monuments, such as the Carrowmore and Carrowkeel tombs, and in the Middle Ages it was ruled largely by the…

corbilo.s: Corbilo was an ancient trading settlement at or near the mouth of the Loire in western Gaul. Strabo, citing Polybius, names it among the leading Gallic emporia, where merchants of Massalia were questioned about the sea route to Britain, a trade linked with Atlantic tin.

cora-people.s: The Cora, who call themselves Náayeri, are an indigenous people of the Sierra del Nayar in the Mexican state of Nayarit, speaking a Uto-Aztecan language. From their mountain stronghold at the Mesa del Nayar they resisted Spanish conquest for nearly two centuries, until it fell…

candi-agung.s: Candi Agung is the ruin of a brick temple at Amuntai in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, associated with the early kingdom of Negara Dipa described in the Hikayat Banjar. Only its brick foundations and some artefacts survive.

cartagena-colombia.s: Cartagena de Indias is a port city on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, founded by Pedro de Heredia in 1533. It was the main Spanish port of the New Kingdom of Granada, a stop of the treasure fleets and a leading market of the transatlantic slave trade, protected by massive…

choco-department.s: The Chocó is a region and department of western Colombia on the Pacific coast, covered by dense rainforest and among the wettest places on earth. In the colonial era its rivers yielded much of the gold, and also platinum, of the New Kingdom of Granada, worked by enslaved…

chitradurga.s: Chitradurga is a town in central Karnataka, India, known for its hill fortress with seven concentric rings of walls on granite hills. Edicts of Ashoka were found nearby.

chuson-ji.s: Chūson-ji is a Tendai Buddhist temple complex at Hiraizumi in Iwate prefecture, northern Japan. It was greatly expanded in the early 12th century by Fujiwara no Kiyohira, founder of the Northern Fujiwara, after the wars in Mutsu.

chihuahua-city.s: Chihuahua is a city in northern Mexico, capital of the state of the same name. It was founded in 1709 as a mining settlement after silver was found nearby, and became the chief town of the northern frontier, linked by the Camino Real to Santa Fe and Mexico City.

coahuiltecan.s: Coahuiltecans is the name given to many small groups of hunter-gatherers who lived in southern Texas and north-eastern Mexico, in present Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, before and during Spanish colonisation. They lived by gathering plants such as prickly pear and…

cotys-i-odrysian.s: Cotys I was king of the Odrysian kingdom of Thrace from 384 to 360 BCE. He strengthened royal power over the Thracian tribes and fought Athens for control of the Thracian Chersonese, although he had married his daughter to the Athenian general Iphicrates.

chapar.s: Chapar was a Mongol khan of the house of Ögedei and son of Kaidu, whom he succeeded as head of the Ögedeid khanate in Central Asia in the early 1300s. Together with the Chagatayid khan Duwa he made peace with the Yuan dynasty in 1304, but Duwa then turned against him.

creek-town.s: Creek Town is an Efik town on the Calabar River in Cross River State, south-eastern Nigeria. Founded in the 17th century, it was one of the trading towns, with Duke Town and Old Town, that Europeans called Old Calabar.

cross-river.s: The Cross River is a river of West Africa that rises in the highlands of western Cameroon and flows through south-eastern Nigeria to the Gulf of Guinea, entering the sea through a wide estuary near Calabar. Its basin was a busy route for the Atlantic slave trade and later the…

cross-river-state.s: Cross River State is a state in south-eastern Nigeria, bordering Cameroon, with its capital at Calabar. Created in 1967 as South-Eastern State, it took its present name in 1976 and lost its western part to the new Akwa Ibom State in 1987.

canning-award.s: The Canning Award was the 1861 arbitration by Lord Canning, Governor-General of India, of the succession dispute between the sons of Sayyid Said of Oman. It separated the Sultanate of Zanzibar under Majid bin Said from the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman under Thuwaini bin Said,…

charites.s: The Charites, or Graces, were goddesses of grace, beauty and festivity in Greek religion, usually three in number: Aglaia, Euphrosyne and Thalia. Their oldest and most famous cult was at Orchomenus in Boeotia, where they were worshipped as stones said to have fallen from the…

caernarfon.s: Caernarfon is a royal town on the Menai Strait in Gwynedd, north-west Wales. It grew beside the Roman fort of Segontium, and after the conquest of Wales Edward I built Caernarfon Castle there from 1283 as the seat of English government in North Wales.

castulo.s: Castulo was an ancient Iberian city in the upper Guadalquivir valley near Linares, in the province of Jaén, Spain, and the chief town of the Oretani. It controlled rich silver and lead mines of the Sierra Morena, and Hannibal's wife Himilce was said to come from there.

colorado-party-uruguay.s: The Colorado Party is one of Uruguay's two traditional parties, founded in 1836 by supporters of Fructuoso Rivera. Allied with the liberal and urban interests of Montevideo, it fought the Blancos in the Guerra Grande of 1839–1851 and held power almost continuously from 1865 to…

carhaix-plouguer.s: Carhaix-Plouguer is a town in central Brittany, in the department of Finistère. Under Roman rule it was Vorgium, the capital of the Osismii, a planned town with a grid of streets, public baths and a long aqueduct.

cotes-darmor.s: Côtes-d'Armor is a department of Brittany in north-western France, on the coast of the English Channel, with its prefecture at Saint-Brieuc. Created in 1790 as Côtes-du-Nord, it took its present name in 1990.

caracalla.s: Caracalla was Roman emperor from 198, jointly with his father Septimius Severus and then his brother Geta, and sole ruler from 211 to 217 after having Geta murdered. His Constitutio Antoniniana of 212 granted Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire, and…

cassiodorus.s: Cassiodorus was a Roman statesman and writer who served the Ostrogothic kings of Italy, holding high offices including praetorian prefect. His Variae preserve official letters of the Gothic court, and his lost History of the Goths was summarised by Jordanes.

cannes.s: Cannes is a city on the French Riviera, in the department of Alpes-Maritimes. In antiquity the area belonged to the Ligurian Oxybii, and in the Middle Ages it was a fishing village under the monks of the nearby Lérins Islands.

chaleion.s: Chaleion was an ancient Greek town of Ozolian Locris on the northern shore of the Gulf of Corinth, west of Delphi. It is known above all for a bronze tablet of the 5th century BCE recording its agreement with neighbouring Oeantheia on the seizure of property and the treatment…

christiaan-snouck-hurgronje.s: Christiaan Snouck Hurgronje was a Dutch scholar of Islam who lived in Mecca in 1885 and became adviser on native and Islamic affairs to the colonial government of the Dutch East Indies. In the Aceh War he urged the Dutch to win over the uleebalang chiefs, crush the religious…

cut-nyak-dhien.s: Cut Nyak Dhien was an Acehnese guerrilla leader in the Aceh War against the Dutch. After her first husband was killed in 1878 she married the commander Teuku Umar and fought beside him, and after his death in 1899 she led resistance in the forests for six more years.

critolaus-achaean-general.s: Critolaus was general of the Achaean League in 147–146 BCE and led it into war with Rome. He rejected Roman demands that Sparta, Corinth and other cities leave the league and stirred the people of Corinth against the Roman envoys.

capelianus.s: Capelianus was the Roman governor of Numidia who crushed the revolt of the Gordians in 238. Loyal to the emperor Maximinus Thrax, he marched the Third Legion Augusta on Carthage, defeated the hastily raised forces of the new emperors and killed Gordian II in battle, after…

chandrakanta-singha.s: Chandrakanta Singha was a king of the Ahom kingdom of Assam who reigned from 1811 to 1818 and again from 1819 to 1821, in a period of court intrigue and foreign intervention. Placed on the throne as a boy by the minister Purnananda Burhagohain, he was deposed by a rival…

claudius-gothicus.s: Claudius Gothicus, or Claudius II, was Roman emperor from 268 to 270, one of the soldier emperors of the third-century crisis. Soon after his accession he defeated an Alemannic army near Lake Garda, and around 269 he won a great victory over the Goths at Naissus, which earned…

crocus-alemannic-king.s: Crocus was an Alemannic king in Roman service in the early fourth century. According to the late Roman Epitome de Caesaribus, he accompanied the emperor Constantius I in Britain and helped bring about the proclamation of Constantius's son Constantine the Great as emperor at…

canillo.s: Canillo is one of the seven parishes of Andorra and the name of its main village, in the north-east of the principality along the upper valley of the Valira d'Orient. The largest parish by area, it includes the ski resort of Soldeu and the Romanesque church of Sant Joan de…

casa-de-la-vall.s: The Casa de la Vall is a stone manor house in Andorra la Vella, built in 1580 as the residence of the Busquets family and acquired in 1702 by the Consell General as its seat. It housed the Andorran parliament and court of justice until 2011, when the Consell General moved to a…

council-of-europe.s: The Council of Europe is an international organisation founded in 1949 by the Treaty of London to uphold human rights, democracy and the rule of law in Europe. Based in Strasbourg, it is distinct from the European Union and has 46 member states.

church-of-santa-coloma-andorra.s: The church of Santa Coloma is a pre-Romanesque and Romanesque church in the parish of Andorra la Vella, Andorra, first documented in the ninth century. It is noted for its rare round bell tower of the twelfth century.

chremonidean-war.s: The Chremonidean War (c. 267–261 BCE) was a conflict in which Athens, Sparta and their allies, backed by Ptolemy II of Egypt, tried to end Macedonian domination of Greece.

caterino-zeno.s: Caterino Zeno was a Venetian merchant and diplomat sent in 1471 as ambassador to the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan, whose wife Despina Khatun was the aunt of Zeno's wife. He worked for an alliance between Venice and Uzun Hasan against the Ottoman Empire and travelled to European…

convertibility-plan.s: The Convertibility Plan was the Argentine monetary system introduced in 1991 by President Carlos Menem's economy minister Domingo Cavallo, which fixed the peso at par with the US dollar and backed the money supply with reserves. It ended hyperinflation and drew foreign…

carlos-saavedra-lamas.s: Carlos Saavedra Lamas was an Argentine jurist and foreign minister from 1932 to 1938. He drafted an anti-war treaty signed by many American states in 1933 and helped mediate the end of the Chaco War between Bolivia and Paraguay, for which he received the Nobel Peace Prize in…

cesar-milstein.s: César Milstein was an Argentine biochemist who worked mainly at Cambridge in England. With Georges Köhler he developed in 1975 the hybridoma technique for producing monoclonal antibodies, now basic tools of medical diagnosis and treatment.

cristina-fernandez-de-kirchner.s: Cristina Fernández de Kirchner is an Argentine Peronist politician who succeeded her husband Néstor Kirchner as president, serving from 2007 to 2015, and was vice-president from 2019 to 2023. Her governments expanded social spending and nationalised the pension funds and the…

carlos-menem.s: Carlos Menem was an Argentine Peronist politician, governor of La Rioja, who served as president from 1989 to 1999. He ended hyperinflation by pegging the peso to the US dollar, privatised state companies, joined in founding Mercosur and pardoned the leaders of the military…

callicrates.s: Callicrates was an Athenian architect of the fifth century BCE who designed the Parthenon together with Ictinus in the building programme of Pericles. He is also credited with the small Ionic Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis and worked on the walls linking Athens to…

callicrates-of-leontion.s: Callicrates of Leontion was a statesman of the Achaean League who led its pro-Roman party in the second century BCE. After the Third Macedonian War he denounced his opponents to Rome, and about a thousand leading Achaeans, including the historian Polybius, were deported to…

carl-menger.s: Carl Menger was an Austrian economist whose Principles of Economics (1871) set out the theory of marginal utility, independently of William Stanley Jevons and Léon Walras. A professor at the University of Vienna and tutor to Crown Prince Rudolf, he founded the Austrian School…

chevalier-de-chaumont.s: Alexandre, Chevalier de Chaumont, was a French naval officer and diplomat who led Louis XIV's first embassy to King Narai of Ayutthaya in 1685. He was instructed to seek the king's conversion to Christianity, which Narai politely declined, but the embassy won privileges for…

constantine-phaulkon.s: Constantine Phaulkon was a Greek adventurer from Cephalonia who came to Ayutthaya with the English East India Company and became the chief minister of King Narai in the 1680s. He promoted close ties with France, which sent embassies and troops, arousing the hostility of…

chalca.s: The Chalca were the Nahuatl-speaking people of Chalco, a confederation of city-states in the south-eastern Valley of Mexico around Lake Chalco. After long wars they were conquered by the Mexica of Tenochtitlan in the mid-fifteenth century and paid tribute to the Aztec Triple…

codex-mendoza.s: The Codex Mendoza is an Aztec pictorial manuscript produced in Mexico City around 1541, probably for the viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, with Spanish glosses and commentary. It records the reigns and conquests of the Mexica rulers, the tribute owed by each province of the empire,…

charles-robin.s: Charles Robin was a Jersey merchant who founded a major cod-fishing business on the Gaspé coast of Quebec after the British conquest of New France. From his base at Paspébiac from 1766 he bought and dried fish caught by local fishermen and shipped it to markets in Europe and…

constitutions-of-king-john.s: The Constitutions of King John are the privileges of the Channel Islands traditionally said to have been granted by King John after the loss of Normandy in 1204. They are in fact known from the record of a royal inquiry held in 1248, which set out the islanders' rights, above…

chhoto-sona-mosque.s: The Chhoto Sona Mosque, the Small Golden Mosque, is a mosque at Shibganj in Chapai Nawabganj district, Bangladesh, on the site of the old city of Gaur. It was built during the reign of Alauddin Husain Shah, between 1493 and 1519, of brick faced with carved stone.

cadmea.s: The Cadmea was the citadel of ancient Thebes in Boeotia, named after the city's legendary founder Cadmus. It held the Mycenaean palace and later the city's chief public buildings.

corinna.s: Corinna was a lyric poet from Tanagra in Boeotia who wrote narrative poems on local myths in the Boeotian dialect. Ancient tradition made her a contemporary and rival of Pindar, said to have beaten him in competition and advised him on the use of myth, but many modern scholars…

charles-canning-1st-earl-canning.s: Charles Canning, 1st Earl Canning, was Governor-General of India from 1856 to 1862 and became the first Viceroy when the Crown took over from the East India Company in 1858. He governed during the rebellion of 1857, when his refusal to permit indiscriminate reprisals earned…

chauri-chaura-incident.s: The Chauri Chaura incident took place on 4 February 1922 at Chauri Chaura in the Gorakhpur district of the United Provinces of British India. After police fired on a procession of protesters, the crowd set fire to the police station, killing 22 policemen.

cripps-mission.s: The Cripps Mission was a British attempt in March and April 1942 to secure Indian cooperation in the Second World War. Sir Stafford Cripps offered India dominion status and an elected constitution-making body after the war, with the right of provinces to stay out.

council-of-india.s: The Council of India was a body in London that advised the Secretary of State for India from 1858 to 1937. Created by the Government of India Act 1858, it was made up mainly of men with long experience of India, and its approval was needed for spending from Indian revenues.

cosmas-indicopleustes.s: Cosmas Indicopleustes, 'the India-voyager', was a sixth-century merchant from Alexandria who travelled the Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade routes and later became a monk. His Christian Topography, written around 550, argued that the world was flat and shaped like the…

chares-of-athens.s: Chares was an Athenian general who held command many times in the mid-fourth century BCE. He fought in the Social War of 357–355 BCE against Athens' rebellious allies, led the Athenian fleet sent to relieve Byzantium when Philip II of Macedon besieged it in 340 BCE, and was…

constitution-act-1867.s: The Constitution Act, 1867, originally the British North America Act, is the act of the British Parliament that created the Dominion of Canada on 1 July 1867 by uniting Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the Province of Canada, divided into Ontario and Quebec. It set up a federal…

charles-best.s: Charles Best was an American-born Canadian medical scientist who, as a student assistant to Frederick Banting at the University of Toronto, helped isolate insulin in 1921–1922. The discovery transformed the treatment of diabetes.

craigellachie-british-columbia.s: Craigellachie is a place in Eagle Pass in the interior of British Columbia, Canada, where the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway was driven on 7 November 1885. The ceremony, performed by the railway's director Donald Smith, completed the line from Montreal to the…

canadian-red-ensign.s: The Canadian Red Ensign was a red flag with the Union Jack in the canton and the Canadian coat of arms in the fly, used as Canada's unofficial and later official national flag on land and at sea from the late nineteenth century. Canadian forces fought under it in the Second…

christoph-froschauer.s: Christoph Froschauer was a Bavarian-born printer who became the leading publisher of the Reformation in Zürich. In 1522 a meal of sausages in his house during Lent, defended by Zwingli, opened the break with Rome.

consensus-tigurinus.s: The Consensus Tigurinus was an agreement on the Lord's Supper concluded in 1549 between the churches of Zürich and Geneva, led by Heinrich Bullinger and John Calvin. By reconciling Zwingli's symbolic view with Calvin's doctrine of a spiritual presence, it united the Swiss…

constaffel.s: The Constaffel was the corporation of the nobility, knights, rentiers and leading merchants of Zürich, created by Rudolf Brun's constitution of 1336 alongside the craft guilds. It sent members to the city's Small and Large Councils and was the political home of the old…

charles-the-younger.s: Charles the Younger was the eldest son of Charlemagne and his queen Hildegard. Crowned king by Pope Leo III in Rome in 800, he led campaigns against the Saxons and Slavs and was assigned the Frankish heartlands in his father's planned division of the empire in 806.

council-of-aghuen.s: The Council of Aghuen was a church assembly convened around 488 by King Vachagan III the Pious of Caucasian Albania. Its canons, preserved in the History of the Country of Albania, regulated the organisation and discipline of the clergy, church dues, marriage and the relations…

carthaginian-iberia.s: Carthaginian Iberia was the territory in southern and eastern Spain ruled by Carthage under the Barcid family from 237 BCE, when Hamilcar Barca landed at Gades, until the Roman conquest in 206 BCE. Its silver mines and manpower rebuilt Carthaginian power after the First Punic…

catullus.s: Gaius Valerius Catullus was a Roman poet from Verona, active in the late Republic. His surviving collection of 116 poems includes love poems to a woman he called Lesbia, invective against public figures and learned poems modelled on Alexandrian Greek verse.

celtiberia.s: Celtiberia was the region of the eastern Meseta of central Spain inhabited by the Celtiberians, around the upper Douro and Tagus and the southern tributaries of the Ebro, roughly the modern provinces of Soria, Guadalajara, Zaragoza, Teruel and Cuenca. Its towns, among them…

clunia.s: Clunia was a town of the Arevaci and later one of the main Roman cities of the Spanish interior, on a plateau near Peñalba de Castro in the province of Burgos. Pompey took it in 72 BCE at the end of the Sertorian War.

chebar.s: The Chebar was a canal near Nippur in southern Babylonia, called the 'great canal' in cuneiform records of the Persian period. In the Book of Ezekiel the prophet lives among the Judean exiles settled by the Chebar and sees his visions there.

centennial-park-sydney.s: Centennial Park is a large public park in eastern Sydney, opened in 1888 to mark the centenary of the British colony of New South Wales. On 1 January 1901 the Commonwealth of Australia was proclaimed there and its first governor-general and ministry were sworn in, an event…

colombo-plan.s: The Colombo Plan is a regional organisation for economic and social development in Asia and the Pacific, conceived at a meeting of Commonwealth foreign ministers in Colombo in 1950 and launched in 1951. Australia was a leading founder, and under the plan thousands of Asian…

commonwealth-of-australia-constitution-a.s: The Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 is the British act, given royal assent on 9 July 1900, that united the six Australian colonies as the Commonwealth of Australia from 1 January 1901. It contains the Constitution of Australia, drafted at conventions in the…

congo-arab-war.s: The Congo Arab war was fought from 1892 to 1894 between the Congo Free State and the Swahili-Arab traders of the eastern Congo, whose power had been built by Tippu Tip. Free State columns under Francis Dhanis, aided by African allies, took the trading towns of Nyangwe and…

charles-the-good.s: Charles the Good was count of Flanders from 1119 until 1127. A son of King Canute IV of Denmark and Adela of Flanders, he was raised at the Flemish court and succeeded his cousin Baldwin VII.

council-of-flanders.s: The Council of Flanders was the high court and governing council of the County of Flanders, founded by Philip the Bold, duke of Burgundy, in 1386. Seated first at Lille and later at Ghent, it heard appeals and cases touching the count's rights and supervised local justice.

collegiate-church-of-saint-waltrude.s: The Collegiate Church of Saint Waltrude in Mons, Belgium, is a Brabantine Gothic church begun in 1450. It served the chapter of noble canonesses that grew out of the community founded by Saint Waltrude, patron of Mons, and that was among the greatest landowners in the County…

consistori-del-gai-saber.s: The Consistori del Gai Saber ('Consistory of the Gay Science') was a literary society founded in Toulouse in 1323 by seven citizens to preserve the poetry of the troubadours. It held a yearly poetry contest with prizes of golden flowers, the Jeux floraux, and its Leys d'amors…

chufut-kale.s: Chufut-Kale is a ruined cliff-top fortress town in the mountains of Crimea, a few kilometres east of Bakhchysarai. Known in the Middle Ages as Qırq Yer, it was the first seat of the Crimean khans before Bakhchysarai was built below it.

crimean-karaites.s: The Crimean Karaites are a Turkic-speaking community of the Karaite faith, a branch of Judaism that accepts the Hebrew Bible but rejects rabbinic tradition. Long settled in Crimea, they lived especially at Chufut-Kale near Bakhchysarai and in Feodosia and Yevpatoria, speaking…

catalan-atlas.s: The Catalan Atlas is a world map drawn on vellum leaves in Majorca around 1375, attributed to the Jewish cartographer Abraham Cresques. Combining the precise coastlines of nautical charts with information from travellers, it shows the Mediterranean, Africa and Asia, including…

charles-ii-of-naples.s: Charles II, called the Lame, was king of Naples from 1285 to 1309. A son of Charles I of Anjou, he was captured by Roger of Lauria in a naval battle in the Bay of Naples in 1284 during the War of the Sicilian Vespers and held by the Aragonese until 1288.

cortes-of-aragon.s: The Cortes of Aragon were the parliament of the Kingdom of Aragon, made up of four estates: the clergy, the great nobles, the knights and lesser nobles, and the towns. Kings had to summon them to obtain taxes and to make or change laws, and they defended the kingdom's fueros.

capitulations-of-santa-fe.s: The Capitulations of Santa Fe were the agreement signed on 17 April 1492 at Santa Fe, near Granada, between Isabella I and Ferdinand II and Christopher Columbus. They granted Columbus the title of Admiral of the Ocean Sea, the offices of viceroy and governor of any lands he…

complutensian-polyglot-bible.s: The Complutensian Polyglot Bible was the first printed polyglot edition of the whole Bible, prepared at the University of Alcalá, Latin Complutum, under the patronage of Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros. Printed in six volumes between 1514 and 1517 and issued in the…

council-of-castile.s: The Council of Castile was the chief governing council of the Crown of Castile, created by John I in 1385 and reorganised by Isabella I and Ferdinand II in 1480 with a majority of university-trained lawyers. It acted as supreme court and administrative body for justice and…

civic-forum.s: Civic Forum was the movement founded in Prague on 19 November 1989 by Václav Havel and other dissidents to lead the Velvet Revolution in the Czech lands, alongside Public Against Violence in Slovakia. It negotiated the end of communist rule and won the elections of June 1990.

comecon.s: Comecon, the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, was the economic organisation of the Soviet bloc, founded in Moscow in January 1949. It coordinated trade and planning among the Soviet Union, the East European communist states and later Mongolia, Cuba and Vietnam, largely…

czechoslovak-national-council.s: The Czechoslovak National Council was the organisation of the Czech and Slovak independence movement abroad, founded in Paris in 1916 with Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk as chairman, Edvard Beneš as secretary and Milan Rastislav Štefánik. Supported by the Czechoslovak Legions, it won…

czechoslovak-new-wave.s: The Czechoslovak New Wave was a movement of young film-makers in the 1960s, among them Miloš Forman, Věra Chytilová and Jiří Menzel. Using irony, improvisation and experiment, their films questioned the official culture of communist Czechoslovakia.

czechoslovak-peoples-army.s: The Czechoslovak People's Army was the name of the armed forces of communist Czechoslovakia from 1954 to 1990. Organised on the Soviet model and controlled by the Communist Party, it formed part of the Warsaw Pact's front line facing NATO.

carpathian-ruthenia.s: Carpathian Ruthenia is a region on the southern slopes of the Carpathian Mountains, part of the Kingdom of Hungary for centuries. Assigned to Czechoslovakia after the First World War as Subcarpathian Ruthenia, it remained its poorest province.

cenel-comgaill.s: The Cenél Comgaill were a kindred of Dál Riata in Cowal, in Argyll, named after Comgall, son of Domangart, a sixth-century king. Not counted among the three main kindreds in the Senchus fer nAlban, they appear in the annals as a separate group, and Conall mac Comgaill, who…

ciniod-i.s: Ciniod, son of Uuredech, was king of the Picts from 763 until his death in 775. The Irish annals record a battle in Fortriu, the Pictish heartland, between him and Áed Find of Dál Riata in 768.

conall-mac-comgaill.s: Conall mac Comgaill was a king of Dál Riata who died in 574. The Irish annals credit him with granting the island of Iona to Columba, who founded his monastery there in 563.

convention-of-druim-cett.s: The Convention of Druim Cett was an assembly held near Limavady in the north of Ireland, around 575 or perhaps later, at which the high king Áed mac Ainmuirech met Áedán mac Gabráin of Dál Riata in the presence of Columba. Recorded by Adomnán, it appears to have settled the…

cowal.s: Cowal is a peninsula in Argyll and Bute in western Scotland, between Loch Fyne and the Firth of Clyde, with Dunoon as its main town. In the early Middle Ages it was the land of the Cenél Comgaill, one of the kindreds of the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata, whose name the peninsula…

cain-adomnain.s: Cáin Adomnáin, the Law of the Innocents, was a law promulgated by Adomnán, abbot of Iona, at the Synod of Birr in Ireland in 697. Guaranteed by many kings and churchmen of Ireland and northern Britain, it sought to protect women, children and clergy from violence in war,…

charioteer-of-delphi.s: The Charioteer of Delphi is a life-size bronze statue of a chariot driver made around 475 BCE, part of a group dedicated at Delphi by Polyzalus, tyrant of Gela in Sicily, for a victory in the Pythian Games. Buried by a rock fall, it was found in 1896 and is one of the finest…

cleisthenes-of-sicyon.s: Cleisthenes was tyrant of Sicyon in the northern Peloponnese in the early sixth century BCE, of the Orthagorid family. He fought in the First Sacred War against Kirrha on behalf of Delphi and won the chariot race at the Pythian Games.

cercamon.s: Cercamon was one of the earliest troubadours, active in Aquitaine and Gascony around 1135–1145. A handful of his songs survive, including a lament on the death of Duke William X of Aquitaine in 1137.

chateau-de-chalus-chabrol.s: Châlus-Chabrol is a castle at Châlus in the Limousin, in west-central France. In March 1199 Richard the Lionheart, besieging it during a dispute with the viscount of Limoges, was struck in the shoulder by a crossbow bolt and died of the wound on 6 April.

council-of-charroux.s: The Council of Charroux was a church synod held in 989 at the abbey of Charroux in Poitou, convened by Archbishop Gunbald of Bordeaux. Its canons threatened excommunication for anyone who robbed churches, attacked unarmed clergy or seized the livestock of peasants and the poor.

charter-of-kortenberg.s: The Charter of Kortenberg was granted on 27 September 1312 by the dying Duke John II of Brabant to secure the succession of his young son. It set up a council of four knights and ten representatives of the towns, meeting every three weeks at Kortenberg, to supervise the…

christophe-plantin.s: Christophe Plantin was a French-born printer and publisher who settled in Antwerp in 1549 and built one of the largest printing businesses in Europe. His press, the Golden Compasses, produced the eight-volume Polyglot Bible for Philip II between 1568 and 1573, besides…

codex-manesse.s: The Codex Manesse is an illuminated songbook compiled in Zürich between about 1300 and 1340, probably for the Manesse family of patricians. It is the most comprehensive surviving collection of Middle High German love poetry, with about 6,000 stanzas by 140 poets, and its 137…

collegium-trilingue.s: The Collegium Trilingue, or College of the Three Languages, was founded at the University of Leuven in 1517 under the will of the humanist Jerome de Busleyden, with Erasmus as its guiding adviser. It offered free public teaching of Latin, Greek and Hebrew, the three languages…

coudenberg-palace.s: The Coudenberg Palace was the main residence of the dukes of Brabant and later of the Burgundian and Habsburg rulers in Brussels, standing on the Coudenberg hill above the lower town. Enlarged by Philip the Good and Charles V, it was where Charles V abdicated in 1555.

council-of-brabant.s: The Council of Brabant was the highest court of justice and chief administrative council of the Duchy of Brabant, organised as a professional body under Philip the Good of Burgundy in the 1430s and headed by a chancellor. Sitting in Brussels, it guarded the privileges of the…

catholicon-breton-dictionary.s: The Catholicon is a Breton–French–Latin dictionary compiled in 1464 by Jehan Lagadeuc, a cleric of the diocese of Tréguier, and printed at Tréguier in 1499. It is the first dictionary of the Breton language and one of the earliest dictionaries to include French, and it is a…

charles-of-blois.s: Charles of Blois was a French nobleman, nephew of King Philip VI, who claimed the Duchy of Brittany by right of his wife Joan of Penthièvre. Backed by France in the War of the Breton Succession against John of Montfort, he was captured by the English in 1347 and held in London…

chateaubriant.s: Châteaubriant is a town in the Loire-Atlantique department of western France, on the old border between Brittany and Anjou. Its castle, begun in the eleventh century and enlarged with a Renaissance palace by Jean de Laval in the sixteenth, was one of the fortresses guarding…

clisson.s: Clisson is a town in the Loire-Atlantique department of western France, on the Sèvre Nantaise south-east of Nantes. Its castle, seat of the powerful Clisson family whose best-known member was the constable Olivier de Clisson, guarded the frontier between Brittany and Poitou.

claude-of-france.s: Claude of France was the eldest daughter of Louis XII and Anne of Brittany, and from 1514 duchess of Brittany. Married in 1514 to Francis of Angoulême, who became Francis I in 1515, she was queen of France until her death in 1524.

combat-of-the-thirty.s: The Combat of the Thirty was an arranged fight on 26 March 1351, during the War of the Breton Succession, between thirty knights and squires from each side. Champions of Charles of Blois led by Jean de Beaumanoir met men of the Anglo-Breton garrison of Ploërmel under Robert…

conan-i-of-brittany.s: Conan I, Count of Rennes, was the first of the house of Rennes to claim the rule of all Brittany, taking the ducal title in about 990 after seizing Nantes. His rivalry with Fulk Nerra of Anjou, protector of the counts of Nantes, ended at the Battle of Conquereuil in 992, where…

conan-ii-duke-of-brittany.s: Conan II was duke of Brittany from 1040 to 1066, the son of Alan III. He ruled under the guardianship of his uncle Eudes until the 1050s and then fought rebellious nobles and the Normans; William of Normandy's campaign against him in 1064 is shown on the Bayeux Tapestry.

conan-iv-duke-of-brittany.s: Conan IV was duke of Brittany from 1156 to 1166 and earl of Richmond in England. Under pressure from Henry II of England, he gave up power in 1166 and betrothed his daughter and heiress Constance to Henry's son Geoffrey, bringing Brittany into the Angevin sphere.

capetian-house-of-burgundy.s: The Capetian House of Burgundy was a branch of the French royal dynasty founded by Robert I, a younger son of King Robert II, who received the Duchy of Burgundy from his brother Henry I in 1032. Its dukes ruled from Dijon until Philip I died without heirs in 1361, after which…

charterhouse-of-champmol.s: The Charterhouse of Champmol was a Carthusian monastery outside Dijon, founded in 1383 by Philip the Bold as the burial place of the Valois dukes of Burgundy. The dukes commissioned works there from Claus Sluter, Melchior Broederlam and Jean de Marville, including the ducal…

claus-sluter.s: Claus Sluter was a Dutch sculptor from Haarlem who worked in Dijon from 1385 for Duke Philip the Bold of Burgundy. His figures for the portal of the Charterhouse of Champmol and the Well of Moses, with their weight, movement and realistic faces, broke with the elegant…

clos-de-vougeot.s: The Clos de Vougeot is a walled vineyard of about 50 hectares in the Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, created by the monks of Cîteaux Abbey from the early twelfth century. Its château, with medieval cellars and a Renaissance building, is the seat of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du…

chateau-salins.s: Château-Salins is a small town in the Moselle department of north-eastern France, in the Seille valley. It grew up around a castle built in the fourteenth century to protect salt springs, and its saltworks were one of the sources of revenue of the dukes of Lorraine.

claude-lorrain.s: Claude Lorrain, born Claude Gellée at Chamagne in the Duchy of Lorraine, was a landscape painter who spent nearly all his career in Rome. His idealised views of the Roman countryside and of harbours bathed in golden light became the model of the classical landscape.

cross-of-lorraine.s: The Cross of Lorraine is a cross with two horizontal bars, originally the Cross of Anjou, which René II brought into use as an emblem of the dukes of Lorraine in the later fifteenth century. It became the symbol of the region of Lorraine and, during the Second World War, of…

charles-borromeo.s: Charles Borromeo was archbishop of Milan from 1564 and a leading figure of the Counter-Reformation. A nephew of Pope Pius IV, he helped bring the Council of Trent to its close and then enforced its decrees in his large diocese through synods, visitations, seminaries and strict…

council-of-italy.s: The Council of Italy was a council of the Spanish monarchy, created under Philip II in the 1550s to advise the king on the government of his Italian possessions: the Duchy of Milan and the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily. Sitting in Madrid, it dealt with appointments, finance,…

consuetudines-et-iusticie.s: The Consuetudines et Iusticie is a record of the rights of the duke of Normandy, drawn up from an inquest held at Caen in July 1091 by Robert Curthose and William Rufus, based on the customs believed to have held under William the Conqueror. It restricted private war, castle…

college-of-cardinals.s: The College of Cardinals is the body of senior clergy of the Catholic Church who advise the pope and, since a decree of 1059, elect a new pope in conclave. Its members are appointed by the pope and hold the rank of cardinal bishop, priest or deacon, many of them heading…

canute-vi-of-denmark.s: Canute VI was king of Denmark from 1182 to 1202, the son of Valdemar I. With his adviser Archbishop Absalon he extended Danish power along the southern Baltic, forcing the Pomeranian duke Bogislaw I to become his vassal in 1185.

croy-tapestry.s: The Croÿ Tapestry is a large tapestry made in 1554 by Peter Heymans for Duke Philip I of Pomerania. It shows Martin Luther preaching before the families of the dukes of Pomerania and the electors of Saxony, celebrating their marriage alliance and Protestant faith.

charles-emmanuel-ii-duke-of-savoy.n: Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy
charles-emmanuel-ii-duke-of-savoy.s: Charles Emmanuel II was duke of Savoy from 1638 to 1675, succeeding as a child under the regency of his mother Christine of France, who remained influential until her death in 1663. His reign saw the massacre of the Waldensians in 1655, known as the Piedmontese Easter, and…

charles-emmanuel-iii-of-sardinia.s: Charles Emmanuel III was duke of Savoy and king of Sardinia from 1730, when his father Victor Amadeus II abdicated, until 1773. He fought in the Wars of the Polish and Austrian Succession, gaining Novara and Tortona in 1738 and further districts of Lombardy in 1748 after the…

christine-of-france.s: Christine of France, daughter of Henry IV and Marie de' Medici, married Victor Amadeus I of Savoy in 1619. After his death in 1637 she ruled as regent for her young sons and faced a civil war in 1639–1642 against her brothers-in-law Cardinal Maurice and Prince Thomas, who were…

county-of-geneva.s: The County of Geneva was a feudal county in the region around Geneva and Annecy, whose counts held the lands about the city from the eleventh century while the city itself was ruled by its bishop. In 1401 Amadeus VIII of Savoy bought the county, known as the Genevois, from the…

chapel-of-the-holy-shroud.s: The Chapel of the Holy Shroud is a baroque chapel in Turin, between the cathedral and the royal palace, built to house the Shroud of Turin. Designed by Guarino Guarini from 1668 and completed in 1694, it is crowned by a dome of stacked arches rising in a cone.

chateau-de-ripaille.s: The Château de Ripaille is a castle and former priory near Thonon-les-Bains on the southern shore of Lake Geneva, in Savoy. The house of Savoy built a residence there in the late fourteenth century, and in 1434 Duke Amadeus VIII retired to it with a small group of knights,…

communist-party-of-indonesia.s: The Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI) grew out of the Indies Social Democratic Association founded in 1914 and took the name Communist Party of the Indies in 1920, one of the first communist parties in Asia. It was banned after its failed uprisings of 1926–1927.

cornelis-van-vollenhoven.s: Cornelis van Vollenhoven was a Dutch legal scholar at Leiden University who founded the systematic study of adat, the customary law of the peoples of the Dutch East Indies. He divided the archipelago into nineteen adat law areas and argued that colonial government should…

council-of-troubles.s: The Council of Troubles was a special tribunal set up in 1567 by the Duke of Alba, governor of the Habsburg Netherlands for Philip II, to punish those involved in the iconoclastic riots and resistance of 1566. Called the Council of Blood by its victims, it condemned more than…

clear-script.s: The Clear script (todo bichig) is an alphabet created in 1648 by the Oirat monk Zaya Pandita, adapted from the traditional Mongolian script to write the Oirat language more exactly. It added marks that distinguished vowels and consonants left ambiguous by the older script.

central-secretariat.s: The Zhongshu Sheng, or Secretariat, was one of the central organs of government in imperial China. It developed from the third century as the office that drafted imperial edicts, and under the Sui and Tang it formed, with the Chancellery and the Department of State Affairs,…

charles-iii-philip-elector-palatine.s: Charles III Philip was Elector Palatine from 1716 to 1742, the last ruler of the Neuburg line. Before his accession he fought the Ottomans as an imperial general and governed Tyrol for the Habsburgs.

conrad-count-palatine-of-the-rhine.n: Conrad, Count Palatine of the Rhine
conrad-count-palatine-of-the-rhine.s: Conrad of Hohenstaufen was count palatine of the Rhine from 1156 until his death in 1195, a half-brother of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. He built up a territorial base around Heidelberg, Alzey and the lower Neckar, laying the foundation of the later Electoral Palatinate.

church-of-the-holy-spirit-heidelberg.n: Church of the Holy Spirit, Heidelberg
church-of-the-holy-spirit-heidelberg.s: The Church of the Holy Spirit is the main church of Heidelberg's old town, built in Gothic style from 1398 and the burial place of several electors palatine. Its galleries once housed the Bibliotheca Palatina.

capitulation-of-wittenberg.s: The Capitulation of Wittenberg of 19 May 1547 was the settlement imposed by Emperor Charles V on the captive Elector John Frederick I of Saxony after the Battle of Mühlberg. John Frederick surrendered the electoral title and much of his territory, including Wittenberg, to his…

corpus-evangelicorum.s: The Corpus Evangelicorum was the body of the Protestant estates at the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire, formally constituted in 1653 under the Peace of Westphalia, which allowed religious questions to be settled by agreement between the Protestant and Catholic bodies…

comares-palace.s: The Comares Palace is the official part of the Nasrid palaces of the Alhambra in Granada, built mainly under Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the fourteenth century. It is arranged around the Court of the Myrtles with its long pool and dominated by the Comares Tower, which houses the…

court-of-the-myrtles.s: The Court of the Myrtles (Patio de los Arrayanes) is the central courtyard of the Comares Palace in the Alhambra, Granada, built mainly in the reign of Yusuf I in the fourteenth century. A long rectangular pool flanked by hedges of myrtle reflects the Comares Tower and the…

chaldia.s: Chaldia was a mountainous region of north-eastern Anatolia inland from Trebizond, around present-day Gümüşhane, named after the ancient Chaldoi. Under Byzantium it became a military province (theme) in the ninth century, with Trebizond as its capital.

carians.s: The Carians were the native people of Caria in south-western Asia Minor, speaking an Anatolian language related to Luwian and written in their own alphabet. Greek writers described them as early inhabitants of the Aegean coasts and islands, and they served widely as…

chersiphron.s: Chersiphron of Knossos was a Cretan architect of the sixth century BCE who, with his son Metagenes, designed and began the archaic Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the first great marble temples of the Ionic order. Vitruvius records the devices they invented to haul its…

cimmerians.s: The Cimmerians were a nomadic people from the steppe north of the Black Sea who invaded Anatolia in the eighth and seventh centuries BCE; Assyrian records call them Gimirri. They overran Phrygia, killed the Lydian king Gyges in the mid-seventh century and raided the Greek…

chernorizets-hrabar.s: Chernorizets Hrabar was a Bulgarian monk and writer of the late 9th or early 10th century, associated with the literary circle of Preslav. His treatise On the Letters defends the Slavonic alphabet created by Cyril against those who held that only Hebrew, Greek and Latin were…

clement-of-ohrid.s: Clement of Ohrid (c. 840–916) was a Slavonic scholar and bishop, one of the disciples of Cyril and Methodius expelled from Moravia in 885–886.

constantine-iv.s: Constantine IV (c. 650–685) was Byzantine emperor from 668 to 685.

constantine-vi.s: Constantine VI (771–c. 797) was Byzantine emperor from 780 to 797, at first under the regency of his mother Irene.

constantine-of-preslav.s: Constantine of Preslav was a Bulgarian writer and churchman of the late 9th and early 10th centuries, a pupil of Methodius and one of the leading figures of the Preslav literary school under Simeon I. He composed the Didactic Gospel, a cycle of sermons, and the Alphabetical…

cosmas-the-priest.s: Cosmas the Priest was a Bulgarian churchman of the 10th century and author of the Sermon against the Heretics, the main source on the early Bogomils. Written probably in the later 10th century, it condemns Bogomil teachings while also criticising lax clergy and describing the…

council-of-preslav.s: The Council of Preslav was an assembly of Bulgarian nobles and clergy held at Preslav in 893. Summoned by the former ruler Boris I, it confirmed the deposition of his son Vladimir-Rasate, who had tried to restore paganism, and placed his younger son Simeon I on the throne.

chararic.s: Chararic was a Frankish king of the late 5th and early 6th centuries who ruled a small kingdom in northern Gaul. Gregory of Tours relates that he stood aside in Clovis I's war against Syagrius, and that Clovis later captured him and his son, had them tonsured as clergy and…

claudius-silvanus.s: Claudius Silvanus (died 355) was a Roman general of Frankish descent, commander of the infantry in Gaul under Constantius II. Accused of plotting against the emperor through forged letters, he had himself proclaimed emperor at Cologne in August 355.

carl-philipp-emanuel-bach.s: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach (1714–1788) was a German composer, the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach. After almost thirty years as harpsichordist to Frederick the Great in Berlin, he succeeded Telemann in 1768 as director of music of Hamburg's five main churches.

chilehaus.s: The Chilehaus is a ten-storey office building in Hamburg's Kontorhaus District, built in 1922–1924 to designs by Fritz Höger for the shipowner Henry Sloman, who had made his fortune in Chilean saltpetre. Its pointed eastern end, resembling a ship's bow, made it a landmark of…

cuxhaven.s: Cuxhaven is a port town in Lower Saxony, Germany, at the mouth of the Elbe on the North Sea. It grew around Ritzebüttel castle, which belonged to Hamburg from 1394 and served as the city's outpost at the river mouth.

chasseurs-d-afrique.s: The Chasseurs d'Afrique were light cavalry regiments of the French Armée d'Afrique, first raised in Algeria in 1831 and recruited mainly from Frenchmen and European settlers. They fought in the conquest of Algeria, the Crimean War, the French intervention in Mexico and both…

cfa-franc.s: The CFA franc is the name of two currencies used in West and Central Africa, created by France in December 1945 for its African colonies. After independence it survived as the West African CFA franc and the Central African CFA franc, each issued by a regional central bank,…

charles-jacques-poncet.s: Charles-Jacques Poncet was a French physician working in Cairo who travelled through the Funj Sultanate to Ethiopia in 1698–1700 to treat the emperor Iyasu I. His account of the journey, published in 1704, gives one of the few European eyewitness descriptions of Sennar at the…

complex-of-koguryo-tombs.s: The Complex of Koguryo Tombs is a group of more than thirty tombs of the Goguryeo kingdom near Pyongyang and Nampo in North Korea, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. Many contain wall paintings of daily life, hunting, processions, guardian animals and constellations.

capital-cities-and-tombs-of-the-ancient-.n: Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom
capital-cities-and-tombs-of-the-ancient-.s: The Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in north-eastern China, inscribed in 2004. It covers the mountain fortresses of Wunü Mountain and Hwando, the walled city of Gungnae and some forty royal and noble tombs around Huanren…

cheongju.s: Cheongju is the capital of North Chungcheong province in central South Korea. In 1377 the Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, was printed at Heungdeoksa temple there, and the city's Early Printing Museum stands on the temple site.

cheontae.s: Cheontae is the Korean form of the Tiantai school of Buddhism, which centres on the Lotus Sutra. It was established as a separate order in Goryeo in 1097 by the monk Uicheon, who sought to reconcile doctrinal study with meditation and to unite the competing Buddhist schools.

choe-chung.s: Choe Chung was a Confucian scholar and chief minister of the Korean kingdom of Goryeo. After retiring from office around 1055 he founded a private academy in Kaegyong, the first of twelve such academies that prepared aristocratic sons for the civil service examinations.

choe-chung-heon.s: Choe Chung-heon was a Korean general who seized power in Goryeo in 1196 and founded a military house that ruled the kingdom for four generations. He deposed two kings, ruled through his own Directorate General for Policy Formulation and private guards, and left the kings as…

choe-mu-seon.s: Choe Mu-seon was a Korean inventor and military commander of the late Goryeo period. Having learned the making of gunpowder from a Chinese merchant, he persuaded the court to found an office for firearms in 1377 and developed cannon and other gunpowder weapons.

choe-seung-ro.s: Choe Seung-ro was a Confucian scholar and statesman of the Korean kingdom of Goryeo. In 982 he presented King Seongjong with a memorial of twenty-eight points on government, urging rule according to Confucian principles, limits on Buddhist expenditure and the sending of…

choe-yeong.s: Choe Yeong was a Korean general of the late Goryeo period, celebrated for his victories over the Red Turban rebels and Japanese pirates and for his incorruptibility. As chief minister under King U he ordered the expedition against Ming forces in Liaodong in 1388.

chungnyeol-of-goryeo.s: Chungnyeol of Goryeo was king of Goryeo from 1274 to 1298 and again from 1298 to 1308. As crown prince he married a daughter of Kublai Khan, making the Goryeo kings imperial sons-in-law of the Yuan dynasty.

constitution-of-cucuta.s: The Constitution of Cúcuta was the constitution of Gran Colombia, adopted by the Congress of Cúcuta in 1821. It created a centralised republic joining Venezuela, New Granada and later Quito, with a president and vice-president elected indirectly for four years, a two-chamber…

crown-of-the-kingdom-of-poland.n: Crown of the Kingdom of Poland
crown-of-the-kingdom-of-poland.s: The Crown of the Kingdom of Poland was the term for the Polish state as a whole, distinct from the person of the king, which developed in the fourteenth century. After the Union of Lublin in 1569 it denoted the Polish part of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, as opposed to…

court-of-justice-of-the-european-union.n: Court of Justice of the European Union
court-of-justice-of-the-european-union.s: The Court of Justice of the European Union is the judicial institution of the European Union, seated in Luxembourg. It began in 1952 as the Court of Justice of the European Coal and Steel Community and became the court of the European Communities.

christina-of-lorraine.s: Christina of Lorraine was a granddaughter of Catherine de' Medici who married Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, in 1589, a match that balanced Spanish influence with ties to France. After the early death of her son Cosimo II she shared the regency for her…

cosimo-iii-de-medici.s: Cosimo III de' Medici was Grand Duke of Tuscany from 1670 to 1723, the longest reign of the dynasty. Deeply pious, he imposed strict religious and moral regulation, including laws against Jews and against sexual offences, while the economy stagnated and taxes rose.

chandela-dynasty.s: The Chandela dynasty ruled the Bundelkhand region of central India from the ninth to the thirteenth century, first as feudatories of the Gurjara-Pratiharas and from the tenth century independently. Their capital was Khajuraho, where they built the famous temple complex, and…

chaturbhuj-temple-gwalior.s: The Chaturbhuj Temple is a small rock-cut Vishnu temple in Gwalior Fort, dedicated in 876 CE under the Pratihara king Mihira Bhoja by Alla, the commander of the fort. Its inscriptions record land grants and gardens, and the zero written in one of them, in the number 270, is…

christoph-willibald-gluck.s: Christoph Willibald Gluck was a German-born composer who worked for much of his career in Vienna for the Habsburg court. With the librettist Ranieri de' Calzabigi he wrote Orfeo ed Euridice of 1762 and Alceste of 1767, reforming opera seria by subordinating virtuoso display to…

carmelites.s: The Carmelites are a Catholic religious order that began among hermits on Mount Carmel in the Holy Land in the late twelfth century and moved to Europe as the crusader states declined. In sixteenth-century Spain Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross led a reform that returned…

council-of-trent.s: The Council of Trent was the ecumenical council of the Catholic Church that met at Trent in northern Italy in three periods between 1545 and 1563. In response to the Reformation it reaffirmed Catholic doctrine on scripture and tradition, justification and the seven sacraments,…

council-of-aragon.s: The Council of Aragon was the royal council that advised the Spanish monarchs on the government of the Crown of Aragon, comprising Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands. Created by Ferdinand II in 1494, it sat at the royal court and handled appointments, justice…

cai-lun.s: Cai Lun was a Chinese court eunuch of the Eastern Han dynasty who, as director of the imperial workshops, presented an improved method of making paper to Emperor He in 105 CE. His paper was made from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets, cheaper than silk and lighter…

confederation-of-cologne.s: The Confederation of Cologne was an alliance formed in Cologne in November 1367 by Hanseatic and Dutch towns against Valdemar IV of Denmark, joined by Holstein, Mecklenburg and Swedish nobles. Its fleets ravaged the Danish and Norwegian coasts and took Copenhagen in 1368.

charibael.s: Charibael was a king of the Himyarites and Sabaeans in south Arabia in the 1st century CE, known from the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. The Periplus says he ruled from Saphar, the Himyarite capital Zafar, and kept friendly relations with the Roman emperors through frequent…

calahorra.s: Calahorra is a town in La Rioja, northern Spain, above the Ebro valley, known in Roman times as Calagurris. It held out for Sertorius in a famine-stricken siege that ended in 72 BCE and later became a Roman municipium.

centcelles.s: Centcelles is a Roman villa near Constantí, close to Tarragona in Catalonia, whose 4th-century domed hall preserves one of the oldest surviving Christian dome mosaics, with hunting and biblical scenes. The hall may have been the mausoleum of the emperor Constans, who was…

constans-i.s: Constans I was a Roman emperor, the youngest son of Constantine the Great, who ruled from 337 to 350. After defeating his brother Constantine II in 340 he controlled the whole western empire, campaigning against the Franks in 341–342 and visiting Britain in 343.

chennakeshava-temple-somanathapura.s: The Chennakeshava Temple at Somanathapura, near Mysore, is a Vaishnava temple built in the 13th century by Somanatha, a general of the Hoysala king Narasimha III. Raised on a star-shaped platform with three shrines, it is among the most complete examples of Hoysala architecture.

chinchaysuyu.s: Chinchaysuyu was the north-western and most populous of the four quarters of the Inca Empire, stretching from Cusco through the central Andes and coast of Peru into Ecuador and southern Colombia. It included the former Chimú kingdom and the northern cities of Tumebamba and Quito.

cuntisuyu.s: Cuntisuyu was the south-western quarter of the Inca Empire, reaching from Cusco to the Pacific coast of southern Peru. It was one of the four suyus into which the Incas divided their realm, each governed by a high official.

chalcuchimac.s: Chalcuchímac was one of the leading generals of the Inca ruler Atahualpa in the civil war against his brother Huáscar. With Quizquiz he defeated Huáscar's army near Cusco in 1532 and captured him.

coricancha.s: The Coricancha was the most important temple of the Inca Empire, in Cusco, dedicated chiefly to the sun god Inti. Its walls of finely fitted stone were covered with sheets of gold, which the Spaniards stripped in 1533.

cusco.s: Cusco is a city in the Andes of southern Peru, about 3,400 metres above sea level, which was the capital of the Inca Empire. Its palaces and temples, including the Coricancha, were rebuilt by the Spaniards after 1533 on Inca foundations, and the fortress-shrine of Sacsayhuamán…

condolence-ceremony.s: The Condolence Ceremony is the central ritual of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, held to mourn a dead chief and to raise up his successor. Set down in the Great Law of Peace, it includes words of comfort that wipe away grief, a recital of the founding chiefs' titles…

cayuga-people.s: The Cayuga are an Iroquoian people, one of the five original nations of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, whose homeland lay around Cayuga Lake in the Finger Lakes region of New York. They held ten of the fifty chiefly titles in the confederacy's Grand Council.

constitution-of-the-united-states.s: The Constitution of the United States was drafted by the Philadelphia Convention in 1787, ratified in 1788 and in force from 1789. It replaced the Articles of Confederation with a federal government divided into legislative, executive and judicial branches, each checking the…

cornelis-matelief-de-jonge.s: Cornelis Matelief de Jonge was a Dutch admiral of the Dutch East India Company (VOC). In 1606, in alliance with the sultan of Johor, he besieged Portuguese Malacca, but failed to take it and fought an indecisive battle with a Portuguese fleet off Cape Rachado.

choe-je-u.s: Choe Je-u was a Korean religious teacher from Gyeongju who founded the Donghak ('Eastern Learning') movement in 1860. After a religious experience he preached a faith drawing on Confucian, Buddhist, Daoist and folk traditions, offered as a Korean answer to the 'Western…

council-of-liubech.s: The Council of Liubech was a meeting of the princes of Kievan Rus' held in 1097 at Liubech on the Dnieper. To end their feuds and unite against the Cumans, the princes, among them Sviatopolk II of Kiev and Vladimir Monomakh, agreed that each should hold his father's patrimony.

charles-gasyonga-ii.s: Charles Gasyonga II was the last Omugabe, or king, of Ankole, succeeding Kahaya II in 1944. His reign saw the late-colonial rivalry between Bahima and Bairu and between Protestant and Catholic factions.

church-of-st-trophime.s: The Church of St. Trophime is a former cathedral in Arles, Provence, dedicated to Trophimus, traditionally the first bishop of Arles.

chronicle-of-albelda.s: The Chronicle of Albelda is a Latin chronicle compiled at the court of Alfonso III of Asturias around 881–883, named after the monastery of Albelda in La Rioja, where a copy was made. It combines a description of Spain with lists of Roman, Visigothic and Asturian kings and a…

chronicle-of-alfonso-iii.s: The Chronicle of Alfonso III is a Latin chronicle written at the court of Alfonso III of Asturias in the late ninth century, surviving in two versions. Continuing Isidore of Seville's history of the Goths, it covers the kings from Wamba in 672 to the death of Ordoño I in 866.

cross-of-the-angels.s: The Cross of the Angels is a jewelled cross of gold, gems and cameos given by Alfonso II of Asturias to the cathedral of Oviedo in 808. A legend says it was made by angels disguised as pilgrims.

cross-of-victory.s: The Cross of Victory is a jewelled processional cross given by Alfonso III of Asturias and Queen Jimena to the cathedral of Oviedo in 908. Its oak core is said by tradition to be the cross carried by Pelagius at the Battle of Covadonga, and it is covered with gold, enamels and…

catholic-university-of-leuven.s: The Catholic University of Leuven was founded by the Belgian bishops in 1834 and settled in Leuven in 1835, taking up the tradition of the medieval University of Leuven of 1425. Disputes between Dutch- and French-speakers came to a head in 1968, when the university was split…

charles-bridge.s: Charles Bridge is a stone bridge across the Vltava in Prague, linking the Old Town with the Lesser Town. Begun in 1357 under Charles IV to replace the flood-damaged Judith Bridge and completed in the early fifteenth century, it was built under the direction of Peter Parler.

charles-university.s: Charles University in Prague was founded by Charles IV in 1348, the first university in Central Europe. In the early fifteenth century it was a centre of the Hussite movement, and the Decree of Kutná Hora of 1409 gave the Czech nation control, prompting German masters to leave.

compacts-of-basel.s: The Compacts of Basel were an agreement between the Council of Basel and the moderate Hussites of Bohemia and Moravia, proclaimed at Jihlava in 1436. They allowed communion in both kinds, bread and wine, to the laity in the Czech lands, making the Utraquist church the first to…

chwezi.s: The Chwezi are the semi-divine rulers of the kingdom of Kitara in the traditions of western Uganda and neighbouring regions, said to have succeeded the Batembuzi and then to have vanished. They are linked with large earthwork sites such as Bigo bya Mugenyi, probably of the…

cortes-of-castile.s: The Cortes of Castile were the representative assembly of the kingdom, made up of the clergy, nobles and representatives of the towns. Rooted in royal councils that admitted townsmen from the late twelfth century, they voted taxes, swore allegiance to heirs and presented…

council-of-burgos.s: The Council of Burgos was a church council held in 1080 under Alfonso VI of León and Castile, with a papal legate present. It decided to replace the old Hispanic or Mozarabic liturgy with the Roman rite in the king's lands, in line with the reforms of Pope Gregory VII and the…

cotonou.s: Cotonou is the largest city and economic capital of Benin, on the coast between Lake Nokoué and the Atlantic. In the nineteenth century it was a small trading post of the Kingdom of Dahomey, and disputes over treaties by which Dahomey had ceded it to France led to the First…

christopher-ii-of-denmark.s: Christopher II was King of Denmark from 1320 to 1326 and again from 1329 to 1332. Forced to accept a harsh coronation charter, he lost control of the kingdom to the nobles and to the counts of Holstein, to whom most of the realm was pawned.

cambridge.s: Cambridge is a city in eastern England on the River Cam, home to the University of Cambridge, the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world, founded around 1209 by scholars leaving Oxford. Its colleges trained clergy, officials and scientists, among them Isaac…

christopher-marlowe.s: Christopher Marlowe was an English playwright and poet of the Elizabethan age whose plays Tamburlaine, Doctor Faustus, The Jew of Malta and Edward II established blank verse as the main form of English drama. Educated at Cambridge, he was linked to government secret service…

constantine-ii-of-scotland.s: Constantine II was king of Alba, the kingdom that became Scotland, from about 900 to 943, one of the longest reigns of early Scottish kings. He submitted to Æthelstan of England at Eamont Bridge in 927 but joined the coalition defeated by Æthelstan at the Battle of Brunanburh…

charles-alexandre-de-calonne.s: Charles Alexandre de Calonne was a French statesman who served as Louis XVI's controller-general of finances from 1783 to 1787. Faced with a growing deficit, he proposed a general land tax paid by all landowners, including the privileged, and summoned an Assembly of Notables…

canal-du-midi.s: The Canal du Midi is a canal in southern France linking Toulouse to the Mediterranean at Sète, which together with the Garonne connects the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Designed by Pierre-Paul Riquet and backed by Colbert and Louis XIV, it was built between 1666 and 1681…

concordat-of-bologna.s: The Concordat of Bologna was an agreement made in 1516 between Francis I of France and Pope Leo X after the French victory at Marignano. It gave the French king the right to nominate bishops, abbots and other senior clergy in his kingdom, while the pope received the first…

chormaqan.s: Chormaqan was a Mongol general who led the conquest of Iran and the Caucasus for the Great Khan Ögedei. Sent in 1230 against the Khwarazmian ruler Jalal al-Din, he drove him out of north-western Iran, and from 1236 his armies overran Georgia and Armenia, forcing Queen Rusudan…

council-of-ruisi-urbnisi.s: The Council of Ruisi-Urbnisi was a church council held in 1103 in Georgia, called by King David IV. It removed hostile bishops tied to the great nobles, restored church discipline and condemned the Monophysite doctrine, affirming Georgian Orthodoxy.

charles-cornwallis-1st-marquess-cornwall.s: Charles Cornwallis was a British army officer and administrator. As a general in the American War of Independence he was besieged by American and French forces at Yorktown, and his surrender in October 1781 effectively ended the war.

charles-edward-stuart.s: Charles Edward Stuart, known as Bonnie Prince Charlie or the Young Pretender, was the elder son of James Francis Edward Stuart and the Jacobite claimant to the British throne. In 1745 he landed in Scotland, raised the Highland clans, took Edinburgh and advanced to Derby before…

church-of-scotland.s: The Church of Scotland, known as the Kirk, is Scotland's national church, Presbyterian in government and Reformed in doctrine. It emerged from the Scottish Reformation of 1560 led by John Knox and, after long conflict with the Stuart kings over bishops, was confirmed as…

central-greece.s: Central Greece, in Greek Sterea Ellada, is the historical and geographical region of mainland Greece north of the Gulf of Corinth and south of Thessaly and Epirus, including Attica and Boeotia in traditional usage. It was one of the main areas of the Greek War of Independence,…

charilaos-trikoupis.s: Charilaos Trikoupis was a Greek statesman who served as Prime Minister seven times between 1875 and 1895. In 1875 he established the principle that the king must appoint governments with the confidence of parliament.

corinth-canal.s: The Corinth Canal is a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece, connecting the Gulf of Corinth with the Saronic Gulf and separating the Peloponnese from the mainland. Projects to cut it date back to antiquity, including Nero's attempt in 67 CE.

castell-y-bere.s: Castell y Bere is a ruined Welsh castle in Gwynedd, north-west Wales, built by Llywelyn the Great from about 1221 to secure the southern border of his lands. Standing on a rocky ridge in the Dysynni valley, it was one of the largest castles of the Welsh princes.

cistercians.s: The Cistercians are a Catholic monastic order founded at Cîteaux in Burgundy in 1098 to follow the Rule of Saint Benedict more strictly. Under Bernard of Clairvaux the order spread across Europe, building remote abbeys and developing large farming estates worked by lay brothers.

clynnog-fawr.s: Clynnog Fawr is a village on the north coast of the Llŷn peninsula in Gwynedd, Wales, associated with Saint Beuno, who founded a monastery there in the seventh century. Its clas church was one of the most important churches of medieval Gwynedd and a stopping place for pilgrims…

chosroid-dynasty.s: The Chosroid dynasty was the royal house of Iberia (Kartli) in eastern Georgia from the early fourth century, when Mirian III took the throne, until the Persians abolished the monarchy around 580. Of Iranian origin, it presided over Iberia's conversion to Christianity and…

catholicate-of-abkhazia.s: The Catholicate of Abkhazia was the autocephalous church of western Georgia, headed by a catholicos who resided at Bichvinta (Pitsunda) and later at Gelati near Kutaisi. It took shape in the medieval kingdom of Abkhazia and continued under the kingdom of Imereti and its vassal…

confederate-ireland.s: Confederate Ireland was the self-governing Irish Catholic government established in 1642, during the Irish Confederate Wars, with its seat at Kilkenny. Led by a general assembly and a supreme council of Catholic nobles, gentry and clergy, it controlled most of Ireland and…

cattle-acts.s: The Cattle Acts were laws passed by the English Parliament in 1663 and 1667 that first restricted and then banned the import of Irish cattle, sheep and pigs into England, to protect English landowners. They struck at Ireland's main export trade, which turned instead to salted…

church-of-ireland.s: The Church of Ireland is the Anglican church in Ireland. After the Reformation it became the established state church, though most of the population remained Catholic, and it held the ancient cathedrals and parish revenues, including tithes paid by Catholics.

college-green.s: College Green is a square in the centre of Dublin, in front of Trinity College. The Parliament House built there from 1729 to designs by Edward Lovett Pearce housed the Irish Parliament from 1731 until the Act of Union of 1800, and later became a branch of the Bank of Ireland.

covenanters.s: The Covenanters were Scottish Presbyterians who bound themselves by the National Covenant of 1638 and the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643 to defend their church against royal religious policy. Their revolt against Charles I began the Wars of the Three Kingdoms, and a…

church-of-the-holy-sepulchre.s: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in the Old City of Jerusalem stands on the site that Christian tradition holds to be the place of Jesus's crucifixion and burial. First built under Constantine the Great in the 4th century, it was destroyed on the orders of the Fatimid caliph…

cluniac-reforms.s: The Cluniac Reforms were a movement of monastic renewal centred on the Benedictine abbey of Cluny in Burgundy, founded in 910. Cluny answered directly to the pope, and its elaborate liturgy and network of dependent priories spread across Latin Europe.

candaules.s: Candaules was the last king of the Heraclid dynasty of Lydia, killed around 680 BCE by Gyges, who founded the Mermnad dynasty. Herodotus tells how Candaules, proud of his wife's beauty, made his bodyguard Gyges see her naked, and how the queen then forced Gyges to kill the…

cearl-of-mercia.s: Cearl was a king of the Mercians in the early 7th century and the first Mercian ruler named by Bede. Bede records that his daughter Cwenburh married Edwin of Northumbria while Edwin was in exile, and that she bore him two sons.

cenwalh-of-wessex.s: Cenwalh was king of Wessex from about 642 to 672. He repudiated his wife, a sister of Penda of Mercia, and was driven into exile by Penda, spending about three years at the court of East Anglia, where he was baptised.

ceolred-of-mercia.s: Ceolred was king of Mercia from 709 to 716, the son of Æthelred. He fought Ine of Wessex at Woden's Barrow in 715.

ceolwulf-ii-of-mercia.s: Ceolwulf II was king of Mercia from 874 to about 879, installed by the Great Heathen Army after Burgred fled. In 877 the Vikings divided Mercia, settling the eastern part and leaving him the west.

clofesho.s: Clofesho was the meeting place of a series of church councils of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in the 8th and early 9th centuries, held under Mercian kings and the archbishops of Canterbury. The councils issued canons on church discipline and settled disputes over monastic lands.

coenwulf-of-mercia.s: Coenwulf was king of Mercia from 796 to 821, a distant kinsman of Offa. He crushed a revolt in Kent in 798, captured its leader Eadberht Præn and later made his own brother king there, keeping Mercia the strongest of the English kingdoms.

castel-nuovo.s: Castel Nuovo is a castle on the harbour of Naples, begun in 1279 by Charles I of Anjou when he moved the capital from Palermo. It was rebuilt in the fifteenth century by Alfonso V of Aragon, whose triumphal entrance arch, celebrating his entry into the city in 1443, is among…

charles-iii-of-naples.s: Charles III of Naples (1345–1386), known as Charles of Durazzo, was a member of the Angevin dynasty. With Hungarian support and the backing of Pope Urban VI he overthrew his cousin Joanna I in 1381 and became king of Naples, and she was killed in 1382.

camino-frances.s: The Camino Francés is the principal route of the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela, crossing the Pyrenees at Roncesvalles and running through Pamplona, Puente la Reina, Burgos and León to Galicia. It developed from the eleventh century with the support of the kings of…

catherine-of-navarre.s: Catherine of Navarre (1468–1517), also called Catherine of Foix, was queen of Navarre from 1483 until her death. She ruled jointly with her husband John III of Albret, and their reign was troubled by the rival ambitions of France and Castile.

charles-prince-of-viana.s: Charles, Prince of Viana (1421–1461), was the son of Blanche I of Navarre and John II of Aragon and the rightful heir to Navarre. His father's refusal to yield the crown led to a civil war in which the Beaumontese supported Charles and the Agramontese his father.

chandra-shumsher-jang-bahadur-rana.s: Chandra Shumsher Jang Bahadur Rana (1863–1929) was the hereditary Rana prime minister of Nepal from 1901 to 1929. He built the Singha Durbar palace, founded Tri-Chandra College, supported Britain in the First World War and obtained the treaty of 1923 in which Britain formally…

chaubisi-rajya.s: The Chaubisi Rajya ("twenty-four kingdoms") were a group of small hill principalities in the Gandaki basin of west-central Nepal, among them Lamjung, Tanahun, Kaski and Palpa, ruled mostly by Thakuri dynasties. With the Baise Rajya ("twenty-two kingdoms") of the Karnali region…

caedmon.s: Cædmon was a cowherd at the monastery of Whitby under Abbess Hild who, according to Bede, received the gift of composing religious verse in a dream. His nine-line hymn on the Creation, preserved in manuscripts of Bede's Ecclesiastical History, is among the earliest recorded…

ceolfrith.s: Ceolfrith (c. 642–716) was abbot of the twin monastery of Wearmouth–Jarrow from 688 and the teacher of Bede.

chalybes.s: The Chalybes were an ancient people of the southern Black Sea coast of north-eastern Anatolia, between the Halys river and Colchis. Greek writers from Herodotus and Xenophon onwards described them as ironworkers, and their name became linked with steel: the Greek word for…

comana-pontica.s: Comana Pontica was an ancient temple city on the Iris river (Yeşilırmak) in Pontus, near modern Tokat in Turkey. It was the seat of the goddess Ma, whose high priest ruled a large temple estate worked, according to Strabo, by more than 6,000 temple slaves.

cius.s: Cius (Kios) was an ancient Greek city on the Gulf of Cius in the Sea of Marmara, at the site of modern Gemlik in Turkey. In the fourth century BCE it was ruled by a family of Persian origin, ancestors of the kings of Pontus.
