cotyora.s: Cotyora (Kotyora) was an ancient Greek colony of Sinope on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Anatolia, near modern Ordu in Turkey. Xenophon's Ten Thousand rested there in 400 BCE on their march home.

cape-bojador.s: Cape Bojador is a headland on the Atlantic coast of Western Sahara, south of the Canary Islands. Its shoals, currents and winds made medieval European sailors fear that ships could not return from beyond it.

cortes-of-coimbra-1385.s: The Cortes of Coimbra was the assembly of clergy, nobles and town representatives that met at Coimbra in March and April 1385, during the succession crisis after the death of Ferdinand I. Persuaded by the jurist João das Regras, it rejected the claims of Beatrice and her…

cortes-of-leiria-1254.s: The Cortes of Leiria, summoned by King Afonso III in 1254, is the first Portuguese Cortes known to have included representatives of the towns alongside the clergy and nobility. Meeting at Leiria in central Portugal, it marked the beginning of the three-estate Cortes, which…

cadwgan-ap-bleddyn.s: Cadwgan ap Bleddyn was a prince of Powys, son of Bleddyn ap Cynfyn. He fought the Normans in Wales from the 1090s and, with his brothers Iorwerth and Maredudd, was drawn into the conflicts of the March and the rebellion of Robert of Bellême in 1102.

canu-llywarch-hen.s: Canu Llywarch Hen is a cycle of early Welsh poems in englyn metre, probably composed in the ninth or tenth century and preserved mainly in the Red Book of Hergest. In them the aged Llywarch Hen laments the sons he urged to their deaths in battle, and much of it is set in Powys.

cynddelw-brydydd-mawr.s: Cynddelw Brydydd Mawr ('the Great Poet') was one of the foremost Welsh court poets of the twelfth century. He was poet to Madog ap Maredudd of Powys, for whom he wrote praise poems and an elegy, and later composed for Owain Gwynedd, the Lord Rhys and other princes.

coup-of-rucunshu.s: The Coup of Rucunshu was a succession struggle at the Rwandan court in late 1896. After the death of Kigeli IV Rwabugiri, his chosen heir Mibambwe IV Rutarindwa was attacked at Rucunshu by the faction of the queen mother Kanjogera and her brothers, and died with many of his…

cyirima-ii-rujugira.s: Cyirima II Rujugira was a king (mwami) of Rwanda in the eighteenth century, whose exact dates are uncertain. Court tradition credits him with defending the kingdom against Burundi, Gisaka and Ndorwa and with stationing permanent armies on the frontiers, a step in the growth of…

charles-i-of-england.s: Charles I was King of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1625 to 1649. His attempt to impose a new prayer book on Scotland in 1637 provoked the National Covenant and the Bishops' Wars, which forced him to recall the English Parliament and led to the civil wars of the 1640s.

charles-ii-duke-of-lorraine.s: Charles II was Duke of Lorraine from 1390 to 1431. An energetic ruler, he allied with the dukes of Burgundy against the Armagnac party in France, and in 1429 Joan of Arc visited him at Nancy.

charles-ii-elector-palatine.s: Charles II was Elector Palatine from 1680 to 1685, the last of the Protestant Simmern line. On his childless death the electorate passed to the Catholic Philip William of Neuburg, while Louis XIV claimed part of the inheritance for Charles's sister Elizabeth Charlotte, Duchess…

college-of-justice.s: The College of Justice is the body of judges and lawyers of Scotland's supreme courts, founded by James V in 1532 with funds from the Scottish church approved by the pope. Its core is the Court of Session, the supreme civil court, whose judges are styled senators of the…

cumberland.s: Cumberland is a historic county in north-west England, between the Solway Firth and the Lake District, with Carlisle as its chief town. Once part of the British kingdom of Strathclyde, it was disputed between Scottish and English kings: David I of Scotland held it during the…

clan-douglas.s: Clan Douglas was a Scottish noble family whose fortune was made by Sir James Douglas, the companion of Robert the Bruce. The earls of Douglas, created in 1358, became the most powerful magnates in late medieval Scotland, dominating the Borders and often the royal government.

chiaramonte-family.s: The Chiaramonte were a Sicilian baronial family, counts of Modica, who became one of the most powerful houses of the island under the Aragonese kings of Sicily in the fourteenth century. They built the Palazzo Chiaramonte, known as the Steri, in Palermo.

carl-linnaeus.s: Carl Linnaeus was a Swedish botanist, physician and zoologist, professor at Uppsala University, who formalised the modern system of naming and classifying living things. His Systema Naturae of 1735 set out a hierarchical classification of nature, and his Species Plantarum of…

carl-xvi-gustaf.s: Carl XVI Gustaf has been King of Sweden since 15 September 1973, succeeding his grandfather Gustaf VI Adolf. The Instrument of Government of 1974 left him a purely ceremonial head of state without political powers, and a change in the law in 1980 made his elder daughter, Crown…

craig-phadrig.s: Craig Phadrig is a hillfort on a wooded hill on the western edge of Inverness in the Scottish Highlands. Its stone ramparts were built in the Iron Age and later burned so fiercely that the stone fused, making it a vitrified fort.

cavustepe.s: Çavuştepe is the site of a Urartian fortress about 25 kilometres south-east of Van in eastern Turkey, known in antiquity as Sardurihinili after its founder, Sarduri II, in the eighth century BCE. Built along a narrow rocky ridge, it has an upper and a lower citadel with…

ceawlin-of-wessex.s: Ceawlin was a king of the West Saxons in the later sixth century, listed by Bede as the second of the kings who held authority over the southern English. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle credits him with victories over the Britons, notably at Dyrham in 577, which brought Gloucester,…

charford.s: Charford is a place on the River Avon in Hampshire, south of Salisbury, usually identified with Cerdicesford, meaning Cerdic's ford. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that Cerdic and his son Cynric fought the Britons there in 519 and took the kingdom, an event treated as the…

chippenham.s: Chippenham is a market town in Wiltshire, south-west England, on the Bristol Avon. It was a royal estate of the West Saxon kings, and in January 878 the Danes under Guthrum seized it in a surprise winter attack that drove Alfred the Great into the marshes of Athelney.

cuthred-of-wessex.s: Cuthred was king of Wessex from 740 to 756. For much of his reign he was subordinate to Æthelbald of Mercia, alongside whom he fought the Welsh, but in 752 he defeated Æthelbald at Burford and briefly freed Wessex from Mercian domination.

cynegils.s: Cynegils was king of the West Saxons from about 611 to about 642. In 635 he was baptised by Bishop Birinus at Dorchester-on-Thames, with King Oswald of Northumbria as his godfather, making him the first Christian king of Wessex.

cynewulf-of-wessex.s: Cynewulf was king of Wessex from 757 to 786, coming to power after the deposition of Sigeberht. He fought the Welsh and was defeated by Offa of Mercia at Bensington in 779, losing lands north of the Thames.

calw.s: Calw is a town in the northern Black Forest in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, on the River Nagold. Seat of the medieval counts of Calw, it later prospered from the timber trade and from the cloth and dyeing business of the Calw trading company.

corfu-declaration.s: The Corfu Declaration was an agreement signed on 20 July 1917 on the Greek island of Corfu by the Serbian government in exile under Nikola Pašić and the Yugoslav Committee under Ante Trumbić. It proposed a single kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes under the Serbian…

cretan-koinon.s: The Cretan Koinon was a federation of the city-states of Crete formed in the Hellenistic period and attested from the late third century BCE. It provided a common assembly and a court for disputes between cities, though rivalries, especially between Knossos and Gortyn, often…

camadevivamsa.s: The Camadevivamsa is a Pali chronicle written by the monk Bodhiramsi in Chiang Mai, probably in the early 15th century. It tells the legendary history of Queen Camadevi and the founding of Haripunjaya, the Mon kingdom at Lamphun that preceded Lan Na, and of the Buddhist relics…

chu-nom.s: Chữ Nôm is a script for writing the Vietnamese language, built from Chinese characters and new characters formed on their model. Used from about the 13th century until the early 20th, it carried a rich vernacular literature, including Nguyễn Du's Tale of Kiều, alongside…

culavamsa.s: The Culavamsa is a Pali chronicle of Sri Lanka continuing the Mahavamsa, compiled in stages by Buddhist monks from the 13th century onwards. It covers the island's history from the 4th century CE to the British conquest of Kandy in 1815, recording the deeds of kings, their…

cathay.s: Cathay is the medieval European name for northern China, derived from the Khitan, the people who ruled the Liao dynasty. The name passed through Central Asian forms such as Khitay and was popularised in Europe by Marco Polo; it survives in the Russian name for China, Kitai.

congo-people-liberia.s: In Liberia, Congo people, or Congoes, were the Africans freed from slave ships by the United States Navy and settled in Liberia in the 19th century, many of them originally taken from the Congo region. They merged largely with the Americo-Liberian elite, and in Liberian usage…

censorius.s: Censorius was a Roman count (comes) of the 5th century, sent as an envoy to the Suebi in Hispania in the 430s. In 440 the Suebic king Rechila besieged him at Myrtilis (Mértola) in Lusitania and forced his surrender, a sign of the collapse of imperial control in the province.

conimbriga.s: Conimbriga is the site of a Roman town near Condeixa-a-Nova, south of Coimbra in central Portugal. A pre-Roman settlement that flourished under the empire, it gained baths, a forum and houses with fine mosaics, and in the late Roman period was enclosed by a new wall that cut…

caceres.s: Cáceres is a city of Extremadura in western Spain. The Roman colony of Norba Caesarina was founded there in the 1st century BCE, in the province of Lusitania.

coptic-pope-of-alexandria.s: The Coptic Pope of Alexandria is the patriarch and head of the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Miaphysite church of Egypt that separated from the Chalcedonian church after 451. The patriarchs consecrated the bishops of the Christian kingdoms of Nubia and the metropolitans of…

conference-of-rulers.s: The Conference of Rulers is the council of the nine hereditary Malay rulers and the governors of the other four states of Malaysia. Its rulers elect the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, the king, and his deputy for five-year terms, in a rotation among the nine royal houses.

czech-silesia.s: Czech Silesia is the part of the historical region of Silesia that lies in the Czech Republic, around Opava and Ostrava. It descends from the small part of Silesia that the Habsburgs kept after Prussia conquered most of the region in 1742, ruled as Austrian Silesia until 1918.

code-of-305-articles.s: The Code of 305 Articles was the law code of the Kingdom of Madagascar, promulgated in 1881 under Queen Ranavalona II and the prime minister Rainilaiarivony. It combined Merina customary law with new rules on government, criminal justice, education and Christian morality, and…

cantarell-field.s: The Cantarell Field is a supergiant offshore oil field in the Bay of Campeche, off the coast of Mexico. Named after the fisherman Rudesindo Cantarell, who reported an oil seep in the area, it began production in 1979 and peaked in 2004 as one of the most productive fields in…

carlos-fuentes.s: Carlos Fuentes was a Mexican novelist and essayist, a leading figure of the Latin American literary boom of the 1960s. His novels, including Where the Air Is Clear, The Death of Artemio Cruz and Terra Nostra, explore Mexican history and identity after the Revolution.

carlos-salinas-de-gortari.s: Carlos Salinas de Gortari was president of Mexico from 1988 to 1994 for the Institutional Revolutionary Party, after an election widely accused of fraud. He privatised state companies, reformed the land-tenure provisions of the constitution and negotiated the North American…

constitutionalist-army.s: The Constitutionalist Army was the force raised in 1913 by Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, to restore constitutional government after Victoriano Huerta's coup. Under commanders such as Álvaro Obregón and Pancho Villa it defeated Huerta in 1914, and after the split…

cristero-war.s: The Cristero War (1926–1929) was an armed uprising in central and western Mexico against the anticlerical laws of President Plutarco Elías Calles. Catholic rebels, the Cristeros, fought federal troops chiefly in Jalisco, Michoacán and neighbouring states, and tens of thousands…

communist-party-of-burma.s: The Communist Party of Burma, founded in 1939, took part in the resistance to Japan within the Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League but went underground in March 1948 and began an armed revolt against the government. Backed by China from the late 1960s, it held large areas…

coxs-bazar.s: Cox's Bazar is a town and district on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, near the border with Myanmar, known for its long sandy beach on the Bay of Bengal. It is named after Hiram Cox, an officer of the East India Company who resettled Arakanese refugees there in the 1790s.

cyclone-nargis.s: Cyclone Nargis was a tropical cyclone that struck Myanmar on 2–3 May 2008, driving a storm surge across the Irrawaddy delta. About 138,000 people were killed or went missing, the worst natural disaster in the country's recorded history.

claus-von-stauffenberg.s: Claus von Stauffenberg was a German army officer who led the 20 July plot of 1944 against Hitler. Badly wounded in North Africa, he became chief of staff of the Replacement Army and placed a bomb in a briefcase at a conference at Hitler's Wolf's Lair headquarters in East Prussia.

condor-legion.s: The Condor Legion was a unit of German air and ground forces sent by Hitler to fight for Franco's Nationalists in the Spanish Civil War. Made up mainly of Luftwaffe aircraft and crews, it gained combat experience and tested new tactics and aircraft, and its bombing of the…

cajuns.s: The Cajuns are a people of southern Louisiana in the United States, descended mainly from Acadians deported by the British from Nova Scotia after 1755. Many exiles settled in Spanish Louisiana from the 1760s, and their descendants kept a distinct French dialect, the Catholic…

cardinal-richelieu.s: Cardinal Richelieu was a French clergyman and statesman who was chief minister of Louis XIII from 1624 until his death. He strengthened royal power by ending the political independence of the Huguenots at La Rochelle in 1628 and curbing the nobility, and brought France into…

carignan-salieres-regiment.s: The Carignan-Salières Regiment was a French infantry regiment sent by Louis XIV to New France in 1665, the first regular troops in the colony. Its roughly 1,200 men built forts along the Richelieu River and in 1666 burned Mohawk villages, forcing the Iroquois to make peace in…

company-of-one-hundred-associates.s: The Company of One Hundred Associates was a French trading company created by Cardinal Richelieu in 1627 and given ownership of New France and a monopoly of the fur trade, in return for bringing out settlers. The capture of its first fleet and of Quebec by the Kirke brothers…

custom-of-paris.s: The Custom of Paris was the body of customary law of the region of Paris, first written down in 1510 and revised in 1580. Made the civil law of New France in 1664, it governed property, inheritance, marriage and the seigneurial system in Canada, survived the British conquest…

carlos-de-siguenza-y-gongora.s: Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora was a Mexican scholar, poet and priest, one of the leading intellectuals of New Spain. A professor of mathematics at the Royal University of Mexico, he wrote on astronomy, history and geography, rejected astrological views of comets, collected…

caxcanes.s: The Caxcanes were an indigenous people of what are now the Mexican states of Zacatecas and Jalisco, in the region the Spaniards called New Galicia. They led the Mixtón War of 1540–1542, the largest rising against Spanish rule in western Mexico, which Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza…

chichimeca-war.s: The Chichimeca War was a long conflict between Spanish colonists and the nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples of northern Mexico known collectively as Chichimecas. Sparked by the opening of the Zacatecas silver mines, it centred on raids along the road between Mexico City and the…

congress-of-chilpancingo.s: The Congress of Chilpancingo, or Congress of Anáhuac, was the first independent legislative assembly of Mexico, convened by José María Morelos at Chilpancingo in September 1813. It formally declared independence from Spain in November 1813 and, after moving under royalist…

christchurch.s: Christchurch is the largest city of New Zealand's South Island, founded in 1850 by the Canterbury Association as an Anglican settlement on the Canterbury Plains. It grew as the commercial centre of a rich farming region.

christchurch-mosque-shootings.s: The Christchurch mosque shootings were terrorist attacks on 15 March 2019, when an Australian white supremacist killed 51 people at the Al Noor Mosque and the Linwood Islamic Centre in Christchurch, New Zealand. Within a month Jacinda Ardern's government banned most…

christchurch-call.s: The Christchurch Call is an international initiative launched in Paris in May 2019 by New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and French President Emmanuel Macron after the Christchurch mosque shootings, which had been livestreamed online. Governments and technology…

christopher-luxon.s: Christopher Luxon is a New Zealand politician and former businessman who became Prime Minister in November 2023. A former chief executive of Air New Zealand, he entered Parliament in 2020 and became leader of the National Party in 2021.

covid-19-pandemic.s: The COVID-19 pandemic was a global outbreak of the disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, first identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. Declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization in March 2020, it caused millions of deaths, lockdowns and border closures…

charles-rigault-de-genouilly.s: Charles Rigault de Genouilly was a French admiral who commanded the Franco-Spanish expedition against Vietnam in 1858. He attacked Da Nang in September 1858 and, when the campaign there stalled, sailed south and captured Saigon in February 1859, the first step in the French…

church-of-the-transfiguration-on-ilyina-.n: Church of the Transfiguration on Ilyina Street
church-of-the-transfiguration-on-ilyina-.s: The Church of the Transfiguration on Ilyina Street is a medieval church on the Trade Side of Veliky Novgorod, Russia, built in 1374. It contains the only surviving frescoes securely attributed to Theophanes the Greek, painted in 1378, whose expressive, almost monochrome…

cabyle.s: Cabyle was an ancient Thracian town on the Tundzha River near present-day Yambol in south-eastern Bulgaria. Philip II of Macedon took it around 341 BCE and settled colonists there, and it later served as a residence and mint of Thracian rulers in the Hellenistic period.

cersobleptes.s: Cersobleptes was a son of Cotys I and the most powerful of the three kings among whom the Odrysian Kingdom was divided in 360 BCE, ruling its eastern part. Aided by the mercenary commander Charidemus, he contested the Thracian Chersonese with Athens before ceding it.

charyapada.s: The Charyapada is a collection of mystical songs by Buddhist poets of the Vajrayana and Sahajiya traditions, usually dated between the eighth and twelfth centuries. A manuscript was discovered in the royal library of Nepal in 1907 by the scholar Haraprasad Shastri.

carlo-maderno.s: Carlo Maderno was an architect from the Swiss–Italian borderland who worked in Rome and helped create the Baroque style. His facade for the church of Santa Susanna was among the first Baroque church fronts, and for Pope Paul V he lengthened the nave of St Peter's Basilica and…

castel-santangelo.s: Castel Sant'Angelo is a fortress in Rome on the right bank of the Tiber, built in the second century as the mausoleum of the emperor Hadrian. Converted into a fortress in late antiquity, it was linked to the Vatican by a fortified corridor and served the popes as a citadel,…

colonna-family.s: The Colonna family is a Roman noble family prominent in the politics of Rome and the papacy from the twelfth century. Long rivals of the Orsini, they produced Pope Martin V, elected in 1417 to end the Great Western Schism, as well as many cardinals and commanders, among them…

constitutio-romana.s: The Constitutio Romana was an agreement issued in 824 by the Frankish co-emperor Lothair I with Pope Eugene II. It placed the government of Rome under joint papal and imperial supervision, created imperial envoys to oversee papal officials, and required each newly elected pope…

chinese-peoples-political-consultative-c.s: The Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference is a political advisory body of the People's Republic of China, bringing together the Communist Party, the minor parties and other groups under the party's leadership. Its first session in September 1949 acted as a…

common-program.s: The Common Program was the provisional constitution of the People's Republic of China, adopted by the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference on 29 September 1949. It defined the new state as a people's democratic dictatorship led by the working class and set out a…

constantin-francois-de-hoensbroeck.s: Constantin-François de Hoensbroeck was prince-bishop of Liège from 1784 to 1792. His conservative rule and a dispute over gaming houses at Spa led to the Liège Revolution of August 1789, which drove him from the city.

consell-de-cent.s: The Consell de Cent ('Council of One Hundred') was the governing council of the city of Barcelona from the 1260s until 1714. Representing citizens, merchants and craftsmen, it ran the city's finances and defence and founded the Taula de Canvi in 1401; it was abolished by the…

capitulation-of-pedralbes.s: The Capitulation of Pedralbes was the agreement of October 1472 by which Barcelona surrendered to King John II of Aragon after a long siege, ending the Catalan Civil War of 1462–1472. The king granted a general pardon and confirmed the constitutions of Catalonia.

catalan-courts.s: The Catalan Courts were the parliament of the Principality of Catalonia, made up of three estates: clergy, nobility and royal towns. Formalised under Peter III, who in 1283 promised to summon them yearly, they passed laws together with the king and voted taxes, until they were…

consulate-of-the-sea.s: The Consolat de Mar is a collection of maritime customs and laws compiled in Catalan, probably in Barcelona in the fourteenth century, and printed in 1484. Used by the sea consulates of the Crown of Aragon, it covered shipping, trade and prize law and was widely followed…

corpus-de-sang.s: The Corpus de Sang ('Bloody Corpus') was the riot of 7 June 1640 in Barcelona, when reapers and townspeople, angered by the billeting of royal troops, killed the viceroy, the Count of Santa Coloma. It began the Reapers' War, the Catalan revolt against Philip IV of Spain.

cervera.s: Cervera is a town in the province of Lleida in Catalonia, Spain. The Catalan Courts met there several times, and in 1717 Philip V closed the other Catalan universities and founded a single university at Cervera, which lasted until it moved to Barcelona in 1842.

council-of-princes.s: The Council of Princes was one of the three colleges of the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire, beside the electors and the imperial cities. It gave individual votes to ecclesiastical and secular princes, and a seat in it required a territory held directly from the…

carte-romaneasca-de-invatatura.s: Carte românească de învățătură ('Romanian book of instruction') is a law code issued in Iași in 1646 by Prince Vasile Lupu of Moldavia. Drawing on Byzantine law, it was one of the first law codes printed in Romanian.

constantine-mavrocordatos.s: Constantine Mavrocordatos was a Phanariot Greek who ruled Wallachia and Moldavia many times between 1730 and 1769. He reformed taxation and administration and abolished serfdom in Wallachia in 1746 and in Moldavia in 1749.

chakrayudha.s: Chakrayudha was a king of Kannauj of the Ayudha dynasty around 800, installed by the Pala emperor Dharmapala in place of his rival Indrayudha. As a Pala client he submitted to the Rashtrakuta emperor Govinda III during his northern campaign.

casbah-of-algiers.s: The Casbah of Algiers is the old walled town of Algiers, rising on a steep hill above the harbour and crowned by the citadel built in the Ottoman period. Its maze of narrow streets, houses, palaces and mosques dates largely from the time of the Regency, when it was the seat of…

carnival-of-oruro.s: The Carnival of Oruro is an annual religious and folk festival in the Bolivian mining city of Oruro, held before Lent in honour of the Virgin of the Mineshaft (Virgen del Socavón). Lasting several days, it combines Andean and Catholic traditions in processions of thousands of…

chapare-province.s: Chapare is a province of the Cochabamba Department of Bolivia, in the humid tropical lowlands at the foot of the Andes. From the 1980s many former tin miners and highland farmers settled there to grow coca, and it became the main source of coca for the cocaine trade.

che-guevara.s: Ernesto 'Che' Guevara was an Argentine-born Marxist revolutionary, a leader of the Cuban Revolution with Fidel Castro and later a minister in Cuba. Seeking to spread guerrilla war, he fought in the Congo and in 1966 went to Bolivia, where his small band failed to win peasant…

cochabamba-water-war.s: The Cochabamba Water War was a series of protests in the Bolivian city of Cochabamba from December 1999 to April 2000 against the privatisation of the municipal water supply. The concession had been given to Aguas del Tunari, a consortium led by the US company Bechtel, and…

chilean-civil-code.s: The Chilean Civil Code, drafted by Andrés Bello and promulgated in December 1855, came into force in 1857. Drawing on Roman law, Spanish legislation and the French Napoleonic Code, it regulated persons, property, contracts and inheritance in clear, systematic language.

carlos-ibanez-del-campo.s: Carlos Ibáñez del Campo was a Chilean army officer who dominated politics after the military interventions of 1924–1925 and ruled as an authoritarian president from 1927 to 1931. His regime built public works but collapsed under the impact of the Great Depression.

chanarcillo.s: Chañarcillo is a former silver-mining district in the Atacama region of northern Chile, south of Copiapó. Its rich deposits, discovered in 1832, set off a silver rush that made it one of the most productive silver mines in the Americas for several decades.

chicago-boys.s: The Chicago Boys were Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago, many through an exchange programme with the Catholic University of Chile begun in the 1950s. From the mid-1970s they directed economic policy under the military regime of Augusto Pinochet, cutting…

chiloe.s: Chiloé is an island, the largest of an archipelago of the same name, off the coast of southern Chile. Settled by the Spanish in 1567, it remained a royalist stronghold after mainland Chile became independent and was annexed to Chile only in January 1826.

chincha-islands-war.s: The Chincha Islands War was a conflict between Spain and its former colonies Peru and Chile, later joined by Ecuador and Bolivia, from 1864 to 1866. It began when a Spanish squadron seized Peru's guano-rich Chincha Islands.

chuquicamata.s: Chuquicamata is a copper mine near Calama in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile, long the largest open-pit mine in the world by excavated volume. Developed by American companies from 1915, it was owned by the Anaconda Copper company until Chile nationalised copper in 1971.

codelco.s: Codelco, the National Copper Corporation of Chile, is the state-owned company created in 1976 to manage the large copper mines nationalised in 1971, including Chuquicamata and El Teniente. It is the world's largest copper producer.

concertacion.s: The Concertación was a coalition of Chilean centre-left parties, including the Christian Democrats and the Socialists, formed to oppose Augusto Pinochet in the plebiscite of 1988. It won every presidential election from 1989 to 2005, governing under Patricio Aylwin, Eduardo…

corfo.s: CORFO, the Production Development Corporation, is a Chilean state agency founded in 1939 by the Popular Front government of Pedro Aguirre Cerda, after the Chillán earthquake. It financed and created key national enterprises in electricity, oil, steel and sugar, becoming the…

cairo-conference.s: The Cairo Conference was a meeting held in Cairo in November 1943 between Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Chiang Kai-shek to plan the war against Japan.

chen-shui-bian.s: Chen Shui-bian is a Taiwanese lawyer and politician of the Democratic Progressive Party who served as mayor of Taipei and as president of the Republic of China from 2000 to 2008. His election ended more than half a century of Kuomintang rule and marked the first peaceful…

chiang-ching-kuo.s: Chiang Ching-kuo, the son of Chiang Kai-shek, was premier of the Republic of China from 1972 and president from 1978 until his death in 1988. He promoted the Ten Major Construction Projects and brought more native Taiwanese into government.

carlos-arroyo-del-rio.s: Carlos Arroyo del Río was a Liberal lawyer from Guayaquil who served as president of Ecuador from 1940 to 1944. His government suffered defeat in the war with Peru in 1941 and signed the Rio de Janeiro Protocol in 1942, which gave most of the disputed Amazon to Peru.

cenepa-war.s: The Cenepa War was a short conflict between Ecuador and Peru fought in January and February 1995 over outposts in the upper Cenepa valley, in an undemarcated stretch of the Cordillera del Cóndor. Ecuadorian forces held most of their positions, and a ceasefire was agreed under…

central-bank-of-ecuador.s: The Central Bank of Ecuador was founded in 1927 on the advice of the American economist Edwin Kemmerer, after the Julian Revolution of 1925 had ended the dominance of the private banks of Guayaquil over money and credit. It issued the sucre until the currency crisis of…

charles-darwin.s: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection transformed biology. As naturalist on the survey voyage of HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, he visited the Galápagos Islands in 1835, where the variation of finches, mockingbirds and tortoises…

conaie.n: Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador
conaie.s: The Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE) is the main organisation of Ecuador's indigenous peoples, founded in 1986. Its uprising of June 1990 put indigenous land and cultural rights on the national agenda, and its protests helped bring down Presidents…

costa-ecuador.s: The Costa is Ecuador's Pacific coastal lowland, lying between the ocean and the Andes and centred on the port of Guayaquil. Its plantations of cacao, then bananas and shrimp farms produced most of the country's exports, and its merchant and banking elite supported the Liberal…

carlos-humberto-romero.s: Carlos Humberto Romero was a Salvadoran army general who became president in 1977 after an election widely denounced as fraudulent. His government met rising protest and guerrilla activity with harsh repression, including the killing of demonstrators and priests.

carlos-melendez.s: Carlos Meléndez was a Salvadoran businessman and politician who became president after the assassination of Manuel Enrique Araujo in 1913 and was elected for the term 1915–1919, stepping down shortly before its end because of illness. He founded the political dominance of his…

central-american-university.s: The José Simeón Cañas Central American University is a Jesuit university in San Salvador founded in 1965. Under its rector Ignacio Ellacuría it became a leading voice for human rights and a negotiated end to the civil war.

chapultepec-peace-accords.s: The Chapultepec Peace Accords were signed in Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City on 16 January 1992 by the government of El Salvador and the FMLN, after negotiations under United Nations mediation. They ended the twelve-year Salvadoran civil war, reduced and reformed the army,…

commission-on-the-truth-for-el-salvador.n: Commission on the Truth for El Salvador
commission-on-the-truth-for-el-salvador.s: The Commission on the Truth for El Salvador was a United Nations body created under the peace accords of 1992 to investigate serious acts of violence during the civil war. Its report of March 1993, From Madness to Hope, attributed the great majority of the cases it examined to…

cooperative-cyber-defence-centre-of-exce.n: Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence
cooperative-cyber-defence-centre-of-exce.s: The NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence is a research and training centre on cyber defence in Tallinn, Estonia. Proposed by Estonia and established in 2008, the year after large cyberattacks on Estonian government and banking websites, it supports NATO members…

council-of-the-european-union.s: The Council of the European Union is the institution in which government ministers of the member states meet to adopt EU laws, usually jointly with the European Parliament, and to coordinate policy. Its presidency rotates among the member states every six months, and the…

centre-party-finland.s: The Centre Party is a Finnish political party founded in 1906 as the Agrarian League to represent small farmers and rural areas. It became one of Finland's three main parties and led many governments; its most prominent figure, Urho Kekkonen, was prime minister several times…

coluccio-salutati.s: Coluccio Salutati (1331–1406) was an Italian humanist and chancellor of the Republic of Florence from 1375 until his death. His public letters defended Florentine liberty against the papacy and the Visconti of Milan, and he invited the Byzantine scholar Manuel Chrysoloras to…

council-of-florence.s: The Council of Florence was an ecumenical council of the Catholic Church that met at Ferrara from 1438 and in Florence from 1439, continuing the Council of Basel. Attended by the Byzantine emperor John VIII Palaiologos and the Patriarch of Constantinople, it proclaimed the…

caffaro-di-rustico-da-caschifellone.s: Caffaro di Rustico da Caschifellone (c. 1080–1166) was a Genoese nobleman, consul, diplomat and naval commander who wrote the first official chronicle of the commune of Genoa.

canary-islands.s: The Canary Islands are an archipelago of volcanic islands in the Atlantic Ocean off the north-west coast of Africa, today an autonomous community of Spain. Inhabited by the indigenous Guanches, they were reached by the Genoese Lanzarotto Malocello in the early fourteenth…

carloforte.s: Carloforte is a town on the island of San Pietro off the south-west coast of Sardinia. It was founded in 1738 by Ligurian families who had lived for two centuries on the Tunisian island of Tabarka, and was named after King Charles Emmanuel III of Sardinia.

carlos-castillo-armas.s: Carlos Castillo Armas (1914–1957) was a Guatemalan army officer who led the small rebel force, organised and armed by the CIA, that invaded from Honduras in June 1954 and brought down the elected government of Jacobo Árbenz. As president from 1954 he reversed the land reform,…

commission-for-historical-clarification.s: The Commission for Historical Clarification was the truth commission created under the Guatemalan peace accords to investigate human rights violations during the civil war of 1960–1996. Its report, Guatemala: Memory of Silence, presented in 1999, estimated that more than…

charles-riviere-herard.s: Charles Rivière-Hérard (1789–1850) was a Haitian army officer who led the Reform movement that overthrew President Jean-Pierre Boyer in 1843. As president from 1843 he faced the Dominican declaration of independence of February 1844 and failed to reconquer the east; peasant…

congress-of-panama.s: The Congress of Panama was a meeting of Spanish American republics called by Simón Bolívar and held in Panama City in June and July 1826 to form a league of the new states. Gran Colombia, Mexico, Peru and the Federal Republic of Central America attended, while the United…

cabbages-and-kings.s: Cabbages and Kings is a book of linked stories by the American writer O. Henry, published in 1904.

contras.s: The Contras were right-wing rebel groups that fought the Sandinista government of Nicaragua in the 1980s. Formed largely around former members of Anastasio Somoza's National Guard, they were armed, trained and funded by the United States and operated from camps in Honduras.

cuyamel-fruit-company.s: The Cuyamel Fruit Company was an American banana company founded by Samuel Zemurray in 1911, with plantations in the lower valleys of north-western Honduras near the Guatemalan border. It competed fiercely with the United Fruit Company for land, railway concessions and…

chandrayaan-3.s: Chandrayaan-3 was a lunar mission of the Indian Space Research Organisation launched in July 2023. On 23 August 2023 its lander Vikram touched down near the Moon's south pole, the first landing in that region, making India the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon.

christmas-battles.s: The Christmas Battles were a Russian offensive against German positions near Riga in late December 1916 and January 1917, in which Latvian Riflemen units broke through the German lines in heavy winter fighting. The breakthrough was not exploited by the Russian command, and the…

courland.s: Courland is a historical region of western Latvia, lying between the Gulf of Riga and the Baltic Sea and including Liepāja and Ventspils. Conquered by the Livonian Order in the thirteenth century, it became the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia under Polish-Lithuanian…

casita-volcano.s: Casita is a volcano in north-western Nicaragua, part of the San Cristóbal volcanic complex near Chinandega. On 30 October 1998, during the torrential rains of Hurricane Mitch, part of its flank collapsed and the resulting mudflow buried the villages of El Porvenir and Rolando…

corinto.s: Corinto is a port city on the Pacific coast of north-western Nicaragua, on Aserradores Island in the department of Chinandega. Developed in the nineteenth century as the country's main Pacific port, it was linked by railway to León and Managua from the 1880s.

cornelius-vanderbilt.s: Cornelius Vanderbilt was an American shipping and railway magnate, one of the richest men of the nineteenth century. During the California Gold Rush his Accessory Transit Company carried travellers between the Atlantic and Pacific across Nicaragua from 1851, and in 1856–1857…

chiriqui-province.s: Chiriquí is a province in western Panama on the Pacific coast, bordering Costa Rica, with its capital at David. It contains the Barú volcano, the country's highest peak, and fertile highlands producing coffee and vegetables, while its lowlands became a centre of banana growing…

civic-crusade.s: The Civic Crusade (Cruzada Civilista Nacional) was a Panamanian opposition movement formed in June 1987 by business, professional and church groups against the military regime of Manuel Noriega. It arose after the former chief of staff Roberto Díaz Herrera accused Noriega of…

colon-panama.s: Colón is a port city at the Caribbean entrance of the Panama Canal and Panama's second city. Founded in 1850 as the Atlantic terminus of the Panama Railroad and first called Aspinwall by the Americans, it grew with the railway and canal and was rebuilt after a great fire in 1885.

coto-war.s: The Coto War was a brief border conflict between Panama and Costa Rica in February and March 1921 over the Coto region on the Pacific side of their disputed frontier. Panamanian forces at first drove back a Costa Rican occupation, but the United States intervened and pressed…

cesar-vallejo.s: César Vallejo was a Peruvian poet, regarded as one of the great innovators of twentieth-century poetry in any language. Born in Santiago de Chuco in the northern Andes, he published Los heraldos negros in 1918 and the radically experimental Trilce in 1922, then lived in Paris…

chincha-islands.s: The Chincha Islands are a group of three small islands off the southern coast of Peru, near Pisco, whose vast deposits of seabird guano made them Peru's chief source of wealth from the 1840s. Guano dug there, largely by Chinese indentured labourers, was exported to Europe and…

civilista-party.s: The Civilista Party was a Peruvian political party founded in 1871 by Manuel Pardo, the country's first organised civilian party, representing merchants, financiers and coastal landowners opposed to military rule. Pardo became its first president in 1872, and the party…

colombia-peru-war.s: The Colombia–Peru War was fought between September 1932 and May 1933 after Peruvian civilians and soldiers seized the Amazon river port of Leticia, which Peru had ceded to Colombia under the Salomón–Lozano Treaty. Fighting along the Putumayo and Amazon rivers ended after the…

cavtat.s: Cavtat is a small town on the Adriatic coast of southern Croatia, south-east of Dubrovnik, on the site of the Greek and Roman town of Epidaurum. According to tradition, refugees from Epidaurum founded Ragusa (Dubrovnik) after the town was destroyed by Avars and Slavs in the…

consilium-rogatorum.s: The Consilium Rogatorum, or Senate, was the chief governing council of the Republic of Ragusa, composed of noblemen elected by the Great Council. Established in the thirteenth century, it directed foreign policy, finance and trade, including the republic's delicate relations…

chris-hani.s: Chris Hani was a South African anti-apartheid leader, chief of staff of Umkhonto we Sizwe and from 1991 general secretary of the South African Communist Party. Highly popular among young black South Africans, he was assassinated outside his home in Boksburg on 10 April 1993 by…

ciskei.s: Ciskei was a Bantustan, or homeland, created by the apartheid government for Xhosa-speaking people in what is now the Eastern Cape of South Africa. Declared independent in 1981, it was recognised by no country except South Africa.

convention-for-a-democratic-south-africa.n: Convention for a Democratic South Africa
convention-for-a-democratic-south-africa.s: The Convention for a Democratic South Africa (CODESA) was the multi-party negotiation on ending apartheid that opened near Johannesburg in December 1991. It brought together the government, the ANC and many other parties, but its second plenary broke down in May 1992 over…

cyril-ramaphosa.s: Cyril Ramaphosa is a South African politician who has been president of South Africa since 2018. A trade unionist who founded the National Union of Mineworkers, he led the ANC's team in the negotiations that ended apartheid, then became a wealthy businessman.

comprehensive-anti-apartheid-act.s: The Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act was a United States law of 1986 that imposed sanctions on South Africa, banning new investment, bank loans and imports of goods such as coal, steel and uranium, and ending direct air links. Congress passed it over the veto of President…

chioggia.s: Chioggia is a town on an island at the southern end of the Venetian lagoon in north-eastern Italy, long a centre of fishing and salt production and one of the oldest lagoon communities. In the War of Chioggia (1378–1381) a Genoese fleet captured it, threatening Venice itself,…

claudio-monteverdi.s: Claudio Monteverdi was an Italian composer whose work bridged Renaissance and Baroque music. After serving the Gonzaga court at Mantua, where he wrote L'Orfeo (1607), one of the first great operas, he became director of music at St Mark's Basilica in Venice in 1613.

collegio-venice.s: The Collegio, or Full College (Pien Collegio), was the steering committee of the government of the Republic of Venice. It brought together the doge, his six councillors, the heads of the criminal court and the boards of savi (sages) responsible for policy, war and the mainland.

canute-guild.s: The Canute Guild was a guild of craftsmen in Reval (Tallinn), named after the Danish saint Canute and dominated by German master artisans. With the Olaf Guild it represented the town's craftsmen, below the Great Guild of merchants that controlled the town council.

church-of-the-holy-spirit-tallinn.n: Church of the Holy Spirit, Tallinn
church-of-the-holy-spirit-tallinn.s: The Church of the Holy Spirit is a medieval Gothic church in the old town of Tallinn (Reval), built in the 14th century as the chapel of the town hall and the almshouse. Its carved and painted high altar of 1483 is by Bernt Notke, and its outer clock is the oldest public clock…

chares-of-lindos.s: Chares of Lindos was a Greek sculptor from Rhodes, a pupil of Lysippus. He designed and built the Colossus of Rhodes, the bronze statue of the sun god Helios, about 33 metres high, which took some twelve years to complete and stood at the harbour of Rhodes from about 280 BCE…

colossus-of-rhodes.s: The Colossus of Rhodes was a bronze statue of the sun god Helios, about 33 metres high, made by Chares of Lindos to celebrate the city's survival of the siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305–304 BCE. Completed around 280 BCE, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

chedworth-roman-villa.s: Chedworth Roman Villa is the site of one of the largest Roman villas in Britain, near Cirencester in Gloucestershire, England, discovered in 1864. Reaching its greatest extent in the fourth century, it had dining rooms with fine mosaics, two bath suites and a water shrine.

clodius-albinus.s: Clodius Albinus was governor of Britain who claimed the Roman throne in the civil wars after 193. Septimius Severus first recognised him as Caesar, but in 196 Albinus declared himself emperor and crossed to Gaul with the British army.

colchester.s: Colchester is a town in Essex, England, on the site of Camulodunum, the chief centre of the Catuvellauni before the Roman conquest. Claudius entered it in 43 CE, and it became the first Roman colonia in Britain, settled by veterans, with a temple to the deified Claudius.

council-of-arles.s: The Council of Arles was a church council summoned by Constantine the Great to Arles in southern Gaul in 314 to settle the Donatist dispute in North Africa. It ruled against the Donatists and issued canons on church discipline.

classis-alexandrina.s: The Classis Alexandrina was the Roman fleet based at Alexandria, created under Augustus after the annexation of Egypt in 30 BCE. It protected the grain ships sailing to Rome, patrolled the eastern Mediterranean and the Nile, and supported the army in Egypt.

catechetical-school-of-alexandria.s: The Catechetical School of Alexandria was a centre of Christian teaching in Alexandria from the late second century. Under Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria and Origen it combined instruction in the faith with Greek philosophy and the allegorical reading of scripture.

clement-of-alexandria.s: Clement of Alexandria was a Christian theologian who taught in Alexandria in the late second century. In works such as the Exhortation to the Greeks and the Stromata he argued that Greek philosophy had prepared the way for Christianity.

caesarion.s: Caesarion, formally Ptolemy XV, was the son of Cleopatra VII and, by her account, of Julius Caesar. Born in 47 BCE, he reigned as co-ruler of Egypt with his mother from 44 BCE.

commonwealth-of-independent-states.s: The Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) is a regional organisation of former Soviet republics, founded by Russia, Ukraine and Belarus in the Belovezha Accords of 8 December 1991 and joined by most other republics at Alma-Ata later that month. It replaced the Soviet Union…

communist-party-of-the-rsfsr.s: The Communist Party of the RSFSR was the branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union for the Russian republic, founded in 1990, until then the only Soviet republic without a party organisation of its own. Led by Ivan Polozkov, it took a conservative line against…

congress-of-peoples-deputies-of-russia.n: Congress of People's Deputies of Russia
congress-of-peoples-deputies-of-russia.s: The Congress of People's Deputies of Russia was the highest legislative body of the Russian SFSR and then the Russian Federation from 1990 to 1993. Elected in March 1990 in the republic's first competitive elections, it chose Boris Yeltsin as chairman of its Supreme Soviet and…

congress-of-peoples-deputies-of-the-sovi.n: Congress of People's Deputies of the Soviet Union
congress-of-peoples-deputies-of-the-sovi.s: The Congress of People's Deputies of the Soviet Union was the highest body of state power in the USSR from 1989 to 1991, created by Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms. Its elections in March 1989 were the first partly competitive national elections in Soviet history, and its…

constructivism-art.s: Constructivism was an avant-garde movement in art and architecture that took shape in Russia after the 1917 revolution, building on the work of Vladimir Tatlin. Its artists, among them Alexander Rodchenko and El Lissitzky, rejected art for its own sake in favour of art serving…

council-of-peoples-commissars.s: The Council of People's Commissars, or Sovnarkom, was the government of Soviet Russia, formed by the Second Congress of Soviets during the October Revolution of 1917 with Lenin as chairman. Its members, the people's commissars, headed the government departments.

czechoslovak-legion.s: The Czechoslovak Legion was a force of Czech and Slovak volunteers, many of them former prisoners of war, who fought for the Allies in the First World War, above all in Russia. In May 1918, while travelling east along the Trans-Siberian Railway to reach France, its troops…

cheka.s: The Cheka, the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission, was the first Soviet secret police, founded in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky to fight counter-revolution and sabotage. During the Russian Civil War it carried out the Red Terror, with mass arrests, hostage-taking and…

chuzan-seikan.s: The Chūzan Seikan (Reflections on Chūzan) is the first official history of the Ryukyu Kingdom, written in Japanese by Haneji Chōshū and completed in 1650. Composed after the Satsuma invasion of 1609, it traced the royal line back to legendary rulers and presented the kingdom's…

celenderis.s: Celenderis was an ancient port city on the coast of Rough Cilicia in southern Anatolia, at modern Aydıncık in Mersin Province, Turkey. Greek tradition credited colonists from Samos with its foundation, and it later belonged to the Persian, Hellenistic and Roman worlds as a…

colaeus.s: Colaeus was a Samian merchant whose voyage is told by Herodotus. Around 638 BCE, bound for Egypt, his ship was driven west by storms through the Strait of Gibraltar to Tartessos in southern Spain, then an untouched market, and he returned with an enormous profit.

chutu-dynasty.s: The Chutu dynasty ruled parts of the western Deccan around Banavasi in present-day Karnataka in the second and third centuries CE, probably first as feudatories and then as successors of the Satavahanas. Known from coins and a few inscriptions, its kings used the name Satakarni.

capitulatio-de-partibus-saxoniae.s: The Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae was a law issued by Charlemagne for conquered Saxony, usually dated to around 782–785. It prescribed death for refusing baptism, cremating the dead, eating meat in Lent and other pagan practices or attacks on the church, and required tithes…

church-of-the-forty-martyrs.s: The Church of the Forty Martyrs is a medieval church in Veliko Tarnovo, Bulgaria, built by Tsar Ivan Asen II to commemorate his victory at Klokotnitsa in 1230. Its columns bear inscriptions including Ivan Asen II's account of his conquests and an earlier column of Khan Omurtag.

constantine-tikh.s: Constantine Tikh was tsar of Bulgaria from 1257 to 1277, chosen by the boyars after the murder of Michael II Asen. A noble of mixed Bulgarian and Serbian descent, he married a granddaughter of Ivan Asen II and later a Byzantine princess to strengthen his claim.

cheomseongdae.s: Cheomseongdae is a stone tower at Gyeongju, South Korea, the capital of Silla, traditionally dated to the reign of Queen Seondeok in the seventh century. About nine metres tall, it has a bottle-shaped body of granite courses with a square window halfway up.

cheonghaejin.s: Cheonghaejin was a maritime garrison founded in 828 by Jang Bogo, with royal permission, on Wando island off the south-western tip of Korea. From it Jang Bogo suppressed piracy and controlled trade between Silla, Tang China and Japan.

cheonmachong.s: Cheonmachong, the 'Heavenly Horse Tomb', is a Silla royal burial mound of the late fifth or early sixth century at Gyeongju, South Korea. Excavated in 1973, it held a gold crown and many other treasures.

choe-chiwon.s: Choe Chiwon was a scholar and poet of late Silla. Sent to Tang China as a boy, he passed the Tang civil service examination and served there, writing a famous proclamation against the rebel Huang Chao.

cam-ranh-bay.s: Cam Ranh Bay is a deep natural harbour in Khánh Hòa province on the south-central coast of Vietnam. The Russian Baltic Fleet anchored there in 1905 on its way to Tsushima, the United States built a large base there during the Vietnam War, and from 1979 to 2002 it was the main…

communist-party-of-vietnam.s: The Communist Party of Vietnam is the ruling and only legal party of Vietnam. Founded by Ho Chi Minh in 1930 and soon renamed the Indochinese Communist Party, it led the Viet Minh against France and ruled North Vietnam as the Workers' Party from 1951.

corrective-move.s: The Corrective Move was the seizure of power on 22 June 1969 by the left wing of South Yemen's ruling National Liberation Front, which removed President Qahtan al-Shaabi. Power passed to a collective leadership including Salim Rubaya Ali and Abdul Fattah Ismail, which renamed…

cuban-missile-crisis.s: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear war. After American reconnaissance flights found Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba, President Kennedy imposed a naval quarantine of the island.

congress-of-soviets-of-the-soviet-union.n: Congress of Soviets of the Soviet Union
congress-of-soviets-of-the-soviet-union.s: The Congress of Soviets of the Soviet Union was the supreme organ of state power in the USSR from 1922 to 1936, made up of delegates from the soviets of the union republics. Its first session, on 30 December 1922, approved the treaty and declaration creating the Soviet Union.

classical-greece.s: Classical Greece is the period of ancient Greek history from the Persian Wars of the early fifth century BCE to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE. It saw the rivalry of Athens and Sparta, Athenian democracy and the Peloponnesian War, and the rise of Macedon, together…

cleombrotus-i.s: Cleombrotus I was an Agiad king of Sparta from 380 to 371 BCE. He led several Spartan expeditions against Thebes in the 370s, and in 371 BCE commanded the army that was defeated at the Battle of Leuctra by the Boeotians under Epaminondas.

constitution-of-the-lacedaemonians.s: The Constitution of the Lacedaemonians is a short treatise on the Spartan state and way of life written by the Athenian historian Xenophon, who lived for years under Spartan protection. It describes the upbringing of boys, the common messes, the army and the privileges of the…

chudamani-vihara.s: The Chudamani Vihara was a Buddhist monastery at Nagapattinam on the Coromandel coast of south India, built in the early eleventh century by the Srivijayan king Sri Mara Vijayottungavarman. The Chola king Rajaraja I granted it the revenue of a village, as recorded in the…

chu-silk-manuscript.s: The Chu Silk Manuscript is a silk sheet with text and painted figures from a Warring States tomb at Zidanku in Changsha, Hunan, looted in 1942 and now held by the Smithsonian's Arthur M. Sackler Gallery in Washington.

chu-ci.s: The Chu Ci (Songs of Chu) is an anthology of Chinese poetry compiled in the Han dynasty, in its received form by Wang Yi in the second century CE. It contains the Li Sao and other poems attributed to Qu Yuan of the State of Chu, the shamanistic Nine Songs, and later works in…

covenant-of-kuiqiu.s: The Covenant of Kuiqiu was an assembly of Chinese feudal lords convened by Duke Huan of Qi in 651 BCE at Kuiqiu, in present-day Henan. King Xiang of Zhou sent his representative with sacrificial meat to honour Duke Huan, confirming his position as hegemon, or ba.

covenant-of-shaoling.s: The Covenant of Shaoling was the agreement of 656 BCE that ended Duke Huan of Qi's campaign against the State of Chu. Leading a coalition of northern lords, Duke Huan marched south after overrunning Cai; the Chu envoy Qu Wan negotiated, and the two sides swore a covenant at…

chen-wan.s: Chen Wan, also called Tian Wan, was a prince of the State of Chen who fled to Qi in 672 BCE after a succession dispute at home. Duke Huan of Qi received him and gave him an office in charge of crafts.

chelmno.s: Chełmno, German Kulm, is a town on the Vistula in the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship of northern Poland. Granted a charter by the Teutonic Order in 1233, it gave its name to the Chełmno law used by hundreds of towns in Prussia and Poland, was a member of the Hanseatic League,…

chelmno-law.s: Chełmno law, German Kulm law, was the town law granted by the Teutonic Order in its charter of 1233 for the towns of Chełmno and Toruń. Based on Magdeburg law, it gave towns self-government and settlers secure property on favourable terms.

chronicon-terrae-prussiae.s: The Chronicon terrae Prussiae, or Chronicle of the Prussian Land, is a Latin history of the Teutonic Order completed in 1326 by Peter of Dusburg, a priest of the Order. It tells of the Order's origins and its conquest of the pagan Prussians and wars with Lithuania up to 1326.

cape-delgado.s: Cape Delgado is a headland on the coast of northern Mozambique, close to the border with Tanzania. In the nineteenth century it marked the southern limit of the East African coast claimed by the sultans of Zanzibar, and it later formed the boundary between German East Africa…

carpenter-agreement.s: The Carpenter Agreement was signed on 22 March 1915 between Frank W. Carpenter, American governor of the Department of Mindanao and Sulu, and Sultan Jamalul Kiram II of Sulu.

ciliwung-river.s: The Ciliwung is a river in western Java, Indonesia, flowing north from the highlands near Bogor through Jakarta to the Java Sea. Sunda Kalapa, the chief port of the Sunda Kingdom, lay at its mouth and served the capital Pakuan Pajajaran upriver.

cimanuk-river.s: The Cimanuk is a river in West Java, Indonesia, flowing north from the Garut highlands to the Java Sea near Indramayu. In the early sixteenth century the Portuguese writer Tomé Pires described it as the eastern boundary of the Sunda Kingdom, and its mouth was one of the…

candide.s: Candide is a satirical novella by Voltaire, published in 1759, in which a naive young man travels the world and meets war, disaster and cruelty while his tutor Pangloss insists that all is for the best. A mockery of philosophical optimism, it is one of the most famous works of…

commewijne-river.s: The Commewijne is a river in north-eastern Suriname that flows into the Suriname River opposite Paramaribo, at the site of Fort Nieuw-Amsterdam. In the colonial period its banks and those of its tributary, the Cottica, were lined with sugar, coffee and cacao plantations worked…

cornelis-van-aerssen-van-sommelsdijck.s: Cornelis van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck was a Dutch nobleman who held a one-third share in the Society of Suriname, formed in 1683 with the Dutch West India Company and the city of Amsterdam, and served as the colony's governor from 1683. He made peace with the Kalina and Lokono…

cottica-river.s: The Cottica is a river in eastern Suriname and a tributary of the Commewijne. In the eighteenth century its banks were lined with plantations, and the swamps and forests nearby sheltered maroon communities, including those of Boni.

charles-denis-bourbaki.s: Charles-Denis Bourbaki was a French general of Greek descent who commanded the Imperial Guard in 1870 and then the Army of the East in the Franco-Prussian War. After failing to relieve Belfort, his defeated army of about 87,000 men crossed into Switzerland in February 1871,…

cabaret-voltaire.s: The Cabaret Voltaire was a nightclub in the Spiegelgasse in Zurich, opened in February 1916 by the German writer Hugo Ball and the performer Emmy Hennings. Its evenings of sound poetry, masks, music and provocation, with artists such as Tristan Tzara, Hans Arp and Marcel…

carl-gustav-jung.s: Carl Gustav Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist and the founder of analytical psychology. An early collaborator of Sigmund Freud, he broke with him in 1913 and developed his own ideas of the collective unconscious, archetypes and the introverted and extraverted personality types.

cern.s: CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, is an intergovernmental particle physics laboratory founded in 1954 on the Franco-Swiss border near Geneva. It operates the world's largest particle accelerators, including the Large Hadron Collider, with which the Higgs…

credit-suisse.s: Credit Suisse was a Swiss bank founded in Zurich in 1856 by Alfred Escher, originally to finance railway building, and for long one of the country's two largest banks. After a series of losses and scandals, a loss of confidence in March 2023 led the Swiss authorities to…

chama-cha-mapinduzi.s: Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), the Party of the Revolution, is the ruling party of Tanzania, formed on 5 February 1977 by the merger of the mainland's Tanganyika African National Union and Zanzibar's Afro-Shirazi Party. It was the sole legal party until 1992 and has won every…

chadema.s: Chadema, the Party for Democracy and Progress, is the main opposition party of mainland Tanzania, founded in 1992 when multi-party politics was restored. It draws much of its support from towns and from the north of the country, and its leaders have faced arrests and attacks.

civic-united-front.s: The Civic United Front is a Tanzanian political party founded in 1992, strongest in Zanzibar and above all on Pemba. Its long rivalry with Chama Cha Mapinduzi produced disputed elections on the islands in 1995, 2000 and 2005 and the killing of opposition protesters in January…

chak-tok-ichaak-i.s: Chak Tok Ich'aak I was a king of the Maya city of Tikal in the fourth century CE. Inscriptions record that he died on the same day in January 378 that Siyaj K'ak', a warrior linked to Teotihuacan, arrived at Tikal, an event widely interpreted as a Teotihuacan-backed…

ciudadela-teotihuacan.s: The Ciudadela is a vast square enclosure at Teotihuacan, on the east side of the Avenue of the Dead, surrounded by platforms topped with temples and enclosing a great plaza. Built in the early third century CE, it contains the Feathered Serpent Pyramid and residential…

coyotlatelco.s: Coyotlatelco is a style of red-on-buff pottery, and by extension the archaeological culture associated with it, found in the Basin of Mexico in the centuries after the decline of Teotihuacan, roughly 600 to 900 CE. Its appearance among the ruins of Teotihuacan and in new…

chongye.s: Chongye is a valley and county in the Lhoka (Shannan) region of southern Tibet, south of the Yarlung Tsangpo. It contains the burial mounds of the Yarlung dynasty, the emperors of imperial Tibet, including the tomb traditionally attributed to Songtsen Gampo.

cossack-hetmanate.s: The Cossack Hetmanate was the state of the Zaporozhian Cossacks in central Ukraine, founded during Bohdan Khmelnytsky's uprising against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1648. By the Pereiaslav agreement of 1654 it came under the protection of the Russian tsar, and after…

chavand.s: Chavand is a village in the Udaipur district of Rajasthan that served as the capital of Maharana Pratap of Mewar in the last years of his struggle against the Mughals, from about 1585. Pratap built a palace and temple there and died at Chavand in 1597, and his cenotaph stands…

chittor-fort.s: Chittor Fort, or Chittorgarh, is a hill fort above the Berach River in southern Rajasthan and one of the largest forts in India. It was the chief seat of the Guhila and Sisodia rulers of Mewar until 1568 and fell three times, to Alauddin Khalji in 1303, Bahadur Shah of Gujarat…

clements-kadalie.s: Clements Kadalie was a trade unionist from Nyasaland, now Malawi, who founded the Industrial and Commercial Workers' Union in Cape Town in 1919. Under his leadership the ICU became the first mass movement of black workers in South Africa in the 1920s, before it split and…

cop28.s: COP28, the 2023 United Nations Climate Change Conference, was held at Expo City Dubai in the United Arab Emirates from 30 November to 13 December 2023 under the presidency of Sultan Al Jaber, head of the national oil company. Its final agreement, the UAE Consensus, called for…

clement-attlee.s: Clement Attlee was a British Labour politician and prime minister of the United Kingdom from 1945 to 1951. Deputy prime minister in Churchill's wartime coalition, he led Labour to a landslide victory in 1945; his government nationalised major industries, created the National…

clydeside.s: Clydeside is the conurbation along the River Clyde in west-central Scotland, centred on Glasgow. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it was one of the world's leading centres of shipbuilding and heavy engineering, and its radical labour movement earned it the name…

cardwell-reforms.s: The Cardwell reforms were a series of changes to the British Army made by Edward Cardwell, secretary of state for war in Gladstone's first government, between 1868 and 1874. They abolished the purchase of officers' commissions and flogging in peacetime, introduced shorter…

charles-dickens.s: Charles Dickens was the most popular English novelist of the Victorian era. Works such as Oliver Twist, A Christmas Carol, David Copperfield, Bleak House and Great Expectations, many first published in monthly instalments, combined comedy and memorable characters with sharp…

charles-stewart-parnell.s: Charles Stewart Parnell was an Irish nationalist politician who led the Irish Parliamentary Party from 1880. A Protestant landowner, he combined parliamentary obstruction with the agitation of the Land League and persuaded Gladstone to adopt Home Rule in 1886, but his career…

conservative-party-uk.s: The Conservative Party is a centre-right political party in the United Kingdom that developed from the Tory party in the 1830s under Robert Peel. It split in 1846 over the repeal of the Corn Laws, revived under Disraeli, and was the dominant party of government in the…

corn-laws.s: The Corn Laws were tariffs and other restrictions on imported grain in the United Kingdom, in force from 1815 to 1846, which kept bread prices high to protect the incomes of landowners. Campaigning by the Anti-Corn Law League and the Irish famine led Robert Peel to repeal them…

cherethites-and-pelethites.s: The Cherethites and Pelethites were the royal bodyguard of King David according to the Hebrew Bible, commanded by Benaiah son of Jehoiada. Their names are usually taken to mean Cretans and Philistines, suggesting a force of foreign mercenaries of Aegean origin loyal to the…

constitution-of-india.s: The Constitution of India is the supreme law of the Republic of India, adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950, a date celebrated as Republic Day. Drafted by a committee chaired by B.

civil-rights-act-of-1964.s: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 is a landmark law of the United States, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson in July 1964, that outlawed discrimination on the basis of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.

constitutional-convention-united-states.s: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia from May to September 1787 to revise the Articles of Confederation, but instead drafted a new Constitution of the United States. Presided over by George Washington, with James Madison as its leading architect, its delegates…

cabimas.s: Cabimas is a city in the state of Zulia in western Venezuela, on the eastern shore of Lake Maracaibo. It grew from a small village after the blowout of the Barroso II well in 1922 revealed the vast oil reserves of the Lake Maracaibo basin, and it remains one of the main…

caracazo.s: The Caracazo was a wave of protests, rioting and looting that began on 27 February 1989 in Guarenas and Caracas, Venezuela, after President Carlos Andrés Pérez's austerity programme raised fuel prices and public transport fares. The army suppressed it with great force, killing…

carlos-andres-perez.s: Carlos Andrés Pérez was a Venezuelan politician of Democratic Action who was president of Venezuela from 1974 to 1979 and from 1989 to 1993. His first term, during the oil boom, saw the nationalisation of the iron and oil industries; his second brought an austerity programme,…

cipriano-castro.s: Cipriano Castro was a Venezuelan military leader from the Andean state of Táchira who seized power in 1899 and ruled as president until 1908. His refusal to pay foreign debts led Britain, Germany and Italy to blockade Venezuelan ports in 1902–1903; while he was abroad for…

cerro-rico.s: Cerro Rico ('rich hill') is a mountain above the city of Potosí in present-day Bolivia whose silver deposits were discovered by the Spanish in 1545. Worked by indigenous labourers under the mita system, it became the largest single source of silver in the world in the late…

cusco-school.s: The Cusco School was a tradition of Catholic religious painting centred on Cusco in the Viceroyalty of Peru from the late sixteenth to the eighteenth century. Its largely indigenous and mestizo painters adapted European models, adding Andean plants, animals and dress,…

cathedral-of-saint-demetrius.s: The Cathedral of Saint Demetrius is a white-stone church in Vladimir, Russia, built in 1194–1197 by Grand Prince Vsevolod the Big Nest as his palace church. It is famous for the hundreds of carved reliefs of saints, animals, birds and mythical beasts that cover its upper walls.

chalukya-vikrama-era.s: The Chalukya-Vikrama era was a calendar era introduced by the Western Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI to count years from his accession in 1076. It replaced the Shaka era in many inscriptions of his empire during his reign and for some time afterwards, before falling out of use…

chengzhou.s: Chengzhou, also called Luoyi, was the eastern capital of the Western Zhou dynasty, built near present-day Luoyang in Henan under the direction of the Duke of Zhou after the suppression of the Rebellion of the Three Guards. It served as a base for controlling the former Shang…

cai-yong.s: Cai Yong was a scholar, calligrapher, musician and official of the Eastern Han dynasty. He supervised the engraving of the Xiping Stone Classics, the official texts of the Confucian classics cut in stone at Luoyang in 175–183.

colony-of-natal.s: The Colony of Natal was a British colony on the south-east coast of Africa, annexed in 1843 after the Boer republic of Natalia was taken over, with its capital at Pietermaritzburg and its port at Durban. Bordering the Zulu Kingdom on the Thukela River, it developed a sugar…

corfinium.s: Corfinium was the chief town of the Paeligni in the Abruzzo mountains of central Italy, near modern Corfinio. In 91 BCE the Italian allies who revolted against Rome in the Social War made it their capital and renamed it Italia.

cetina.s: The Cetina is a river of Dalmatia in southern Croatia, flowing about 100 kilometres from the Dinaric mountains to the Adriatic at Omiš. In the early Middle Ages it marked the western limit of the Narentine principality of Pagania, and the Poljica district lay between its lower…

christian-august-of-saxe-zeitz.s: Christian August of Saxe-Zeitz was a German prince of the Wettin house who converted to Catholicism and became a churchman in the Habsburg lands. He was made Archbishop of Esztergom, primate of Hungary, in 1707 and a cardinal, and in 1712 he crowned Charles VI king of Hungary.

christian-knorr-von-rosenroth.s: Christian Knorr von Rosenroth was a German scholar, poet and Christian Kabbalist who served as chancellor at the court of Christian August of Palatinate-Sulzbach. His Kabbala Denudata (1677–1684) translated parts of the Zohar and other Kabbalistic texts into Latin, making them…

cross-group.s: The Cross Group is a set of three temple-pyramids at Palenque, the Temple of the Cross, the Temple of the Foliated Cross and the Temple of the Sun, dedicated in 692 by King K'inich Kan B'ahlam II. Their carved panels show the king with his father Pakal and record the mythical…

cassius-longinus.s: Cassius Longinus was a Greek rhetorician and Platonist philosopher who taught for many years at Athens, where Porphyry was among his pupils. He later joined the court of Queen Zenobia at Palmyra as her adviser.

chhattisgarh.s: Chhattisgarh is a state of central India, formed in November 2000 from the south-eastern districts of Madhya Pradesh, with its capital at Raipur. It covers the upper Mahanadi basin, historically known as Dakshina Kosala, and the forested Bastar plateau, and has a large Adivasi…

communards.s: The Communards were the supporters and defenders of the Paris Commune, the revolutionary government that ruled Paris from March to May 1871. Thousands of them were killed during the 'Bloody Week' of May 1871, when government troops retook the city, and many more were…

camulogenus.s: Camulogenus was an elderly leader of the Aulerci in Gaul who commanded the Gallic forces around Lutetia during the revolt of Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Facing Caesar's legate Titus Labienus, he burned Lutetia and its bridges and held the marshes along the Seine.

cis-sutlej-states.s: The Cis-Sutlej states were the Sikh and other states of the Malwa region of Punjab between the Sutlej and Yamuna rivers, among them Patiala, Nabha and Jind. To avoid absorption by Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire, they accepted British protection in 1809, and the Treaty of Amritsar…

camilo-henriquez.s: Camilo Henríquez was a Chilean priest, writer and patriot of the independence era. Born in Valdivia and educated in Lima, he edited Aurora de Chile, the country's first newspaper, from 1812, using it to promote independence and republican ideas.

chrysocheir.s: Chrysocheir was the last leader of the Paulicians of Tephrike, a nephew and son-in-law of Karbeas, whom he succeeded in 863. Allied with the Arab emirs of the frontier, he led deep raids into Byzantine Anatolia, reaching Nicaea and Ephesus around 869, and rejected the peace…

cultural-revolution.s: The Cultural Revolution was a political campaign launched by Mao Zedong in China in 1966 to reassert his authority and purge the Communist Party of supposed capitalist and traditional elements. Students organised as Red Guards attacked officials, teachers and 'old' culture,…

cambodian-peoples-party.s: The Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party was the ruling communist party of the People's Republic of Kampuchea, set up after Vietnam overthrew the Khmer Rouge in 1979 and claiming descent from the party founded in 1951. Led by former Khmer Rouge cadres such as Heng Samrin…

committee-for-the-preparation-of-korean-.n: Committee for the Preparation of Korean Independence
committee-for-the-preparation-of-korean-.s: The Committee for the Preparation of Korean Independence was formed in Seoul on 15 August 1945, the day of Japan's surrender, by the moderate leftist Lyuh Woon-hyung. Its local committees took over administration and kept order across Korea, and in September it proclaimed the…

committee-for-the-relief-of-the-black-po.n: Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor
committee-for-the-relief-of-the-black-po.s: The Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor was a charitable body formed in London in 1786 to help destitute Black people in the city, many of them Black Loyalists who had served Britain in the American War of Independence. With government funding and the encouragement of…

connecticut.s: Connecticut is a state in the New England region of the north-eastern United States, named after the Connecticut River. Its lands were home to Algonquian peoples such as the Pequot, Mohegan and Niantic before English colonists founded settlements in the 1630s, and the colonies…

calchas.s: Calchas is a seer of Greek mythology who served the Greek army in the Trojan War, demanding the sacrifice of Iphigenia and explaining the plague sent by Apollo in the Iliad. Later legends said that after the war he wandered with Mopsus and other heroes into southern Anatolia,…

congress-of-tacna.s: The Pact of Tacna was the agreement of May 1837 by which delegates of the North Peruvian Republic, the South Peruvian Republic and Bolivia defined the Peru–Bolivian Confederation. It made Andrés de Santa Cruz Supreme Protector for ten years, with control of foreign affairs and…

cippus-perusinus.s: The Cippus Perusinus is a stone boundary marker inscribed with about 130 words of Etruscan, found near Perugia in 1822. It is one of the longest surviving Etruscan texts and appears to record a legal agreement over land between two families, the Velthina and the Afuna.

cephissus-boeotia.s: The Cephissus is a river of central Greece that rises near Mount Parnassus in Phocis and flows east through Phocis and Boeotia. In antiquity it fed the marshy Lake Copais, which was drained in the late 19th century.

charles-emmanuel-iv-of-sardinia.s: Charles Emmanuel IV was King of Sardinia and Duke of Savoy from 1796 to 1802. In December 1798 French troops occupied Turin and forced him to give up his mainland states, and he withdrew to the island of Sardinia.

cen-yuying.s: Cen Yuying was a Qing dynasty official from Guangxi who rose to prominence suppressing the Panthay Rebellion of the Hui Muslims in Yunnan. As governor of Yunnan he led the campaign that besieged and took Dali in 1872–1873, ending Du Wenxiu's state.

cape-cod-bay.s: Cape Cod Bay is a large bay of the Atlantic Ocean in Massachusetts, enclosed by the hooked peninsula of Cape Cod. The Mayflower anchored at its tip, in Provincetown Harbor, in November 1620, and the Pilgrims then founded their settlement at Plymouth on its western shore in…

caligula.s: Caligula, properly Gaius Caesar, was Roman emperor from 37 to 41 CE, the son of Germanicus and successor of Tiberius. Popular at first, his reign became notorious in the ancient sources for cruelty, extravagance and claims to divine honours.

cape-verdean-creole.s: Cape Verdean Creole, known as Kriolu, is a Portuguese-based creole language spoken in Cape Verde and by its emigrant communities. It arose from contact between Portuguese settlers and enslaved West Africans on the islands from the late 15th century, making it one of the oldest…
